And that appears to a scholar <note>original: "Clerke"; a learned person or student of alchemy</note>,
In the working of the white work <note>original: "white Werke"; the "albedo" stage of the alchemical process where the material is purified to a white state</note>;
Liquors wash and make clean
Both the extremes and the middle <note>original: "Meane"</note>;
God made liquors for man's use,
To cleanse foul things in every house;
Liquor brings, without doubt,
Hidden things out of bodies,
As laundresses witness evidently,
When they make their lye <note>an alkaline solution made from vegetable ashes used for washing</note> from ashes;
Liquor comforts the roots of grass,
And of trees that were dry;
For liquors of nature will restore
Humors <note>the vital fluids or moisture within a living thing</note> that were lost before.
Liquors separate qualities from one another,
Resolving substance into atoms <note>original: "Attomes"; refers to the smallest constituent parts</note> with wonder;
Liquors also bring into one
Many things to be one Stone <note>the Philosopher's Stone</note>.
Liquors help many things to flux <note>to melt or become fluid</note> and to flow,
And now you may learn
How liquor is found in many ways
From things that are on the ground:
Some by cutting, such as turpentine;
Some with pressing, such as cider and wine;
Some with grinding, as oil is obtained;
Some with distilling <note>original: "stilling"</note>, as waters are made;
Some with burning <note>original: "Brenning"</note>, such as colophony <note>a type of resin or rosin</note>;
And some with water, as women make lye;
Some are brought about in other ways,
And set out by natural processes <note>original: "working"</note>,
Such as urine, sweat, milk, and also blood,
And rennet <note>original: "Renniet"</note>, which is good for cheese.
By as many ways, and one more,
We seek liquors for our Stone.

## Chapter 5.

Every one of the aforementioned liquids will stick
To what they touch, and leave some part behind;
But quicksilver <note>Mercury</note>, although it is fleeting,
Yet it will never stick to anything,
Except to a metal of one kind or another,
For there it finds a sister or a brother <note>Alchemists used familial terms to describe the chemical affinity or "attraction" between substances.</note>.
Mixing it with subtle <note>original: "suttill," meaning fine-grained or refined</note> earth prevents it
From sticking to the things it meets.
All the said liquors which have been mentioned
Contain the four elements just as it does;
As milk contains whey, butter, and cheese,
So truly does every single one of these.
These four may be separated apart,
And afterwards joined together to make you succeed.
But they are sought here much more skillfully
Than cheese, and butter, and whey are made;
And they draw nearer to simplicity <note>In alchemy, "simplicity" refers to elemental purity or the most basic state of matter.</note>,
Than cheese, butter, or whey can be.
Of all the liquors which are in our Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note>,
None is called "simple" except water alone.
For every liquor which shall go into our Stone,
You must also know its complexion and degree <note>The specific balance of qualities—hot, cold, moist, or dry—and their intensity.</note>.
And then with liquor you may diminish
The principal agent from its current state,
If it remains permanent and unchanging
In any point of excess <note>original: "superfluity"</note>:
As if the reigning quality is dryness,
You may correct it with the humor of moisture.
Now more, now less, as you see the need,
And so in all qualities proceed;
And in such a way, order at your will
The principal agent, to fulfill your purpose.
With knowledge of diversity, contrariety, and agreement,
You may choose which quality shall be the master.

# Ashmole (Elias), 1617–1692.

**The British Alchemical Theater <note>original: *Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum*</note>. Containing several poetic pieces by our famous English philosophers, who have written the Hermetic <note>Refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> mysteries in their own ancient language. Faithfully collected into one volume, with annotations included.** Thick small quarto <note>original: "4to," a book size where each sheet of paper is folded twice to form four leaves</note>. Title printed in red and black with a very fine engraved title vignette. With a folding plate by John Goddard, seven full-page and several smaller engravings by Robert Vaughan. Old calf leather, neatly rebacked, with a gilded title-piece.

->London: J. Grismond for Nath. Brooke, 1652<-

<margin>of Ashmole</margin>
Ashmole, "perhaps the most remarkable antiquarian adventurer of the century" (Gunther) and founder of the Ashmolean Museum at Oxford, provided in *The British Alchemical Theater* the most valuable collection of old English alchemical writings in verse—29 in total. The first and longest (106 pages) of them is the original English version of ***The Ordinal of Alchemy*** <insert>by</insert> Thomas Norton of Bristol (active around 1477), a true storehouse of medieval science. Two other contributions of primary importance are ***The Compound of Alchemy*** by George Ripley (c. 1415–1490) and ***The Canon's Yeoman's Tale*** by Geoffrey Chaucer.

Ashmole's collection was one of the favorite books of Sir Isaac Newton. An entry in one of his notebooks shows that he bought it in 1669 for 1 pound and 8 shillings. Manuscript transcripts of parts of this book, in Newton's handwriting, still exist, and his richly annotated copy of the printed book is also preserved. The fine engravings by Vaughan are of unusual interest.

One of the very rarest books in English alchemy. Ours is a fine, well-preserved copy, but without the unnumbered plate between pages 436–437, which is found

It is surer to act by their advice,
Nevertheless, seven may suffice for your work,
By discoveries lately found anew,
Of later philosophers whose works are true.
But regarding the circulations of elements,
Some scholars <note>original: "Clerks"</note> think to achieve their goals
When they arrange for [the process] to descend from Fire
To Air (they think they do not err),
If they then proceed to Water,
And from there to Earth when they see the need,
And in such a way fall by order,
From the highest to the lowest of all:
Upon these words they based their reasoning:
That *Air is the food of fire* <note>original: "Aer est cibus ignis"</note> was found.
But trust me, that such circulation
Is only a rectification <term>the purification of a substance, often through repeated distillation</term>,
Better serving for separation
And for correction than for transmutation.
But the truth is that the appetite of the Fire
Has its chief desire to work in Earth,
As upon its chief material food,
For Fire has the most harmony <note>original: "concord"</note> with Earth;
Because dryness <note>original: "ficcitie"</note> is the fuel <note>original: "lyme"</note> of heat,
But Air by its nature is mostly wet;
Yet Fire does not work without Air,
For the aspects <note>original: "Faces"</note> of elements are joined with a knot
By God's hand so that they may not separate
By any device <note>original: "engine"</note> nor craft of man's art;
As in pumps <note>original: "Plomps"</note> you have a fair example,
Where heavy water rises after air;
Of which you shall find no reasonable cause
But the connection of elemental properties.
But our circulation is from Fire on high,
Which ends with Water, its most extreme opposite.

Chapter 5. Another circulation begins with Air,
Ending with its contrary, clean and fair Earth.
From Fire to Earth, from there to clean Water,
From there to Air, then from there by a medium <note>original: "meane"</note>,
Passing to Earth, then soon after <note>original: "eftsoones"</note> to Fire;
The Red Work <note>The final stage of the alchemical process, known as the *rubedo*.</note> desires such circulations.
Other circulations are better for the White Work <note>The second stage of the alchemical process, known as the *albedo*.</note>,
Which are described according to its needs.
Every circulation has its proper season,
As its lightness accords with reason.
For just as one planet is more heavy <note>original: "ponderous"</note>
And slower in its course than another,
So some circulations which scholars <note>original: "Clerks"</note> seek
Must have a full thirty weeks for their time;
Other circulations shall often take less,
Just as one planet is lighter than another was.
But the total time of one compared with another will amount
To twenty-six weeks, as proved by calculation <note>original: "accompt"</note>.
After all preliminary <note>original: "groſſe"</note> work is done beforehand,
And after I have understood all the circumstances;
Ignorance of this deceives many a man,
Causing them to stop where wise men began.
Common people who have sought this science
Think <note>original: "Ween"</note> that it might <note>original: "mought"</note> be accomplished in forty days.
They do not know how Nature and the things of Art <note>In alchemy, "Art" refers to the human manipulation of natural processes.</note>
Have a specific time assigned for their role,
As it appears by this comparison <note>original: "Similitude"</note>:
The elephant, because she is large and rugged <note>original: "rude"</note>,
Carries a calf <note>original: "Foale"</note> for two full years,
And it is fifty years before that calf produces offspring <note>original: "gender"</note> again.
Anaxagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 500–428 BCE) who theorized about the composition of matter.</note> said in his deliberations
That metals took a thousand years for their generation;
Therefore he chose to say that,
In respect to that, our Work is but one day.
Also <note>original: "Alfoc"; this is a catchword for the following page.</note>

# TO
## All Ingeniously Diligent <note>original: "Elaborate"</note> Students,
## In the most Divine Mysteries of
## Hermetic <note>original: "Hermetique"</note> Learning.

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial 'T' decorated with scrolling foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

*The subject of this following work is a philosophical account of that eminent secret treasured up in the bosom of Nature. It has been sought by many, but found by few, despite the fact that experienced antiquity has provided faithful (though infrequent) discoveries of it. Past ages, like rivers, have carried down to us on the surface <note>original: "upon the floate"</note> the more light and superficial <note>original: "Sophisticall"</note> pieces of learning; but those that were profound and mysterious sank to the bottom due to their weight and solidity. From there, not everyone who attempts to dive can easily retrieve them. Thus, what our Savior said to his disciples may (I hope without offense) be spoken to the chosen <note>original: "Elected"</note> <term>Sons of Art</term>: "Unto you it is given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of God; but to others in parables, that seeing they might not see, and hearing they might not understand" (Luke 8:10).*

<term>Sons of Art</term> — A traditional term used by alchemists to describe those initiated into the "Art" of alchemy or the Great Work.

*Our English philosophers generally (like prophets) have received little honor in their own country (unless it was paid to them privately). Nor have they performed any mighty works among us, except in secretly administering their medicine to a few sick people and healing them. (For they never publicly showed any greater experiments than what the medicine performs in <term>physick</term>.)*

<term>Physick</term> — The early modern term for the practice of medicine and the study of the natural world.

*This is what I.O. (one of the first four fellows of the Brothers of the Rosie Cross <note>original: "Fratres R. C."</note>) did in curing the young Earl of Norfolk of leprosy; and Doctor B. <note>Likely Dr. Butler, a famous physician of the era.</note> did in twice removing the virulence of the smallpox from Queen Elizabeth, so effectively that the marks never appeared. But in foreign countries, they have found a more noble reception, and the world is greedy to obtain their works; indeed (rather than go without seeing them), they are content to view*

<summary>In this preface, Elias Ashmole introduces his collection of alchemical texts by arguing that profound spiritual and natural truths are often hidden from the public and preserved only by a few "Sons of Art." He laments that English alchemists are more respected abroad than at home, despite their miraculous medical cures.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Prolegomena" or preface to Elias Ashmole’s "Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum" (1652). Ashmole is arguing for the value of English alchemical heritage, noting that while English scholars often neglect their own history, foreign scholars have historically traveled to England specifically to study and translate these works.</meta>

...them through a translation, no matter how imperfect. Consider what Michael Maier, Hermannus, Combachius, Faber, and many others have achieved; the first of these came from Germany to live in England specifically so he could understand our English language well enough to translate Thomas Norton’s *Ordinal* into Latin verse. He did this with great judgment and learning; yet (to our shame) he was treated far too poorly <note>original: "too too course"</note> for such a deserving scholar.

*How great a disgrace it is for us to refuse to read such famous authors in our native language, while foreigners find it necessary to read them in ours just to understand them in their own—believing the importance of the subject is worth far more than the effort they spend.*

*If we consider this honestly <note>original: "ingeniously"</note>, we will see it is more reasonable to look back on, rather than neglect, the works of learning produced in our own country. Through this investigation, we will find that no* **nation** *has written more or better works, although at present—due to both our own laziness <note>original: "supinenesse"</note> and the* **decrees of fate**—*few of their works can be found.* **John Leland** <note>John Leland (1503–1552) was an English antiquary who traveled throughout England recording its history and libraries just before the monasteries were dissolved.</note> *went to great lengths, even as our* **English** *learning was breathing its last, to preserve its final (though weak and nearly exhausted) breath. From his work,* **John Bale** *and* **John Pitts (who is actually just a plagiarist of Bale)** *have left us a catalog of this nation’s writers, and that is nearly all we have. Yet future generations <note>original: "posterity"</note> are deeply indebted to them even for this. What punishment then did the destructive malice of those who robbed us of their complete works deserve?*

A wise author, speaking of the dissolution of our monasteries, says this: "Many manuscripts, guilty of no other superstition than having red letters <note>Red ink was commonly used for headings and instructions (rubrics) in religious texts; reformers often viewed these as "popish" and destroyed them.</note> on their front pages, were condemned to the fire; thus, a vital key to antiquity was lost, to the great harm of future generations." Indeed, such was learning's misfortune during that great destruction of English libraries that whenever a red letter or a mathematical diagram appeared, it was enough to label the book as either "popish" or "diabolical."

*Our* **English** *nation has always been blessed with learning and learned men, and I hope it will not be unpleasant if I illustrate this.*

*First, there were the* **Druids** *(the famous and mysterious* **Druids** *) who were priests, diviners, and wise men. They took their origin and name from* **Druys Sarronyus**, *the fourth king of the* Celts *(styled the* **Teacher of Wise Men and Augurs** <note>original: "Sapientum & Augurum Doctor"</note> *), who died in the* **Year of the World 2069.** <note>original: "Anno Mundi. 2069." This refers to a dating system that counts years starting from the biblical creation of the world.</note>

# Prolegomena.

Next were the **Bards**, who celebrated the *illustrious deeds of famous men*. They skillfully arranged these stories in *heroic verse* and sang them to the *sweet melody of the harp*. Among other testimonies to this, consider **Chaucer’s**:

> The noble Britons of old, in their time,
> Composed songs <note>original: "Layes"</note> about various adventures,
> Which were first written in their mother tongue,
> And these songs they sang to their instruments.

These philosophers took their name from **Bardus Druidus** (the fifth King of the **Celts**), who was the first inventor of *verses*, as **Berosus** <note>original: "Berofius"</note> tells us; he died in the *Year of the World* <note>original: "An. Mundi"</note> 2138. Neither of these groups <note>The Bards and the Druids</note> of philosophers used any writing—indeed, it was not permitted. *Such was the strategy and carefulness of ancient times (to protect their learning and mysteries from the damage of ignorant interpretations) that they passed them on to posterity by tradition only.*

**Julius Caesar** testifies (and it is a noble testimony) *that the learning of the* **Druids** *was first invented in* **Britain** *and then transferred to* **Gaul** <note>original: "France"</note>; *and that in his time, those in France came over here to be instructed.* **Agricola** (as recorded by the historian **Tacitus**) *prefers the Britons over the students of France (even though the French had a teachable mind and were quick to learn) because the Britons were eager to master the eloquence of the* **Latin language**.

*As for* **Magic**, **Pliny** *tells us it flourished in Britain, and that the people there were so devoted to it (performing it with every possible ceremony) that one would think even the* **Persians** *learned their magic from there.*

A **German** poet says *that when the world was troubled by* **Pannonian** <note>Invasions from the region of Pannonia, a Roman province in central Europe.</note> *invasions, England flourished in the knowledge of all good arts and was able to send her learned men into other countries to spread learning. He cites* **Winifrid** (also known as **Saint Boniface**, the man from Devonshire) *and* **Willibrord** (the man from the North) *who were sent to Germany.*

Nay, more—England was twice a "school-mistress" to France (as **Peter Ramus** <note>A famous 16th-century French humanist and logician.</note> says). *Specifically: first through the* **Druids** (who taught them their discipline) *and later through* **Alcuin** <note>original: "Alcunius"</note> *during* **Charlemagne’s** <note>original: "Charles the Great's"</note> *time. It was through Alcuin’s persuasion that the Emperor founded the* **University of Paris**.

As for the **Saxons**, it cannot be denied that many of them, after...

<meta>This page continues the "Prolegomena" (preface) of Elias Ashmole's *Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum*. Ashmole is discussing the ancient wisdom of the Germanic and Saxon ancestors of the English, specifically their religious symbols and their connection to alchemical concepts.</meta>

# Prolegomena.

After their conversion to Christianity, they were exceedingly learned; and before that, they were much addicted to soothsaying, augury, and divination by the neighing of horses, etc. *And it is worth the inquiry (there being more in it than we ordinarily realize) why they in general worshiped* Hertha <note>original: "Herthus"</note> [that is, **Mother Earth**] *as a goddess, and honored* Mercury *above all the gods of the* Germans, *whom they called* **Woden** <note>original: "Wooden"</note> (*from which comes* **Woden's Day**, *now our* **Wednesday**?). *For they believed that this* **Mother Earth** *interceded in human affairs and relieved the poor. Her image was depicted as an armed woman standing among* flowers, *holding a staff in her right hand with a banner on it wherein a* rose *was painted. # Prolegomena.

In whichever field they excelled, there was no liberal science or any feat concerning learning in which they have not shown clear evidence of great talent and intelligence. And so much for the general state of learning.

Now for a specific account of the *Hermetic science* <note>The study of alchemy and occult philosophy, attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, please deign (*intelligent reader*) to accept the following collections. However, do not think that they contain all the works of our *English Hermetic philosophers* (for more are planned in a second part to follow and complete this into a full *theatre* <note>original: "Theatrum"</note>; which, if **GOD** allows me further time and peace to complete as I have this one, I intend shortly to make ready for the press). In this way, I will further reveal what men we have had, who were no less famous for this kind of *philosophy* than for all other *praiseworthy arts and sciences*.

To add anything to the praise of this science would be like holding a candle before the sun. If I were to provide a full account here of its marvelous operations and effects, it would be as far beyond the limits of a preface as it is distant from the belief of the general public. Nor do I expect that all my readers should come committed to believing what I write here, or that there was ever any such thing in *nature* <note>original: "rerum natura"</note> as what we call *a philosopher's stone*. Nor will I try to persuade them of it (though I must tell them I am not so vain as to publish these sacred and serious mysteries and *secrets* <note>original: "Arcana"</note> as if they were *fictional stories* <note>original: "Romances"</note>). And first, concerning the **Mineral Stone**: it is refined only to the degree that has the power of **transmuting** any **imperfect earthy matter** into its highest degree of **perfection**. That is, to convert the basest of **metals** into perfect **gold** and **silver**; **flints** into all manner of **precious stones** (such as rubies, sapphires, emeralds, and diamonds, etc.) and many more experiments of a similar nature. This can be done not only instantly, for the sake of the experiment <note>original: *Experimenti gratia*</note>, *but daily, monthly, and yearly, at any time and in any season; yes, even in the depth of winter. For though they are both made from one natural substance, they have contrary qualities in operation. Nevertheless, there is such a natural cooperation between them that what the one cannot do, the other both can and will perform.

In a word, it clearly presents the whole world to your view, allowing you to behold, hear, or see whatever you desire. And yet—*oh, mysterious wonder!*—it is a stone that can stay in the fire for eternity without being harmed. It possesses a divine, celestial, and invisible power above all the others, and it endows its possessor with divine gifts. It provides the appearance of angels and grants the power of conversing with them through dreams and revelations; no evil spirit dares approach the place where it is kept. This is because it is a <term>Quintessence</term> <note>the "fifth element" in ancient science, believed to be the pure essence of the heavens</note> containing nothing corruptible, and where the elements are not corrupt, no devil can remain.

Saint Dunstan <note>a 10th-century Archbishop of Canterbury who, in later legends, was claimed to be an alchemist</note> calls it the "food of angels," and others term it the <term>Heavenly Viaticum</term> <note>original: "Heavenly Viaticum"; a viaticum is a provision for a journey, often used to refer to the final Eucharist given to the dying</note> or the "Tree of Life." For by it, the human body is preserved from corruption, enabling one to live a long time without food; indeed, some question whether any person who uses it can ever die. I do not wonder at this so much as I wonder why those who possess it would even desire to live, having seen these manifestations of glory and eternity with their own mortal eyes. I would think they would rather desire to be released from the body <note>original: "Dissolved"</note> to enjoy the full reality of heaven, rather than living where they must be content with mere contemplation <note>original: "Speculation"</note>.

<meta>This page continues the "Prolegomena" or introduction to Elias Ashmole's "Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum." # Prolegomena.

But while I was doing this, I raised a question (considering that some philosophers had written in verse and others in prose): which of these should take precedence? After some consideration, I awarded it to the poetic part. This was not only because its origins likely precede the time of Orpheus—even though he is noted by Michael Maier <note>original: "Maierus," a famous German alchemist and physician (1568–1622).</note> as the **First Leader, Priest, Theologian, PROPHET, and Teacher of the entire Greek nation** <note>original: "Primus Antistes, Sacerdos, Theologus, VATES, & Doctor totius Græcorum nationis"</note>—but also because Linus is said to be the most **skilled** <note>original: "Perite"</note> of any **lyric poet**. Linus was so ancient that some suppose him to be the master of Orpheus, who wrote that admirable allegory of the **Golden Fleece** <note>In alchemical traditions, the quest for the Golden Fleece was often interpreted as a metaphor for the search for the Philosopher's Stone.</note>. Orpheus was the first of all the Greeks to bring **alchemical learning** <term>Chemick Learning</term> (along with other sciences) out of Egypt, just as Linus was the first to bring **Phoenician learning** to the Greeks. *I say I chose poetry not only because it is the most ancient form, while prose is of more recent use among other nations, but because poetry has been most anciently used among us in England and—as if by a grant of nature—is held to be unquestionable.*

Again, the excellent melody of poetry is so natural and universal that it seems to be born with all the nations of the world, **as an inborn eloquence proper to all mankind.** Nor was this all, for I considered that it claims a general succession and reception in all nations and all ages, which were never without a Homer, a Virgil, or an Ovid. Even this small segment of the world, England, was not without a Rafis of Chester <note>original: "Rafis Cestrensis"</note> and a Hortulanus <note>Latin for "The Gardener."</note>. Regarding the first of these, his **Book of Lights** <note>original: "Liber Luminum"</note> and his **Light of Lights** <note>original: "Lumen de Luminum"</note> are the oldest works now surviving in Latin verse. In the latter of these, I cannot omit this title of his: **The Answer of Rafis of Chester to his son Merlin** <note>original: "Responsio Rafis Cestrensis Filio suo Merlino"</note>. From this, it appears he was Merlin's contemporary (at least), if not his master, in this **hidden mystery** <note>original: "Abstruse Mystery," referring to alchemy.</note>. Both of these works were published by Hermannus, but very imperfectly, as I found by comparing them with a manuscript as ancient as King John’s time. As for the second, Hortulanus, he was the first **Christian philosopher** after Morienus <note>A legendary alchemist said to have taught the Umayyad prince Khalid ibn Yazid.</note>. Because he was the first to transplant the "alchemical muses" from the most remote parts into his own country (traveling abroad and returning here during the reign of William the Conqueror), he is called **Garland, for the Hermetic and Poetic crown** <note>original: "Garland, ab Coronam Hermeticam & Poeticam." This likely refers to John de Garlandia, an 11th-century grammarian and alchemist.</note>.

But, to return to our matter.

Even if neither its antiquity, nor its natural confirmation, nor its general succession and reception were enough to allow poetry the "right hand of fellowship," I still believe its effects are sufficient. These effects so affect and delight the ear, rejoice the heart, and satisfy the judge-

<meta>This page continues the "Prolegomena" or introduction to Elias Ashmole's *Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum*. Ashmole is concluding his argument for why he chose to publish alchemical works written in verse rather than prose, emphasizing poetry's power to move the mind and its historical use as a "sacred" veil for secrets. He also reflects on his role in rescuing these rare manuscripts from the destruction that followed the Reformation.</meta>

# Prolegomena.

[...judgment, and please the listeners] as they justly may. This is because **poetry** has a life, a pulse, and such a secret energy that it leaves a far deeper impression on the mind than the flow and uneven rhythms of prose. Through this power, poetry won over the world so completely that in unrefined times <note>original: "Rude Times"</note>, and even among uncivilized nations where other types of learning were excluded, nothing was held in higher esteem. 

As for what we call rhythm <term>Rythme</term>, the custom of many of our Saxon and Norman poets shows the high opinion they had of it. Even the Latin language—despite its excellence—could not sufficiently delight their ears unless their verses in that language were formed with a harmonious cadence and brought into rhyme. Nor did the ancients hide their greatest mysteries anywhere else but in the symbolic and metaphorical <note>original: "Parabolical & Allusive"</note> parts of poetry. They considered this the most sacred and venerable form, and the safest way to keep secrets from the uninitiated and the common-minded <note>original: "Prophane and Vulgar Wits"</note>. 

For such was the goodness of our ancestors <term>Fathers</term> that they would not willingly risk (much less throw) their "children’s bread" to the "dogs." Therefore, their wisdom and strategy was first to find a way to teach, and then to find an art—which was poetry—to conceal. In short, to prefer prose over poetry is no better than letting a crude peasant <term>Rough-hewen-Clowne</term> take the place of honor <note>original: "take the Wall," a phrase referring to the cleaner, safer path next to a wall in narrow streets, reserved for social superiors.</note> over a noble lady, or to hang a royal reception room <term>Presence Chamber</term> with coarse tarpaulin instead of fine tapestry.

And for these reasons, and out of these considerations, I believed the poetic works deserved to come first.

However, it is likely that some of these pieces—now brought to public light—would have nearly perished in silent ruin. Destruction would have achieved a complete victory over them if my diligence and laborious investigation <term>Inquisition</term> had not rescued them from its jaws. They were almost entirely shrouded in the dust of antiquity and lost in the obscurity of forgotten things, with their pages half worm-eaten. It is a wonder that, like the creatures in Noah’s Ark, they were preserved so safely until now from that universal flood which—at the time of the dissolution of the monasteries <term>Dissolution of Abbies</term>—overflowed our greatest libraries. 

In doing this, I do not think it arrogant to claim the reputation of performing a work nearly as significant as if it were my own original creation. In fact, it is something more: as if I possessed the Elixir <term>Elixir</term> itself, I have made old age become young and lively again. I have restored each of these ancient writers not only to the "spring" of their various beauties but to the "summer" of their strength and perfection.

<summary>Ashmole argues that poetry is superior to prose for conveying alchemical mysteries because it is more memorable and serves as a "sacred" veil to hide secrets from the unworthy. He also compares his editorial work to the Elixir of Life, claiming to have rescued these "worm-eaten" manuscripts from the destruction of monastic libraries.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Prolegomena" or introduction to Elias Ashmole's *Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum*. Ashmole is justifying his editorial choices, specifically regarding the preservation of the original language and spelling of the ancient alchemical poems he has collected.</meta>

# Prolegomena.

*As for the whole work itself, it has been gathered together <note>original: "sheav'd up"</note> from a few gleanings in some of our English fields. Although I have put in the effort <note>original: "bestow-ed my Industry"</note> to pick up here and there what I could find in my path, I believe there are many other pieces of this nature in private hands. If anyone is pleased to share these with me (out of the same high-minded <note>original: "Ingenious"</note> motive for which I have published these), I shall value their generosity as it deserves and let the world know of its obligation to them as well.*

*The style and language of these works may, I confess, seem tedious and strange <note>original: "Irksome and Uncouth"</note> to some, and it is indeed so to those who are strangers to it; however, it is also very meaningful. Old words have great power <note>original: "strong Emphasis"</note>. Others may look upon them as garbage or trivialities, but they are completely mistaken; for what some shallow minds <note>original: "light Braines"</note> may regard as silly trifles <note>original: "Foolish Toys"</note>, deeper judgments can and will value as sound and serious matter.*

*We English have often changed our fashions (such is the fickleness of our tastes), and therefore if you encounter spellings different from those currently in use, or strange words as oddly ridiculous as a <term>Manche</term> <note>A large, hanging sleeve fashionable in the Middle Ages</note>, a <term>Hood</term>, a <term>Codpiece</term>, or <term>Trunk-hose</term> <note>Short, puffy breeches worn in the 16th century</note>, know that just as those were the fashionable clothes, these were the usual dialects of those times. Posterity will pay us back in our own coin if we should mock the behavior and dress of our ancestors. For we must consider that languages used in daily conversation are in constant change <note>original: "Mutation"</note>. Whatever custom brings into fashion is liked best for the present—whether it is to revive what was lost, introduce something new, or patch up the present with the retained shreds of what came before. But literary languages <note>original: "learned Tongues"</note> preserved in books enjoy a more unchanging fate because they are not subject to being washed away by the daily tide and flow of time. They are like the fashion and clothing carved on marble statues, which must always be kept without alteration.*

*And therefore, so that the truth and worth of their works would not be diminished by my transcription, I purposely kept the old words and their way of spelling just as I found them in the originals (excepting only some obvious mistakes and flaws of previous transcribers, which I took it upon myself to correct as little more than clerical errors). Yet, so as not to leave the reader unsatisfied, I have added a concise table <note>original: "Compendious Table"</note> for the interpretation of old, unusual, and obsolete words. By this, I have smoothed (I believe) the path for those who have not previously been familiar with these ancient, unrefined <note>original: "Rough-hew'd"</note> expressions.*

<summary>Elias Ashmole explains his decision to preserve the original archaic spelling and vocabulary of the alchemical texts, comparing linguistic evolution to changing fashions in clothing. He also invites other collectors to share similar manuscripts and mentions he has provided a glossary to help modern readers understand the old terminology.</summary>
<keywords>Elias Ashmole, Prolegomena, linguistic evolution, archaic spelling, glossary, English alchemy, manuscript preservation, fashion metaphors</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the "Prolegomena" (introduction) to Elias Ashmole's *Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum* (1652). Ashmole invites his readers to learn from the writings of deceased alchemists and explains that his own notes focus on historical context rather than explaining the secret philosophical processes themselves.</meta>

# Prolegomena.

Therefore, you who love to converse with the dead, or consult with their monuments, draw near; perhaps you may find more benefit in them than in the living. There you may meet with the guiding spirits <note>original: "Genii"</note> of our Hermetic philosophers <note>Practitioners of alchemy and esoteric wisdom based on the teachings of Hermes Trismegistus</note>, learn the language in which they wooed and courted Dame Nature, and enjoy their company more freely and with greater command (to satisfy your doubts) than when they were in the flesh. For they have written more than they would speak, and they left their writing <note>original: "Lines"</note> so rich, as if they had dissolved gold in their ink and clothed their words with the sovereign moisture <note>original: "Soveraign Moysture"; an alchemical term referring to the "mercury of the philosophers" or the universal solvent</note>.

My annotations are limited within the bounds of what is historical, or what must occasionally overlap <note>original: "intrench"</note> with the territory of other arts. I have purposely omitted all commentary <note>original: "Glosses"</note> upon the actual philosophical work <note>The secret alchemical process of creating the Philosopher's Stone</note> for the same reasons that I chose to send forth other men's "children" <note>Referring to the poems and texts by other authors in this collection</note> into the world rather than my own. And whatever arrogant mistakes or errors the sincere <note>original: "Candid"</note> reader shall encounter, I hope they will be judged with no less favor and charity than that with which people are accustomed to judge the faults of those they consider their friends and well-wishers.

And now to conclude: may the **GOD** of **NATURE** be graciously pleased (out of the immense treasury of his goodness) to grant <note>original: "vouchsafe"</note> all those—whose good angels direct them to, or have already religiously engaged them in, this mysterious knowledge—the full and entire accomplishments of a true and pious philosopher. [Namely: learning, humility, judgment, courage, hope, patience, discretion, charity, and secrecy.] May this be so that they may enjoy the fruits of their labors, which otherwise will be only vain and unpleasant, and would cause this divine science and the secret itself to be wrongly viewed as contemptible.

*Farewell* (*industrious students*), and let your goodness continue to invite me to accomplish the goal I have proposed. In doing so, I trust <note>original: "presume"</note> you may one day consider me better deserving of your support <note>original: "Patronage"</note>; at the very least, your charitable judgment <note>original: "Censure"</note>, which is all the reward expected or deserved by him who is

->Yours truly devoted,<-

->26 January 1651/2 <note>In the old calendar, the year changed in March; this is 1652 by modern reckoning.</note><-

# The Prologue <note>original: "The Prohême"</note>

All masters who write of this solemn work,
They made their books very obscure <note>original: "derke"</note> to many men,
In poems <note>original: "Poyses"</note>, parables, and in metaphors also,
Which causes pain and woe to scholars:

They lose their money <note>original: "Costs"</note>, as people see every day.
*Hermes*, *Rhazes* <note>original: "Rafis"</note>, *Geber*, and *Avicenna* <note>original: "Avicen"</note>,
*Merlin*, *Hortulanus* <note>original: "Hortolan"</note>, *Democritus* <note>original: "Democrit"</note>, and *Morienus* <note>original: "Morien"</note>,

Their obscure <note>original: "Cloudy"</note> sentences confused <note>original: "dulled"</note> many men;
From laypeople, from scholars <note>original: "Clearks"</note>, and so from every man,
They hid this *Art* so that no man can find it.

Of the old fathers that I ever found,

Intending that men should not turn to him:
For he was generous <note>original: "large"</note> with his knowledge <term>original: "cunning"; meaning specialized skill or hidden knowledge</term> and love—

Like the monk who wrote a book

Which are copied in many a place,
Whereby many a face has been made pale;
And many gowns have been made threadbare <note>original: "bare of hewe"</note>,
And men made false who before that time were true.

# The Prologue <note>original: "The Prohême"</note>

Therefore my pity compels me
To show the truth in words few and plain,
So that you may flee from false doctrine,
If you give belief to this book and me;
Avoid your books written of recipes <note>original: "Receipts"</note>,
For all such recipes are full of deceits;
Trust not such recipes, and learn this principle <note>original: "Clause"</note> well:
Nothing is produced except by its proper cause.
Therefore, practice falls far short
When knowledge of the cause is not kept in mind.
<margin>Why.</margin>

Therefore, you must never slip into falsehood.

The "*Believe me*" <note>original: "Crede mihi"</note>, the *Perpetual Standard*.

# The Prologue <note>original: "The Prohême"</note>

For just as the *Ordinal* for *priests* sets out
The daily services as they occur throughout the year:

Is a book of incomparable value;
Its truth shall never be corrupted <note>original: "defiled"</note>,
Even though it appears compiled in a simple <note>original: "homely"</note> manner:
And as I received this *Art* by Grace from Heaven,
I give the same to you here in *seven chapters*:
As fully as my oath of loyalty allows,
By the license of the awesome <note>original: "dreadfull"</note> Judge at the Day of Judgment <note>original: "domes daye"</note>.
The first chapter shall teach all men
What kind of people may attain this *science*,
And why the true *science* of *alchemy*

The fourth chapter teaches the "gross work" <term>the initial, physical stages of alchemical processing, often involving raw or "unclean" materials</term>,

And helps further our wonderful works.

# The Epistle

And he immediately adds these two things as the best
For those who practice alchemy to take,
In order to make our Gold and our Silver alone;
Therefore I say, whoever wishes to make our Pearl and Ruby <note>original: "Pearle and Ruby"; these terms refer to the White Elixir (which transmutes metals into silver) and the Red Elixir or Philosopher's Stone (which transmutes them into gold).</note>,

For if his principles are true at the beginning,

Truly, in the end, he shall not regret his work.

But it is very necessary to know one great secret,
That though the Philosophers speak in the plural <note>Alchemists often used multiple names (like "Green Lion," "Adrop," or "Mercury") for the same single substance to hide their secrets from the uninitiated.</note>,
It is all but one thing, you may believe me,
In "kind" <note>original: "kinde," meaning its nature or species</note>, which is principally our Base,

And yet the White must come before the Red:
Which thing is not achieved manually,
But naturally, with Craft helping to draw it out of our Lead <note>In alchemy, "Lead" often refers to the raw, unrefined starting material (Materia Prima) rather than the common metal.</note>.

For all the parts of our most precious Stone,
As I can prove, are <term>co-essential</term> <note>Sharing the same fundamental essence or substance.</note> and concrete;
Moreover, there is no true principle but one,
It was a very long time before I could find it:
Whoever can <term>reduce</term> <note>To bring back to a simpler or more fundamental state.</note> it, and knows its Heat,
And can redress Nature only with its own Nature,
Until original filth is cleansed from its seat,
He is likely to find our secrets, both great and small.

Therefore, work only Nature with its own Nature,
And join all your elements so that they do not struggle;
Also, bear this point in mind above all else:
That you turn passive natures into active ones,
From Water, Fire, and Wind, quickly make Earth;
And from the <term>Quadrangle</term> <note>The square, representing the four physical elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note> make a round figure <note>A reference to "squaring the circle," a symbol for the union of opposites and the creation of the perfect Philosopher's Stone.</note>,
Then you shall have the honey <note>original: "bonie," likely a variation of "honey."</note> of our beehive;
One ounce is well worth a thousand pounds.

## CHAPTER I.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial letter 'M' featuring a central bearded figure with long hair, surrounded by ornamental foliage, scrolls, and floral patterns.</image-desc>

Masterful, marvelous, and an arch-mastery
Is the <term>tincture</term> <note>original: "tincture"; in alchemy, a potent substance (like the Philosopher's Stone) capable of transmuting or "dyeing" base metals into gold or silver.</note> of holy Alchemy:
A wonderful science, a secret philosophy,
A singular grace and gift of the Almighty;
Which was never found by the labor of man,
But through teaching or revelation it began.
It was never sold or bought for any amount of money
By any man who has sought after it;
But it is given to a capable man by grace,
Wrought with great cost, and with long leisure and time.
It helps a man when he is in need;
It removes <note>original: "voydeth"</note> vainglory, hope, and also dread.
It removes ambition, extortion, and excess;
It wards off adversity so that it does not oppress.
He who achieves his full purpose in it
Forsakes extremes and is content with moderation <note>original: "Measure"</note>.
Some people would not have it called "holy,"
And they argue in this way:
They say that <term>pagans</term> <note>original: "Painims"; non-Christians, specifically referring here to the many famous Arabic and Greek alchemical authorities like Geber or Hermes.</note> may possess this art,
Whom our Lord God will never save;
Because of their willful, false infidelity,
They cannot be the possessors of the source of goodness.
Also, it creates nothing else
But gold or silver for money, cups, or rings,
Which wise men have proven and found
To be the least virtuous things upon the earth.
Therefore, all men of that mindset conclude
And say that this science is not holy in its effect.
To this we say and bear witness as best we can,
That this science was never taught to man [by human means alone];

For *God* has ordained by his wisdom and grace,
All things to grow in their natural place.

<summary>Norton argues that fraudulent alchemists lie about the nature of metals, which do not "multiply" like animals but require specific natural conditions—namely putrefaction and being in their "proper place" underground—to grow or transform.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Thomas Norton’s *Ordinal of Alchemy*, Chapter 1. Having previously argued that metals do not multiply like living things through biological propagation, Norton now addresses counter-arguments from those who believe metals grow underground and should therefore be able to be "multiplied" in a laboratory setting.</meta>

<page-num>19</page-num>
<header>ORDINALL.</header>

<margin>Chapter 1.</margin>
Against this doctrine some men reply,
And say that metals do multiply:
For of silver, lead, tin, and also brass,
some veins are larger, and some are smaller;
Regarding which diversity, Nature would cease
if metals did not multiply and increase.
Therefore they say that reason shows now
how they multiply and grow under the earth;
Why not then above the earth in vessels closed and fair,
such as should preserve them from fire, water, and air?
To this we say this reasoning is but crude,
for this is no perfect comparison <note>original: "similitude"</note>.
For you shall find the efficient cause of metals
to be only the "mineral virtue,"
which is not found in every kind of earth,
but in certain places of eligible ground;
into which places the heavenly sphere
sends its beams directly every year.
And as the matters there are disposed,
so shall you see such metals formed from it.
Few grounds are suited for such generation;
how then should there be multiplication above ground?
Also all men who are wise perceive
how water congealed with cold is ice;
and before the time it was hardened,
some lay in more places and some in less—
just as water in the ruts <note>original: "fosses"</note> of a cart-wheel
were small veins when they began to cool <note>original: "keele"</note>,
but water in ditches made larger veins
because of the plenty of water that was frozen <note>original: "froare"</note> therein.
Based on this, it would be poor logic to say
that therefore more ice should multiply from ice.
So, though there are larger and smaller veins of metals,
it does not prove that they increase more than they originally were.

<summary>Norton refutes the idea that metals "grow" like plants by explaining that their varying sizes in the earth are due to initial conditions and "mineral virtue" rather than biological reproduction. He uses the analogy of ice forming in different sized puddles to show that volume does not equal active multiplication.</summary>

<page-num>20</page-num>
<header>Norton's</header>

<margin>Chapter 1.</margin>
Also, you may trust without any doubt,
If multiplication were to be achieved:
All the ingredients must be reduced to simplicity,
And break their composition, as you may see every year.
For see how *Nature* has provided for the multiplication of herbs:
She requires that all things joined in the seed be divided;
Otherwise, the stalk and leaves, which are potentially <note>original: "vertually"</note> within it,
May not come forth actually so that the eye might see them.
But metal keeps its whole composition,
Even when corrosive waters have dissolved it.
Therefore, since ice is closer to simplicity
Than metal is, and yet cannot be increased,
Truly you may trust, as I said before,
That from one ounce of silver, there can be no more silver.
Also, you shall find nothing multiplied
Unless it is of a vegetable or "sensitive" <note>living or animal</note> kind;
Whereas metals are only elemental <note>original: "Elamentative"</note>,
Having no seed, nor any feeling of life.
Therefore, concluding that all "multipliers" <note>those who claim to increase the quantity of a metal</note> must stop,
For once metals are metals, they shall increase no further.
Nonetheless, we find one metal transmuted
Into a metal of another kind,
Because of the proximity <note>original: "propinquity"</note> of the matter that was in them,
As it is known to happen between *iron* and *brass* <note>Norton likely refers here to the "cementation" process where iron is coated or transformed in appearance</note>.
But to make true *silver* or *gold* there is no engine <note>method or device</note>,
Except only the *Philosopher's Medicine*.
Therefore, such lies <note>original: "leasings"</note> as "multipliers" use,
Scholars <note>original: "clerks"</note> reprove and utterly reject.
Such an art of multiplication is to be condemned,
But holy *Alchemy* is rightly to be loved,
Which deals with a precious Medicine,
Such as truly makes fine *gold* and *silver*;
Of which an example for testimony
Is found in a city of *Catalonia* <note>original: "Catilony"</note>.

<summary>Norton argues that metals cannot "multiply" like plants because they lack seeds and biological life; however, he asserts that one metal can be "transmuted" into another through the true "holy alchemy" of the Philosopher's Medicine.</summary>

<margin>Chapter 1.</margin>
Which *Raymond Lully* <note>original: "Raymond Lully, Knight"; a 13th-century Majorcan philosopher and legendary alchemist</note>, Knight, men suppose,
Made in seven images the truth to disclose;
Three were good *Silver*, in shape like *Ladies* bright,
Each of the other four were *Gold* and looked like a *Knight*:
In the borders of their clothing, letters appear,
Signifying in sentences as it is shown here.
1. "From old horseshoes," said one, "I was *iron* <note>original: "yre"</note>,
Now I am good *Silver*, as good as you desire."
2. "I was," said another, " *Iron* taken from the mine,
But now I am *Gold*, pure, perfect, and fine."
3. "Formerly <note>original: "Whilome"</note> I was *Copper* from an old red pan,
Now am I good *Silver*," said the third woman.
4. The fourth said, "I was *Copper* grown in a filthy <insert>place</insert>,
Now am I perfect *Gold* made by *God's* grace."
5. The fifth said, "I was *Silver*, perfect and fine,
Now am I perfect *Gold*, excellent, better than the best <note>original: "prime"</note>."
6. "I was a pipe of *Lead* for nearly two hundred years,
And now to all men, good *Silver* I appear."
7. The seventh said, "I, *Lead*, am *Gold* made by a mastery <note>term: "maistrie" refers to the Magisterium, the successful completion of the alchemical process</note>,
But truly my fellows are nearer to it than I."
This science bears its name from a king,
Called *Alchimus* <note>A legendary figure often cited in the Middle Ages as the founder of alchemy; the name is a folk etymology for "alchemy"</note>, without lying:
A glorious prince of most noble mind,
His noble virtues helped him this art to find;
He searched Nature; he was a noble scholar <note>original: "Clerke"</note>,
He left extortion, then sought and found this work.
King *Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical "thrice-great" founder of Hermetic philosophy and alchemy</note> also did the same,
Being a scholar of excellent fame;
In his *Quadripartite* <note>original: "Quadripartite"; referring to a four-part work attributed to Hermes</note> made of *Astrology*,
Of *Medicine* <note>original: "Phisique"</note> and of this *Art of Alchemy*,
And also of *Natural Magic*,
As of four sciences in nature surpassing all others.
And there he said that blessed is he
That knows things truly as they be.

<margin>Chapter 1.</margin> And blessed is he who makes proper proof <note>original: "due proofe"; here meaning experimental verification or demonstration</note>,
For that is the root and the roof of knowledge <note>term: "cunning" in this context refers to specialized knowledge, wisdom, or skill, rather than deceit</note>;
For by mere opinion, many a man is
Deceived, who knows little of this art.
*An old proverb: In a bushel of guessing <note>original: "weeninge"</note>,*
*There is not found one handful of knowledge:*
With proper proof and with careful testing <note>term: "assaye"; the chemical trial of a metal's purity</note>,
Wise men may learn new things every day.
By knowledge, men know themselves and everything;
A man is but a beast—and worse—without knowledge:
But every man has little favor
For a science of which he knows little;
And a little knowledge makes men proud and wild,
But sufficient knowledge makes men very humble <note>original: "milde"</note>.
Noble men nowadays, in a way, have contempt
For those who have an appetite for knowledge:
But noble kings in ancient days
Ordained (as old authors <note>original: "Auctors"</note> say)
That to learn and master the seven sciences,
None should be allowed but only a nobleman;
And at the least, he should be so free
That he might study with liberty;
Therefore, old sages called them
*The seven liberal sciences:*
For he who would learn them perfectly and well
Must live in clear liberty.
He must withdraw from worldly works
Who would learn even man's law;
Much more must he forsake the world
Who would master many sciences.
And for that reason, men may well see
Why knowledgeable men are despised.
Yet noble memory shall never cease
Regarding him who increases knowledge.

<margin>Chapter 2.</margin>
He who loves knowledge, <note>original: "Cunning"; in this context, it refers to wisdom, skill, or specialized knowledge rather than trickery.</note> justice, and grace
Is cast aside in many a place;
But he who brings to Court, with guile,

Are lost and have departed from you all.
And furthermore, remember what I say:
Sin hastens fast toward its final day.
Greed and knowledge are naturally at odds;
He who covets wealth shall not find this *Science*;
But he who loves *Science* for its own sake,
He may acquire both for his blessed mind.
Of this *Chapter* I need teach no more,
For here it appears which men may reach it:
That is, to remember to be only truthful,
And he who is constant in mind to pursue it,
And is not ambitious, and has no need to borrow,
And can be patient, not in a hurry to succeed;
And that he sets his trust fully in *God*,
And all his desire <note>original: "lust"; used here in the archaic sense of a strong desire, passion, or intense interest.</note> be fixed on knowledge;
And with all this, he leads a righteous life,
Subduing falsehood and supporting no sinful strife:
Such men are fit to attain this *Science*.
The chapter following is of joy and pain.

<margin>Chapter 2.</margin>
The first *pain* <note>original: "Paine"; refers here to a hardship or trial</note> is to remember in one's mind,
How many seek and how few actually find,
And yet no man may win <note>attain</note> this *science*,
Unless it is taught to him before he begins.
He is well-learned and of very clear wit <note>intellect</note>,
Who can surely learn it through teaching.
He must be certain of many complexities <note>original: "diversities"</note>,
If he wishes to know the secrets of working **nature**.
Yet teaching may not surely succeed <note>original: "availe"</note>,
But it will sometimes happen that a man fails;
Just as all those who are now dead and gone

One time or another, sooner or later,
All men failed until true **practice** was accomplished <note>original: "paste"</note>.
No man fails sooner in heat and cold <note>referring to laboratory operations</note>,

For no man may ruin <note>original: "spill"</note> our **work** sooner,

But he who shall truly do the deed,

For of all pains, the most grievous pain,

Every man shall have great *pain*,
When he shall first covet and crave this *art*.
He shall often **change** his desire,

It is a great risk <note>original: "adventure"</note> for him to succeed.
So, no matter how eager <note>original: "faine"</note> you are for this *art*,
Yet you must taste many a bitter pain.

Of *pains* <note>original: "Paines"; hardships or trials</note> yet I must show more,

As to beguile <note>deceive</note> you with hastiness;

<summary>Norton warns that the alchemist's progress is threatened by the difficulty of finding a master and by the Devil's traps, particularly the "peril of haste." He argues that rushing the alchemical process is a diabolical impulse that inevitably leads to failure and impurity.</summary>

Therefore, he will often assault
Your mind with haste to make you fail;
He shall find grace in town and country
Who can withstand hastiness at all times.
I say at all times, for in a single moment,
Haste may destroy all your progress <note>original: "engine"; refers to the alchemical apparatus, the process, or the alchemist's ingenuity</note>;
Therefore, avoid and fear all haste
As if she were a *Devil*.
Truly, my wit cannot suffice
To despise haste sufficiently;
Many men have been cast into great sorrow
Because they would not beware of haste,
But always cried out to see an end,
Which is a temptation of the Fiend <note>original: "Fende"; the Devil</note>.
No more of haste at this present time,
But blessed be the Patient person forever.

When the Fiend has no success with *Haste*,
Then he will assault your mind with *Despair*;
And often present this thought to your mind:
How many seek, and how few may find,
Even among men wiser than you ever were—
What certainty can there be for you then?
He will move you to doubt also
Whether your teacher had the knowledge <note>the secret of the Philosopher's Stone</note> or not;
And also how it might so happen
That he taught you part, but not all.
He will cast out such uncertainty
To set your mind with grievous doubt;
And so he will renew your pains
With faint hope <note>original: "wann hope"; despair or waning hope</note> and with much *Despair*.
Against this assault there is no defense
But only the virtue of Confidence,
To which reason should lead you,
So that you shall have no cause to fear;

Think <note>original: "Ween"</note> that it will be accomplished <note>original: "wrought"</note> in forty days.
Now you may see that between forty days of work
And forty days of learning, there is a great difference.

# THE ORDINAL. CHAPTER 3.

Tonfile was a laborer in the fire
Sixty years and more to win his desire;
Brian was another, with Holton in the West,
These were ever busy, and could practice with <margin>the best :</margin>
But yet this science they never found,
For they knew not the materials, nor the foundation,
But rumbled along, and evermore they sought,
They spent their life and their goods for nothing;
Much loss, much cost, much anguish they bought,
Among the recipes <note>original: "receipts"</note> which they had worked:
Then Tonfile made to me his great complaint,
With weeping tears he said his heart was faint,
For he had spent all his vigorous <note>original: "lusty"</note> days
In false recipes, and in such ignorant <note>original: "lewde"</note> attempts;
Of herbs, gums, of roots, and of grass,
Many kinds were tested by him,
Such as <term>Crowfoot</term>, <term>Celandine</term>, and <term>Mezereon</term>,
<term>Vervain</term>, <term>Lunary</term>, and <term>Martagon</term>: <note>These are various plants traditionally used in herbalism and alchemy for their supposed magical or transformative properties.</note>
In antimony, arsenic, honey, wax, and wine,
In hair, in eggs, in dung <note>original: "merds"</note>, and urine,
In quicklime <note>original: "calx vive"</note>, glass-gall <note>original: "sandifer"</note>, and vitriol,
In marcasites, tutty <note>original: "tutits," an impure form of zinc oxide</note>, and every mineral,
In amalgams, in whitening agents <note>original: "blanchers"</note>, and yellowing processes <note>original: "citrinacions," a stage in alchemy where the substance turns yellow</note>,
All fell to nothing in his operations:
For he did not consider how he acted blindly <note>original: "did rage"</note>,
When he added excess <note>original: "surcharge"</note> to God's proportions:
After all this, he thought nothing so good,
To work upon as human blood;
Until I said how blood would waste and smoke
In mighty fire, and be utterly consumed.

"For the love of Christ," he said then, "teach me

"Tonsile," I said, "how would it benefit you
To know such a thing? Your limbs fail you
From very age; therefore, cease your study <note>original: "lay"</note>

"Tonsile," I said, "it is no small thing
Of which you want true news;
For many authors write of this mystery <note>original: "doubte"</note>, 
But none of them show it clearly.
For authors who write of this *Art* 
Besought God (as *Democritus* <note>Democritus of Abdera (c. 460 – c. 370 BC) was an ancient Greek philosopher often cited in alchemical texts as a foundational authority.</note> testifies)
That He would take their souls from this world without pain
After He taught them how to write books about it;
For all such men greatly doubted evermore
That they might write too much of this *science*. 
Each of them taught only one point or two,
By which his fellows were made certain 
That he was a *brother* to them,
For they each understood one another.
Also, they did not write to teach every man,
But to show themselves through a secret speech.
Do not trust, therefore, in the reading of one book,
But you should look into the works of many authors;
'One book opens another' <note>original: "Liber librum aperit"</note> says *Arnold* the great scholar <note>original: "Clerke"; referring to Arnold of Villanova, a famous medieval physician and alchemist.</note>,
*Anaxagoras* <note>An ancient Greek philosopher whose theories on the composition of matter were influential in alchemy.</note> said the same for his work:
Whoever is too lazy to look into many books,
Such a person shall never be quick in the actual practice."

Such as is found between *Male* and *Female*.
These two kinds shall do all your service,
For the *White Work* <note>The albedo, or second stage of the alchemical process, which results in the "White Stone" capable of turning metals into silver.</note> (if you can be wise).
One of these kinds you shall find to be a *Stone*,
For it withstands fire as stones do by nature <note>original: "by kinde"</note>;
But it is no stone to the touch nor in sight,
But a subtle *Earth*, brown, ruddy, and not bright.
And when it is separated and brought to its appearance,
Then we name it our ground *Litharge* <note>A lead oxide mineral, though here used in a specific alchemical sense.</note>.
First it is brown, ruddy, and afterward somewhat white,
And then it is called our chosen *Marcasite* <note>In historical alchemy, "marcasite" referred to various metallic minerals, often bismuth or iron pyrites, believed to contain the "seed" of metals.</note>."

12. Which, if they were not by skill made alive <note>original: "quick"</note>,
And their essence <note>original: "fatness"</note> drawn out with water;

The last secret I will tell to you:
Your water must be sublimated seven times,

That is our *Dragon*, as I tell you,
Fiercely burning as the fire of hell.

Do not stop until it may simmer no more,

For in this work you shall find nothing

# Of Putrefaction.

4. And therefore, as I have said before, when your elements are mixed and wisely equalized, you must maintain a temperate heat, always avoiding their incineration <note>original: incynerat; turned to ash</note> by violent heat—lest they be unprofitably turned into a dry red powder <note>original: Rubyfycate; a premature or incorrect reddening of the matter</note>. Instead, they should become a powder as black as a crow’s bill, using the heat of a water bath <note>original: Balne; a *balneum Mariae*</note> or else our dunghill <note>Decomposing manure was often used by alchemists as a source of gentle, steady heat</note>.

5. Until ninety nights have passed, keep them in moist heat away from anything else. Soon after, you shall perceive by the blackness that they are moving quickly toward putrefaction; after which, through many changing colors, you shall easily and with patience bring them to perfect whiteness. Thus, your "seed" shall multiply according to its nature.

6. Make each one embrace <note>original: hawse</note> and kiss the other, and like children, let them play up and down <note>This likely refers to the "ascent and descent" of vapors during distillation or circulation within a sealed vessel</note>. And when their shirts are soiled with urine <note>original: pysse; a metaphor for the foul-smelling or dark liquid state of the matter</note>, then let the Woman be bound to wash them; she who often, from faintness, will fall into a swoon <note>original: sound</note> and at last die along with all her children, going to Purgatory to purge their original filth.

7. When they are there, little by little increase their pains by applying more and more heat. Never let the fire cease from them, and ensure your furnace is suitable for the task—the kind which wise men call an Athanor <note>A self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a constant temperature for long periods</note>. It maintains the required heat most temperately, by which the water naturally <note>original: kindly</note> putrefies.

Nothing is fully achieved except through Heat and Cold;
Nevertheless, the passive qualities <note>In Aristotelian physics, Heat and Cold are "active" qualities, while Moisture and Dryness are "passive."</note> have some activity,
As you may daily see in craftsmen;
In baking, brewing, and all other crafts,
Moisture is active and so shall dryness be.
*Aristotle* in his *Physics* <note>Aristotle's *Physica*, a foundational text for medieval science</note> and many others more,
Said that knowledge comes from action <note>original: *ab actionibus procedit speculatio*</note>;
They said that practice is the root and beginning
Of theory <note>original: Speculation</note> and of all skill <note>original: Cunning</note>;
For the properties of every thing
Are perceived by how they work;
Just as by the colors of *urines* we may be bold
To give judgment on heat and cold;
By these aforementioned four primary qualities,
We seek colors over a length of time;
Of the white color we are not fully sure
To find it except in a pure substance:
You may now learn great doctrine from this,
When you know how colors develop every day.

Color is the outermost layer of a clear body,
A clear substance well-bounded <note>original: termined; meaning having defined limits or boundaries</note> is its material here;
If heat has mastery in matter that is dry,
*White color is always certainly the result*;
As it appears in the look of burnt <note>original: brent</note> bones,
And in the making of all lime stones.
Where cold works in matter moist and clear,
Yet from such working whiteness will appear:
As it shows in ice and hoary <note>original: hore</note> frost,
The cause of which is set out in philosophy before:
I do not write here of common philosophy,
But by example to teach *Alchemy* <note>original: *Alkimy*</note>;
So that one may be understood by the other,
As the child is understood by the mother.

<margin>Chapter 5.</margin>
If heat works in matter that is moist
And gross <note>Meaning thick, dense, or impure</note> as well, it shall produce **black** color;
If you desire an example of this from me,
Observe what happens when you set green wood on fire.
When cold works in matter that is thick and dry,
**Black** color shall also result; this is the reason why:
Such matter is compacted and made denser
By the constriction of cold, which is the enemy to all things living <note>original: quick; meaning vital or alive</note>.
Density creates darkness through the deprivation of light;
Thus, color is absent <note>original: private; meaning deprived or lacking</note>, appearing **black** to the sight.
Therefore, always remember this:
Clear matter is the material of **whiteness**.
The efficient cause <note>The primary source of change or action in Aristotelian science</note> may be manifold;
For sometimes it is heat, and sometimes it is cold.
But **white** and **black**, as all people may see,
Are contrary colors at the furthest extremes;
Therefore, your work must begin with **black**
If you wish to win **whiteness** in the end.

The middle color, as *philosophers* write,
Is *red* color, located between **black** and **white**;
Nevertheless, trust me certainly,
*Red* is the last stage in the work of *alchemy*.
They also say in their **doctrine**
That these two colors, *rufous* <note>original: Rufe; a brownish-red or rust color</note> and *citrine* <note>A lemon-yellow color</note>,
Are intermediate colors between **white** and *red*;
And they say that **green**, and a color pale as lead,
Are intermediate colors between *red* and **black**,
And the freshest color comes from the purest matter.

*Physicians* recognize nineteen colors in *urines* <note>Alchemists often used the color charts developed by doctors for diagnosing illness through urine to describe the stages of their chemical reactions</note>,
Between **white** and **black**, as they believe;
One of these is the "whitish" color, *subalbidus* <note>original Latin: subalbidus; meaning somewhat white or off-white</note>,
Similar in color to the *onyx* stone.
*Magnesia* <note>original: Magnetia; an alchemical term for a primary mineral substance, not necessarily modern magnesium</note> is found to be of a similar color,
But *Magnesia* glitters with clarity.

In which three rest all that **God** created:
For **God** made all things and established them securely,

In Number, Weight <note>original: "Ponder"</note>, and in Measure—

Therefore **Anaxagoras** <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BC) was a Pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who argued that all things existed in some part in all things</note> said, "Take good heed

Until you know the weights in full completeness
Of all the components which should meet therein."
**Bacon** <note>Roger Bacon (c. 1220–1292), an English philosopher and Franciscan friar renowned for his work in alchemy and science</note> said that the old masters hid nothing
Except for **Proportion**, in which there was no guide;
For no ancient author, king, prince, or lord,
Writing of this science, agreed with any other
In the proportions. But if you wish to achieve them,
**Raymond** <note>Ramon Lull (c. 1232–1316)</note>, with **Bacon** and **Albert** <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), a German Dominican friar and bishop who wrote extensively on the natural sciences</note>, teach it.

Have perfect knowledge—though you will not have it all from just one.

Such as Water and Earth, according to your desire,
Well-compounded with Air and Fire.
Know the worthiest in its activity,
The second, the third—each in its degree;
The fourth and the lowliest <note>original: "vilest"</note> may not be refused,
For it is profitable and best to be used.
And it may best extend its **Multiplication** <term>Multiplication: the process of increasing the quantity or the transmutative power of the Alchemical Stone</term>,

And that is the earthly **litharge** <term>litharge: lead oxide, but here used symbolically for the solid, "earthy" foundation of the Alchemical Stone</term> of our Stone;
Without it, there shall be no generation,

For nothing is fixed but Earth alone.
All other elements are movable—
Fire, Air, and Water, as you see daily.
But Fire is the cause of **extendibility** <term>extendibility: the ability of the substance to spread or penetrate through other matter</term>,
And causes matters to be **mixable** <term>permiscible: capable of being thoroughly mixed or blended</term>,
And creates clear brightness in fair colors.

During all that season, they have more obedience
To the influence of the stars than to their own formed natures.
And the science of **Optics** <note>original: "Perspective"; in the Middle Ages and Renaissance, this referred to the study of light, sight, and the laws of reflection and refraction</note> gives great evidence

<margin>Chapter 5.</margin>
When the four elements are wisely joined,
And each one of them is set in its proper degree,
Then, from various degrees and various **maturation** <note>original: "digestion"; in alchemy, the process of slow heating to ripen or transform a substance</note>,
Colors will arise toward perfection.
For then the inward natural heat works,
Which in our substance is only **subtle** <note>original: "Intellectual"; meaning a non-physical or spiritual quality perceived by the mind rather than the senses</note>:
It is unknown to the sight, and the hand may not feel it;
Its working is known to few men, and even then, seldom.
And when this natural heat is activated
By our outward artificial heat,
Then Nature, stimulated to labor, will not cease
To increase many various stages.
Which is one reason you may see
Why there are so many colors in our work:
Therefore, in this **Art**, great uncertainty is caused by
Ignorance of the heat both within and without—
To know how these two heats should harmonize,
And which of them should be the master in the work.

**Maturation** <note>original: "Digestion"</note> in this work has a great likeness
To the digestion in living things:
And above others (as I can witness),
It is most like the digestion of a human being.

**Physicians** say of good and sweet <note>original: "soote"</note> herbs,

->### Of your principal Agent truly to discern.###<-

As White and Black are colors at the extremes,
So it is with odors: sweet and stinking.
But just as fish do not know by sight
Any intermediate <term>Intermediate: The original word "meane" refers to the middle or average state between two extremes.</term> colors, because their bright eyes
Have no eyelids for closing their sight,
So intermediate odors shall not, through smelling,
Be known by you; this is the reason why:
For nostrils are as open as the fish's eye.
Therefore, intermediate odors are not certainly
Smelled by the nose, as intermediate colors are seen.
A heavy smell is not, as scholars think,
The middle odor, but only a lesser stink.
The old Fathers wrote by their doctrine,
From their experience which is mature <note>original: "maturine"—meaning ripened, well-developed, or based on long experience.</note>,
That if you mix sweet and fragrant <note>original: "redolent"</note> scents
Equally with stinking ones to test your intent;
The sweet <note>original: "soote"</note> shall be smelled, but the stinking not so.
The cause you may learn now before you go:
All sweet-smelling things have more purity,
And are more spiritual than stinking things can be.
Therefore, sweetness is more penetrative in the air,
And is more extendable, and is also to life
More acceptable, as a friend to Nature,
And therefore more readily received, you can be sure.

**Odor** is a smoky vapor released by heat,
Out of a substance, by an invisible sweat;
Which has free entry into the air,
And changes the air and your smelling;
Just as the flavor <note>original: "Sapor"</note> of foods changes your tasting,
And as sounds change your hearing,
And as color changes your sight,
So odor changes smelling by its power.

To know the cause of odors, if you so desire,
Four things are required for them:
First, that subtle matter must be responsive
To the action of heat, so as to present—
By a vapor—the likeness of the very thing
From which that vapor originated.
Also, to carry that pure and beautiful vapor,
Clear and thin air is required;
For thick air will not carry it far,
But will instead trap it much more tightly.
And similarly, dense matter is not responsive
To the action of heat, as is seen in stone.
Heat creates odors, while cold contracts them; for this reason,
Dunghills in summer stink more than in the winter season.
Pleasant odors shall be created
From clean and pure substances that can be vaporized <note>original: "fumigale"—meaning capable of being turned into a fume or vapor.</note>,
As is seen in amber, nard <note>original: "Narde"—an aromatic oil (spikenard) derived from a Himalayan plant.</note>, and myrrh;
These are good for a woman; such things please her.
But from a pure substance with moderate <term>Moderate: original "Meane"—referring to the middle point between two extremes of temperature.</term> heat,
Mild odors are produced, as in the violet.
From moderate heat acting on an impure substance,
Unpleasant odors arise, such as aloes and sulfur.
But when natural heat begins to fail <note>original: "spill"—in this context meaning to waste away, perish, or lose its vital force.</note>,
Then a heavy smell arises from it;
Just as fish smells when it is kept too long,
Natural heat causes rot, so the smell is strong.

**Stench** is a vapor, a dissolved smokiness
Of things that have bad compositions <term>Complexions: In medieval science, "complexion" referred to the specific balance of the four humors or qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) within a substance.</term>.
And when only the moisture <note>original: "Humor"</note> is corrupt,
So that the substance itself is not destroyed,
Only a heavy smell will arise from it,
But a true stench does not come about in that way.
Of every stench, the cause of that occurrence—
