# Of Putrefaction.

## *The Fifth Gate.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Now begins the chapter on Putrefaction <term>Putrefaction: in alchemy, a stage of "rotting" or breakdown where the matter turns black (the *nigredo*), believed to be essential for spiritual and physical rebirth.</term>,
Without which foundation <note>original: "Pole"; referring to the North Star or a guiding principle.</note> no seed may multiply.
This must be done only by the continual action
Of heat in the body—moist heat, not by hand <note>original: "not manually"; meaning the change happens through the internal chemistry of heat rather than physical manipulation.</note>,
<margin>Wheat</margin>
For otherwise, bodies cannot be naturally altered:
Since Christ witnesses to it: unless the grain of wheat
Dies in the ground, you cannot gain an increase <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 12:24: "Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit."</note>.

<margin>2.</margin>
And likewise, unless your matter putrefies,
It can in no way truly be altered,
Nor can your elements be naturally <note>original: "kyndly"</note> divided,
Nor can your *conjunction* <term>Conjunction: the alchemical union of the elements, often symbolized as a marriage.</term> of them be perfectly celebrated.
So that your labor is not frustrated,
Understand the secret <note>original: "prevyte"</note> of putrefying well
Before you ever take this work in hand.

<margin>3.</margin>
And *putrefaction* may be defined in this way,
According to the sayings of philosophers: it is the slaying <note>original: "fleyng"; meaning the "killing" or breaking down of the physical form.</note> of bodies.
In our "Compound" <term>Compound: the specific mixture of substances being transformed into the Philosopher's Stone.</term>, it is a division of three things:
Leading the "killed" bodies into corruption,
And afterward making them capable of regeneration;
For things existing in the Earth, without doubt,
Are engendered by the rotation of the heavens above <note>Alchemists believed that the movements of the celestial spheres influenced the growth and decay of minerals and life on Earth.</note>.

<summary>This page introduces Putrefaction, the fifth stage of the alchemical process, explaining that matter must "die" and decay (like a seed in the ground) before it can be transformed and multiplied. The author emphasizes that this breakdown is a natural process driven by heat and celestial influence rather than manual labor.</summary>

<keywords>Putrefaction, Fifth Gate, Nigredo, Regeneration, Alchemical Compound, Seed of Wheat, Celestial Influence</keywords>

# Of Putrefaction

<margin>4.</margin>
And therefore, as I have said before,
Once your elements are mixed and wisely made equal <note>original: "coequat"; balanced in proportion or quality</note>,
Maintain them in a temperate <note>original: "intemperat"; likely a printer's error for "in temperate" or "temperate," given the instruction to avoid extreme heat</note> heat, always avoiding 
The possibility that they might be incinerated <note>original: "incynerat"; reduced to ash</note> by violent heat,
Or unprofitably turned into a dry red powder <note>original: "Rubyfycate"</note>;
Instead, they should turn into a powder as black as a crow's bill,
Using the heat of a bath <note>original: "Balne"; referring to a *balneum Mariae* or water bath</note>, or else of our dunghill <note>original: "Dounghyll"; decomposing manure used by alchemists as a source of steady, gentle heat</note>.

<margin>5.</margin>
Until ninety nights have passed,
Keep them in moist heat, away from anything else;
Soon after, you shall see by the blackness
That they are quickly moving toward putrefaction.
After this, you shall lead the matter through many colors
To perfect whiteness, easily and with patience,
And so your "seed" shall multiply in its own nature.

<margin>6.</margin>
Make each element embrace <note>original: "hawse"</note> and kiss the other,
And like children, let them play up and down;
And when their shirts are soiled with urine <note>original: "pysse"</note>,
Then the woman must be bound to wash them—
She who will often fall into a swoon <note>original: "found"</note> from exhaustion,
And at last die along with all her children,
Going to Purgatory to purge their original filth <note>This stanza uses the common alchemical allegory of the "chemical wedding" and "death" of the matter to describe the process of dissolution and the cleaning of impurities during the stage of Nigredo, or blackness</note>.

<margin>7.</margin>
When they are there, increase their pains 
Little by little with more and more heat;
Never let the fire cease from them,
And see that your furnace is suitable for this task—
The one which wise men call an *Athanor* <note>original: "Athenor"; from the Arabic *al-tannūr*, a self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a constant, steady temperature for long periods</note>.
This furnace conserves the required heat most temperately,
By which the water naturally <note>original: "kyndly"; according to its kind or nature</note> putrefies.

<summary>This page describes the alchemical stage of Putrefaction, emphasizing the need for gentle, steady heat to turn the mixture black (Nigredo) before it can be purified into whiteness. The process is illustrated through metaphors of death, washing, and purgatory.</summary>

# Of Putrefaction

<margin>8.</margin> Of this principle speaks the wise <note>original: "Sapyent"</note> Guido <note>likely Guido de Montanor, an alchemical authority</note>,
And says that by rotting, the physical compound dies;
And then, according to Morienus <note>original: "Moryen"; a 7th-century legendary alchemist</note> and others,
It rises again—regenerated, simple, and spiritual.
And if heat and moisture were not continuous,
->Sperm could not remain within the womb,<-
->And so no fruit would grow from it.<-

---

<margin>9.</margin> Therefore, at the beginning, take our "Stones" <note>the primary alchemical materials</note>,
And bury each one with the other within their "Grave" <note>the alchemical vessel or crucible</note>;
Then create an equal marriage between them
To lie together for six weeks; then let them have
Their seed conceived to naturally <note>original: "kyndly"</note> nourish and save;
->Not rising from the bottom of their grave during that time,<-
->Which secret point deceives many a person.<-

---

<margin>10.</margin> Wait for this time of conception with gentle heat;
The appearing blackness shall tell you when they die.
For at that time, they—like liquid pitch—
Shall swell and bubble, settle, and putrefy;
Then you shall see shining colors within,
->Like a rainbow, marvelous to the sight;<-
->The water then begins to dry up completely.<-

---

<margin>11.</margin> For in moist bodies, a temperate, nourishing heat
Engenders blackness first of all, which is 
The assigned sign <note>original: "tokyn affygnate"</note> of a natural mixing <note>original: "Commyxyon"</note>;
And remember this regarding true putrefying:
For then you cannot fail to transform it perfectly.
->And thus you must enter through the Gate of Blackness,<-
->If you wish to reach the light of Paradise in Whiteness.<-

<margin>12.</margin>
For first the Sun in his rising shall be darkened <note>original: "obscurate"</note>,

The heart of an oak that is constantly soaked in water

For though it lies in water for a hundred years or more,
Yet you would find it as sound as it ever was before.

# Of Putrefaction.

<margin>16.</margin>
If you keep wood sometimes wet and sometimes dry,
As you may see in timber through common experience,
In the process of time that oak shall utterly rot <note>original: "Putrefy"</note>:
And in the same way, according to our intention,
Sometimes our Tree must be burned by the Sun <note>The "Sun" refers to the heat of the furnace; the "Tree" refers to the growing alchemical matter.</note>:
And then with Water soon after we must cool <note>original: "kele"</note> it,
So that by these means you shall bring it to rot
well.

<margin>17.</margin>
For being now in wet and then again in dry,
Now in great heat and now again in cold,
Shall cause it soon to rot:
And so you shall bring your Gold to rotting.
Treat <note>original: "Entrete"</note> your bodies, therefore, as I have told you:
And in your putrefying, do not be so swift with heat,
Lest you have to search through the ashes for your lost profit <note>original: "thryft"; meaning the work is ruined by too much heat, leaving only worthless ash.</note>.

<margin>18.</margin>
Therefore, draw your water out of the earth,
And make the soul <note>The "soul" refers to the volatile spirit or gas that rises during heating.</note> ascend with it;
Then throw it down again into the earth,
Letting them often ascend and descend.
Defend your glass vessel from violent heat and sudden cold,
And make your fire so temperate
That your Water is never turned to glass <note>original: "vytryfycate"</note> against the sides.

<margin>19.</margin>
And be wise in choosing your water;
Meddle with no salt, sulfur, nor low-grade <note>original: "mene"</note> mineral,
No matter what anyone prattles <note>original: "clatter"</note> to you about any water;
Our Sulfur and Mercury are only found in Metal,
Which some men call "Oils" and "Waters":
Also "fowls" and "birds" and many other names,
Because fools should never know the secret of our Stone.

"Drink on," says another, "the method is found;
I am a Master of that Art <note>Referring to alchemy</note>,
I guarantee us we shall have a part."

<margin>37.</margin>
Such talk causes the monks then to do evil,
To waste their wages through their foolishness <note>original: "dotage"; a state of weak-mindedness or infatuation</note>;
Some bring a wooden bowl <term>original: "Mazer"; a traditional drinking bowl, often highly decorated or made of expensive wood</term> and some bring a spoon;
There, the *Philosophers* give them such encouragement,
Promising them <note>original: "Behotyng"</note> profit without any loss:
At least a pound back for every penny spent,
And so fair promises make fools glad <note>original: "fayne"</note>.

<margin>38.</margin>
A Royal Medicine <note>The alchemical elixir or "Philosopher's Stone" believed to transform base metals into gold</note> at a ratio of one to twelve,
They promise them that they shall have;
Which they themselves could never
Yet bring about, as God may save me:
Beware such *Philosophers*—let no man disparage <note>original: "deprave"</note> them:
Who "help" these monks to such "riches"
That they go about in threadbare cowls <note>term: Cowl; the hooded habit worn by a monk</note>.

<margin>39.</margin>
The *Abbot* ought to cherish this company well,
For they can teach his monks to live in poverty,
And to go clothed and monied religiously,
As did *Saint Benedict* <note>original: "Seynt Benet"; the 6th-century founder of Western monasticism whose "Rule" emphasizes poverty and simplicity</note>, avoiding excess <note>original: "superfluyte"</note>,
Easing them also of the heavy weight <note>original: "ponderosyte"</note>
Of their purses, which are so weighed down with pounds,
But which by *Philosophy* are now lightened <note>original: "allevyat"</note>.

# ON CONGELATION.

## *The Sixth Gate.*

<margin>1.</margin> I do not need to write much about *Congelation* <term>Congelacyon</term>, but I will first declare what it is now: it is the hardening <term>Induracyon</term> of soft things into a white color, and the solidification <term>confyxacyon</term> of spirits which are volatile <note>original: "fleyng"; referring to substances that easily evaporate or escape during heating</note>. You do not need to worry much about how to congeal, for the elements will soon knit together, provided that *Putrefaction* has been properly <note>original: "kyndly"; meaning according to its natural kind or proper method</note> performed.

<margin>2.</margin> But *congelations* are made in various ways: spirits and bodies dissolved into clear water, or salts dissolved once or twice and then congealed into a fusible <note>original: "fluxyble"; capable of being melted</note> matter. Fools chatter about such *congealing*. Some also dissolve by manually dividing the elements, afterward congealing them into a dry powder.

<margin>3.</margin> But such *congealing* is not what we desire, for it is contrary to ours. Our *Congelation* does not fear the fire, for it must always remain unctuous <term>unctuos</term> <note>oily, greasy, or resinous in texture; a quality desired to prevent the stone from being brittle</note> within it. It must also be very abundant in its tincture <term>Tincture</term> <note>the coloring or transforming essence of the Stone</note>. Once congealed, it will not dissolve <note>original: "relent"</note> back into water when exposed to the air; if it did, our work would be ruined <term>shent</term>.

<summary>This page introduces Congelation, the sixth stage of the alchemical Great Work, defining it as the solidification of volatile spirits into a stable, white, and unctuous substance. The author distinguishes his "true" congelation from the ineffective methods used by "fools," emphasizing that the final product must resist dissolving when exposed to air.</summary>
<keywords>Congelation, sixth gate, induration, spirits, unctuous, tincture, alchemical process, George Ripley</keywords>

--- Page 186 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the sixth gate, Congelation. The author provides specific instructions on the physical properties the substance should exhibit during this stage, distinguishing true alchemical congelation from common or "vulgar" chemical processes.</meta>

<page-num>162</page-num>

<margin>4.</margin> Moreover, do not congeal it into a stone as hard as glass or crystal which melts only through fusion <term>fusyon</term> <note>original: "fusyon"; melting through the application of high heat</note>; but rather so that it will melt instantly like wax, without a forced blast of air <note>original: "wythouten blast"; refers to the use of bellows to reach high temperatures</note. Beware of delusion, for that kind of congealing does not belong to our objective <term>Conclusyon</term>—that which will not flow and run back into water, like congealed salts, means you labor in vain.

<margin>5.</margin> Such common congelation <term>Congelacyon</term> is of no use to us at all; it belongs to the "Multipliers" <note>original: "Multyplyers"; a derogatory term for amateur alchemists or charlatans who attempted to increase the quantity of precious metals through deceptive or purely physical means</note> who congeal substances in a common <term>vulgarly</term> way. Therefore, if you wish to succeed (since your Medicine shall never flow naturally, nor congeal, unless you first putrefy <term>Putrefye</term> it), first purge and fix the elements of our Stone until they congeal and flow together instantly.

<margin>6.</margin> For when the matter is made perfectly **White**, then your Spirit <term>Spryte</term> shall be congealed with the Body. But you must wait a long time before it appears congealed like pearls to you; be glad to see such a congelation! And afterward, it will appear like grains as red as blood—richer than any worldly treasure.

<margin>7.</margin> The earthly grossness <term>Grosnes</term> must therefore first be mortified <term>mortyfyed</term> <note>the alchemical "killing" or breakdown of the substance's physical form during putrefaction</note> in moisture, and then blackness is engendered. This principle cannot be denied, for the natural *Philosophers* <note>original: "Phylofophers"; referring to the "Adepts" or masters of alchemy</note> say as much. Once that is achieved, you cannot fail to reach Whiteness. And if you congeal it into **Whiteness** once, you have a Stone more precious than all other stones.

# Of Congelation

8. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Just as the **Dry** caused the **Moist** to putrefy—which caused the color black to appear—so too does the **Moist**, when congealed by the **Dry**, produce a shining **Whiteness** with great clarity. Dryness proceeds as it whitens the matter:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Just as moisture shows itself during the "blackening" stage,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;It does so through various colors that are constantly changing.

9. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The cause of all this is a most temperate heat, which works and moves the matter continually. Through this, the matter is substantially altered, both inwardly and outwardly—not superficially to the eye as the fools do. Instead, every part must be made to endure the fire, being both capable of flowing <term>fluxibly</term> and stable in its color <term>tyncture</term> <note>original: "tyncture"; the medicinal or transforming power of the Stone, often associated with its color</note>.

10. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And medicine <term>Phyfycke</term> <note>original: "Phyfycke"; here referring to the study of natural physics or the biological processes of the body</note> describes each type of digestion. The first occurs in the stomach, where there is dryness, which undoubtedly causes whiteness. Similarly, the second digestion, completed in the liver by temperate heat, results in redness. Thus, our Stone is digested by dryness and heat until it is perfectly **White** and **Red**.

11. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;But here you must learn another secret: how the "Philosophers' Child" <note>a symbolic name for the Alchemical Stone or the perfected Medicine</note> is born in the air. Do not be too eager to blow on the coals too fast—take this neither as a joke nor as an insult—but trust me truly, or else your work is entirely lost. Unless your Earth is revived with Water, you shall never see our true Congealing.

<margin>16.</margin> And truly, that is the principal cause why *philosophers* charged us to be patient until the time the water was dried entirely to powder, with nourishing heat that is continuous but not violent. For the qualities of every element are contrary until, after the **Black** stage, a union is made in the **White** stage <note>In alchemy, the "Nigredo" (Blackness) must precede the "Albedo" (Whiteness) to achieve the first level of perfection.</note>, and then it is forever congealed without division.

<margin>17.</margin> Furthermore, the preparation of this conversion from thing to thing, and from one state to another, is done only by the natural <note>original: "kindly"</note> and discreet operation of Nature, just as it is with sperm within the mother. For sperm and heat are like sister and brother, which are converted within themselves (as Nature knows how to do) by action and passion <note>In traditional philosophy, "action and passion" refer to the active force acting upon a passive substance.</note>, until at last they become a perfect man.

<margin>18.</margin> For just as the bodily part, which is perfected into a man by Nature, is the same as its beginning was—and though it was thus altered from thing to thing, it did not go out of its kind <note>original: "kynd"; meaning its species or natural essence</note> to mingle with other kinds—so our spermatic matter within one glass must turn within itself from thing to thing,

<margin>19.</margin> I may tell you another natural example: how the substance of an egg is wrought by nature into a chick without passing out of the shell. Only keep this in mind.

Through heat and moisture by natural operation;
And therefore minerals are nourished by the administration
    Of radical moisture <note>original: "Moysture radycall"; the essential, life-giving fluid thought to be the basis of all matter</note>, which was their beginning,

And so the sperm is altered within its own nature,
    Able to multiply its own kind after its likeness,
    Just as all other things do naturally within their kind.

While the conceived sperm is growing,
The substance is nourished by its own menstrual fluid <note>original: "Menstruall"; in alchemy, the "menstruum" is the solvent or "blood" that nourishes the growing philosophical child or stone</note>,
Which only water brought out of the earth,

# Of Congelation

<margin>24.</margin> The said menstrual fluid <note>original: "Menstrue"; in alchemy, a solvent or nourishing substance that dissolves and feeds the "seed" of the stone</note> is (I tell you in confidence)
The blood of our *Green Lion* <note>original: "Grene Lyon"; a term often referring to raw mineral ores or specialized solvents, such as vitriol or antimony</note>, and not of *Vitriol*.
Dame *Venus* <note>the alchemical name for copper</note> can tell you the truth of this,
If you call her to counsel at your beginning.
This secret is hidden by *Philosophers* great and small;
Which blood, drawn out of the said *Lion*,
Had not achieved perfect *digestion* <note>original: "Dygestyon"; the process of maturing a substance through gentle, continuous heat</note> for lack of heat.

<margin>25.</margin> But this blood, our secret menstrual fluid,
With which our sperm is nourished temperately,
When it is turned into the physical dregs <note>original: "fecys Corporall"; the solid matter or residue remaining after a chemical process</note>,
And becomes perfectly white and very dry,
Congealed and fixed into its own body;
Then to the sight it may well seem like bruised blood <note>original: "brustyn blod"; likely referring to the dark, thickened appearance of the substance before it whitens</note>,
Resulting from this work named the *milk-white Diadem*.

<margin>26.</margin> Understand now that our fiery water, thus sharpened <note>original: "acuate"; increased in power or acidity</note>,
Is called our menstrual water, wherein
Our earth is dissolved <note>original: "losyd"</note> and naturally calcined <note>original: "Calcenat"; reduced to a powder through heat</note>
By *Congelation* so that they may never separate <note>original: "twyne"</note>.
Yet you must not cease <note>original: "blyn"</note> to congeal more water:
Use three parts of the sharpened water mentioned before,
With the fourth part of the congealed earth, and no more.

<margin>27.</margin> Therefore, to that substance so congealed,
Add the fourth part of crystalline water,
And then make them to be joined together <note>original: "Dysponsat"; from the Latin *desponsatus*, meaning betrothed or married in a chemical union</note>
By *Congelation* into a metallic mineral,
Which will then shine like a newly polished <note>original: "slypyd"</note> sword.
After the blackness which will first appear,
Give them the fourth part of new water.

<margin>28.</margin> We must still perform many more imbibitions <note>original: "Inbybycyons"; the process of adding liquid to a solid to nourish or saturate it</note>;
Give it the second, and then the third also,
Keep the said proportion well in your mind;
Then proceed to the fourth time,
And do not stop at the fifth or sixth time:
->But add two parts at each of those three times,<-
->And at the seventh time, let there be five parts.<-

<margin>29.</margin> When you have performed imbibition seven times in this way,
You must then turn your *Wheel* <note>original: "Whele"; the cycle of alchemical processes, often referring to the repeated distillation or circulation of matter</note> again,
And putrefy <note>original: "Putrefy"; the breaking down of matter through heat and moisture, often the first step in a new stage of the work</note> all that matter without adding anything else:
Wait for the first stage of blackness if you wish to succeed,
Then congeal it entirely into whiteness,
->And through redness, ascend into the South <note>in alchemy, the 'South' represents the highest degree of heat and the final 'Red' stage of the Great Work</note>,<-
->Then you have brought your base to an end.<-

<margin>30.</margin> In this way, your water is divided into two parts:
The bodies are putrefied <note>original: "Putryfycat"</note> with the first part,
And the second part must go toward your imbibitions,
By which the matter is afterward blackened <note>original: "Denygrat"; from the Latin 'denigrate', meaning to turn black</note>,
And soon after, it is whitened <note>original: "Albyfycate"; from the Latin 'albify', meaning to turn white</note> by gentle boiling <note>original: "Decoccyon"; the process of heating or boiling a substance in a liquid</note>:
->Then it is named by the *Philosophers* our *Starry Stone* <note>original: "Sterry Stone"; a stage where the matter begins to glitter or show crystalline structures</note>,<-
->Bring that to redness, and then the sixth Gate is won.<-

# Of Cibation <note>original: "Cibacion"; the process of "feeding" the alchemical material with liquid to increase its substance and prepare it for further stages</note>.

## The Seventh Gate.

<margin>1.</margin> Now I turn my pen to write of Cibation,
Since it must occupy the seventh place here;
But I will explain it quickly in few words;
Pay attention to it, and understand me wisely;
Cibation is called a feeding of our dry Matter
->With Milk and Meat, which they do moderately,<-
->Until it is brought to the third order.<-

<margin>2.</margin> But do not give it so much that you glut <note>original: "glut"; to overfeed or saturate to the point of ruining the substance</note> it,
Beware of the Dropsy <note>original: "Dropsy"; a historical term for edema or the swelling caused by excess fluid</note>, and also of Noah’s Flood;
Therefore, add to it little by little
Food and Drink as seems to do it good,
So that watery humors <note>original: "humors"; the various fluids within the alchemical vessel</note> do not overwhelm the blood:
->Therefore, let the Drink be measured so,<-
->That you never quench its natural appetite.<-

<margin>3.</margin> For if it drinks too much, then it must have
A Vomit <note>original: "Vomyte"; in an alchemical context, a process to remove or evaporate excess moisture</note>, otherwise it will be sick for too long;
Therefore, save your Womb <note>original: "Wombe"; the alchemical vessel or furnace where the matter gestates</note> from the Dropsy,
And from the Flux <note>original: "Flux"; an excessive or unnatural flow of liquid</note>, or else it will go wrong;
Instead, let it occasionally thirst for drink:
->Rather than giving it too much at once,<-
->Because in its youth it must be dieted for this purpose <note>original: "for the nons" (for the nonce); for the specific occasion or purpose</note>.<-

# OF SUBLIMATION.

## *The eighth Gate.*

<margin>1.</margin> Here I have a word or two to speak concerning our **Sublimation** <note>original: "Sublimacion"; the alchemical process of purifying a substance by heating it into vapor and then condensing it back into a solid</note>, which is the eighth Gate. Fools perform **sublimation**, but do not sublimate as they do; for we certainly <note>original: "I wys"</note> do not sublimate like them. Therefore, you shall not fail to sublimate truly if you can first make your bodies spiritual, and then make your spirits physical <note>original: "corporall"; meaning to fix volatile substances into a solid state</note> as I have taught you.

<margin>2.</margin> Some sublimate *mercury* from *vitriol* <note>original: "Vitriall"; sulfuric acid or sulfate minerals</note> and *salt*, and other spirits from scales of iron or steel, from <term>calcined</term> <note>original: "calcynyd"; reduced to a powder by roasting or burning</note> eggshells and quicklime. In their own way, they sublimate quite well; however, such sublimation does not accord at all <note>original: "never adele"</note> with our intent, for we do not sublimate in that manner. Therefore, I will now proceed to true sublimation.

<margin>3.</margin> In **sublimation**, first beware of one thing: that you do not sublimate to the very top of your vessel. For you shall not be able to bring it back down again without violence <note>meaning harsh force or breaking the vessel</note>, but it will instead remain and dwell there. I tell you, it rejoices in cooling <note>original: "refrygeracion"</note>. Therefore, keep it down with temperate heat for a full forty days, until it becomes black on top.

<summary>This page introduces the "Eighth Gate" of alchemy, Sublimation, distinguishing between the common chemical methods used by "fools" and the true philosophical method. Ripley warns the practitioner to keep the material at the bottom of the vessel using temperate heat to ensure it turns black, rather than letting it rise too high.</summary>

# OF FERMENTATION.
## *The ninth Gate.*

<margin>1.</margin>
Few workers understand true **fermentation**,
Therefore I will expound that secret to you;
I traveled truly through many a land
Before I could find anyone who could tell it to me;
Yet as God willed (evermore blessed may He be),
At last I came to perfect knowledge of it;
Take heed, therefore, to what I write of it.

<margin>2.</margin>
**Fermenting** is done in various ways,
By which our medicines must be made permanent <note>original: "perpetuate"; rendered stable and lasting</note>;
Some dissolve **Sun** and **Moon** <note>original: "Son and Mone"; alchemical terms for Gold and Silver</note> into a clear water,
And with their medicines make them congeal <note>original: "Congelate"; to solidify or thicken</note>;
Which, when they are examined in the fire,
May not remain nor change completely <note>original: "Complement"; with full perfection</note>,
For such **ferments** are not our intention.

# Of Fermentation.

<margin>11.</margin> But true *Fermentation*, as I tell you,
Is the incorporation of the Soul with the Body,
Restoring to it the natural <note>original: "kyndly"; meaning natural or according to its kind</note> smell,
With taste and color by the natural union <note>original: "conspyfacyon" (conspiration); here meaning a "breathing together" or harmonious blending of elements</note>

<margin>12.</margin> For just as bodies in their physical density <note>original: "compaccyon corporall"</note>

Unless they are first fixed <note>original: "confyxat"; made stable or non-volatile</note> with them in the right proportion.
For then the Body teaches the Spirit to endure the fire,
And the Spirit teaches the Body to endure according to your desire.

<margin>13.</margin> Therefore, you must ferment your Gold with Gold—

Draws iron <note>original: "Yern"</note> to itself, so our Earth by its nature

Make elements run together with elements,

In this way, our *Fermentation* must be done.

   So into air your water [shall turn], as I tell you;
   When heat has gained dominance over cold,
   It shall be converted by the craft of circulation <term>circulation</term> <note>the process of continuous distillation in a closed vessel, where vapors rise, condense, and fall back down, mimicking natural weather cycles</note>.

6. And from the fire you shall then have air,
   By loosening, putrefying, and subliming;
   And you have fire from the material earth:
   Thus separating <note>original: "dyſſeveryng"</note> your elements by craft,
   Especially calcining <note>original: "Calcenyng"; reducing a substance to a fine powder through heat</note> the earth well:
   And when they are each made pure,
   Then they all possess the fifth nature <note>The "quintessence" which transcends the four physical elements</note>.

This transformation is achieved through "circulation," a process of continuous heating and cooling that purifies the "body" and "soul" of the medicine.</summary>

# Of Exaltation.

7. In this way, therefore, make them circulate <term>circulate</term> <note>original: "Cyrculat"; the process of rotating or recycling substances through different states</note>,
Exalting each into the other one by one,
And in one glass vessel surely seal <term>seal</term> <note>original: "sygylate"; from the Latin *sigillum*, to hermetically seal a flask</note> all of this,
Not with your hands, but naturally as I teach you:
First, firmly turn Fire into Water;
    For Fire is in Air, which is present in Water,
    And this conversion aligns with our intention.

8. Then, furthermore, turn your wheel,
So that your Air is converted into Earth,
Which will also be done very well:
For Air is in Water, which is in the Earth, trust me;
Then turn Water into Fire, which are contrary in their quality:
    You may soon turn them, for Water is in Earth,
    Which is in the conversion of Fire; this is true.

9. Your wheel is now nearly turned all the way around;
Turn Earth into Air, which is the proper nest
Of other elements, there is no doubt,
For Earth is in Fire, which takes its rest in Air.
You must begin this circulation in the West:
    Then forward into the South until they are exalted;
    Proceed duly as I have taught you in the diagram <note>original: "Fygure"</note>.

10. In which process you may clearly see
How you may not go from one extreme to another,
But only by a medium <term>mean</term> <note>original: "mene"; an intermediate substance or state that links two opposites</note>, since they are contrary in quality;
And reason truly dictates that it be so,
As with heat into cold and other opposites:
    Without their mediums—such as moisture between heat and cold—
    I have already given sufficient examples of this.

# OF MULTIPLICATION.

## The eleventh Gate.

<margin>1.</margin>
I now proceed to declare *multiplication* <note>original: "Multyplycacyon"</note>,
Which is defined by the *philosophers* <note>original: "Phylosophers"</note> in this way:
It is indeed the augmentation <term>increase</term> <note>original: "Augmentacyon"</note> of that *elixir* <note>original: "Elixer"</note>,
In quality and quantity, for both the White and the Red <note>The "White" and "Red" refer to the two grades of the Philosopher's Stone: one for transmuting metals into silver, the other into gold</note>.
*Multiplication* is therefore, as they have said: <margin>(degree)</margin>
That thing which increases the medicines in every degree,
In color, in scent, in power <term>virtue</term> <note>original: "Vertue"</note>, and also in quantity.

<margin>2.</margin>

As musk in perfumes <term>aromatics</term> <note>original: "Pygments"; here referring to aromatic mixtures or spiced wines rather than paint</note> and other various spices

# OF PROJECTION.
## The twelfth Gate.

1. **IN** *Projection* it shall be proved if our practice be profitable <note>original: "profy-"; likely "profitable" based on the rhyme with "variable" and "table" in the margin</note>,
<margin>table</margin>Of which it behooves me to reveal the secrets here;
Therefore if your *Tincture* is sure and not variable,
By a little of your *Medicine* you shall thus prove it:
With metal or with Mercury, it will stick like pitch <note>original: "cleve"; meaning to adhere or stick firmly</note>;
And colored <note>original: "Tynct"</note> in *Projection* to endure all fires,
And soon it will enter and spread itself very wide.

2. But many, through ignorance, mar <note>original: "mar"; to spoil or ruin</note> what they have made,
When they perform *Projection* upon uncleaned metals,
For because of corruption, their *Tinctures* must fade <note>original: "vade"; meaning to fade, vanish, or lose strength</note>;
Which corruption they would not first take away from the bodies <note>In alchemy, "bodies" refers to the base metals being transformed.</note>,
Which after *Projection* are brittle, livid <note>original: "bloe"; meaning a bluish-grey or leaden color</note>, and black:
So that your *Tincture* therefore may last forevermore,
See that you first cast your *Medicine* upon *Ferment*.

3. Then your *Ferment* will be as brittle as any glass;
Upon bodies cleansed and made very pure,
Cast your brittle substance and soon you shall see,
That they shall be skillfully colored with *Tincture*,
Which at all assays <note>original: "affays"; tests for the purity and quality of metals</note> shall endure forever:
But take the Psalms of the Psalter <note>original: "Sawter"; the Book of Psalms. This may refer to a specific number of repetitions or the spiritual state required for the final stage.</note> as an example
To perfectly make profitable *Projection*.

## *declares his failed experiments.* <note>original: "Erroneous experiments".</note>

<margin>1.</margin> After all this, I want you to understand,

Beginning with <term>Vermilion</term> <note>original: "Vermylion"; a red pigment made from mercury sulfide.</note> which proved worthless,

<margin>2.</margin> I made very many <term>solutions</term> <note>original: "Solucyons"; the chemical process of dissolving a solid into a liquid.</note>,
Of <term>Spirits</term> <note>Volatile substances like sulfur or arsenic.</note>, <term>Ferments</term> <note>Substances used to trigger a transformation.</note>, salts, iron <note>original: "Yerne".</note>, and steel;
Thinking <note>original: "Wenyng".</note> that way to make the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term>:
But finally I lost every bit <note>original: "eche dele".</note> of it.
Yet I worked hard according to my books,
Which I always found to be untrue,
Which often made me very deeply distressed <note>original: "sore agrevyd".</note>.

<header>Experiments.</header>

<margin>7.</margin>
I made **Oil of the Moon** <note>original: "Oyle of Lune"; an alchemical preparation of silver (associated with the Moon).</note> with great labor,

<margin>8.</margin>

But I always failed in my purpose:

There was always something missing.

<term>Celandine</term> <note>An herb used in folk medicine and alchemy.</note> and <term>secundines</term> <note>Placental tissue or afterbirth.</note> with many others yet—
I practiced with these as I found them in my books,
I gained nothing at all, but lost many a pound;
From <term>mercury</term> and metals I made crystal stones,
Thinking that it had been the great work for that very purpose.

<margin>10.</margin>
Thus I roasted and boiled like one of **Geber's Cooks** <note>original: "Gebers Cooks"; a reference to the famous alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan. His "cooks" were amateur alchemists who followed literal "recipes" without understanding the underlying philosophy.</note>,
And often I sought my profit in the ashes;
For I was deceived by many false books
Through which I worked truly at what was untrue:
But all such experiments were of no use to me;
Instead, they brought me into danger and trouble,
Through the loss of my goods and other grievances.

11. For the love of our Lady, avoid such ignorance <note>original: "lewdnes"; here meaning folly or lack of skill rather than sexual impropriety.</note>;

Of which I have told the truth in this treatise.
Study only how to make our ***Stone***;
For by that, you may win both silver and gold.
Therefore, be bold to ground yourself upon my writing;
If God is your guide, you shall lose nothing;
Trust my doctrine and stick by it.

13. Remember how Man is the most noble creature

In whom the four elements are proportioned by nature.

For our metals are nothing else but mines also

Descends secretly into these two mines,
Although that brightness is hidden from your sight.
By craft you shall make it appear openly;
Therefore, <term>putrefy</term> <note>The alchemical stage of "death" or breakdown, where the material is heated until it turns black and "rots."</note> this hidden ***Stone***, this one thing.

Then <term>ferment</term> <note>The stage where the "Stone" is given the power to transform or "ripen" base metals into gold.</note> him wisely; now here is the sum total of it all.

<meta>This page concludes the "Compound of Alchemy" by George Ripley. It transitions from the final instructional verses into a formal closing statement and a Latin-to-English translation of the author's colophon.</meta>

# Experiments.

Now to God Almighty I recommend you,
Who grants you by Grace to know this one thing,
For now is this treatise <note>original: "Treatys"</note> brought to an end:
And may God of His mercy bring us to His bliss,
Holy, Holy, Holy <note>original: "Sanctus, Sanctus, Sanctus"</note>, where Angels do sing:
Praising without ceasing His glorious Majesty,
Which may He grant us to see in His Kingdom.

---

->In the Year of Our Lord 1471.<-

*Here ends the Philosophical Treatise of Alchemy,* <note>original: "Explicit Alchimiae Tractatus Philosophiae"</note>
*Of which George Ripley, Canon, was the author;* <note>original: "Cujus Rypla George, Canonicus, Auctor erat"</note>
*In the year one thousand, four hundred and seventy-one,* <note>original: "Mille, quadringentis septuaginta unoq;"</note>
*It was written and composed.* <note>original: "Annis qui scriptus compositusq; fuit"</note>
*Reader, I pray you, offer help to the author through prayer,* <note>original: "Auctori lector praebe prece, quaeso Iuvamen"</note>
*So that his purgation after life may be light. Amen.* <note>original: "Illi purgamen leve post vitam ut sit Amen." This refers to the Catholic belief in Purgatory, asking for prayers to shorten the author's time there.</note>

->Translated into English.<-

Thus here the *Treatise* <note>original: "Tract"</note> of *Alchemy* does end,
Which (*Treatise*) was penned by *George Ripley*, Canon <note>term: "Chanon" - A member of certain bodies of Christian clergy subject to a religious rule (in Ripley's case, the Augustinians).</note>;
It was composed, written, and signed as his own,
In the *Year* <note>original: "Anno"</note> fourteen hundred seventy-one: <note>original: "twice Seven hundred seventy-one"</note>
Reader! Assist him, make it your desire,
That after life he may have gentle fire. <note>A poetic reference to the fires of Purgatory being mild.</note>
->*Amen.*<-

# THE BOOK OF THE FATHER
## OF WISDOM.
<note>original: "LIBER PATRIS SAPIENTIAE"</note>

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap 'T' within a square border, decorated with stylized leaves and vines.</image-desc>You who begin to read in this book, keep this advice well so that you shall prosper <note>original: "spede"</note> the better. Be in a secret place by yourself alone, so that no one sees or hears what you shall say or do.

2. Yet before you begin to read much, take good heed of whom you keep company with; I truly advise you: do not trust your friend too much wherever you go, for he whom you trust best may sometimes be your foe.

3. And take heed to the words of the Father of Wisdom, how he teaches his son how he should act: to keep his precepts of bodily governance <term>bodily governance: the management of one's physical health, conduct, and moral behavior</term>, and with his knowledge <note>original: "Conyng"</note> he will greatly advance you.

4. And if you will not take heed of his words, you shall often stand here in great fear and dread. For he who has foresight <note>original: "fore wytt"</note> does not need to go astray, and he who acts foolishly—the folly shall be his own.

5. Now my dear *Son*, do not make yourself known <note>original: "be thow not a know"</note> to the learned or the unlearned <note>original: "Leud"</note>, to high or to low; neither to young nor old, rich nor poor. To them, teach nothing of my teaching <term>lore: secret knowledge or traditional learning, often specifically regarding alchemy here</term>.

-> **The Father of Wisdom** <-
<note>original: "Pater Sapientiæ"</note>

6. Also to those men who consider themselves wise, and likewise to the fools who "glide on the ice" <note>This likely refers to people taking unstable or dangerous risks</note>: they think the *Art* of the science of *Alchemy* should be found in great books, but those books are not worth a thing <note>original: "fart"</note>.

7. Therefore, my Son, I may well teach this *Science* to you; and if you wish to take revenge <note>original: "be wreach"</note> upon your enemy, or to purchase or build any good thing, it shall be to your great advancement.

8. If you wish to learn <note>original: "leare"</note> this worthy *Science* of *Alchemy*, you must part with a little money from your purse to buy the *Flower of Flowers* <note>original: "Flos Florum"</note>—it is the most worthy thing—and to build her cabin and her nest well.

9. And if you spend money on any other thing, it is to your loss and your great hindrance, unless it is for your work’s natural food, which is obtained from stone, air, and wood.

10. And if you have all things growing within you, then you do not need to buy any kind of thing that should belong to this *Science*; but watch yourself for fear of hanging <note>Alchemical practice was often legally restricted or associated with counterfeiting, making it a capital offense</note>.

11. For then you and this *Science* would be lost forever if you make any kind of boast about it to any man or woman, old or young. Watch yourself for fear of being discovered.

12. For if you make any man privy to your secrets <note>original: "make any man privie of thy Councell"</note>, whether he is rich or needy, you must be careful whether you are sleeping or waking, for even the mere thought of making money <note>Refers to the illegal creation of gold or currency through transmutation</note> could be dangerous.

13. For if God sends you grace and understanding, you may have a good life with this *Science*. But beware of the talk of loose <note>original: "liberall"</note> women, and of the voices and sight of children in general.

-> **The Father of Wisdom** <-

14. Son, in your own house you may well obtain a good morsel of meat to sweeten your mouth—both pheasant, partridge, plover, and leveret <note>a young hare</note>—even though you do not shout about it in the public market.

15. 17. Also, you must be sure of another thing: to purchase a license from your King. Then, whatever doubts may befall you, you may work better and travel freely <note>original: "both go and ride"</note>.

18. I shall also teach <note>original: "lere"</note> you another thing: do not charge the poor people dearly. Instead, always serve your God first at the beginning, and your life will be better among the poor.

19. Now, my *Child*, pay heed to my precepts; whatever happens afterward, you shall succeed better. It is better to have a thing than to wish for it, for when you feel a wound, it is hard to find a physician <note>original: "leech"</note>.

20. Now, my dear *Son*, I will declare more of this Work <note>The "Great Work" or "Magnum Opus" of alchemy</note> to you, which shall be for your welfare. If you can consider all my sayings, you may find a most precious thing through them.

21. And *Son*, though this writing is made in rhyme, do not feel any great disdain for it. Until you have proved my words in both deed and thought, I know <note>original: "wot"</note> well that it shall be valued as nothing.

22. Therefore, out of all bodies and spirits, more or less,
*Mercury* is called the *Flower of Flowers* <note>original: "Flos Florum"</note> and the worthiest princess:
For her birth and marvelous behavior,
she is most worthy to have been King.

23. For she is Earth and Water, the heaviest of things,

and so forth with her love she will run and fly,
for she delights in no other game or entertainment.

24. Some say that from *Sulphur* and *Mercury* all mineral bodies <margin>are made,</margin>

25. I will first begin with *Saturn* <note>the alchemical name for Lead</note>, following the sayings of others,

And of *Mercury* he is the heaviest, mixed <margin>mixed,</margin> with black, sulfurous earth,
except that he is soft in fusion <note>melting</note>, and his *Sulphur* is not at all fixed <note>chemically stable or resistant to heat</note>.

26. *Jupiter* <note>the alchemical name for Tin</note> is a white body made of pure *Mercury* on the outside,
and of clear *Sulphur*, somewhat earthy and white on the inside;
he is by nature the softest and well on his way to fixation,
for he is almost fixed, but he lacks decoction <note>prolonged heating to reach maturity</note>.

27. *Mars* <note>the alchemical name for Iron</note> is a white body made mostly of unclean Mercury <note>represented by the symbol ☿</note> in the earth,
and he is hardest to melt <note>original: "of fusion"</note>, being clothed in earthy *Sulphur*;
to blackness and redness he will soonest be consumed,
by heat or by corrosive agents when the spirit begins to fume.

28. *Sol* <note>the Sun, representing Gold</note> is the purest and somewhat red, and is made of clean Mercury and fixed <margin>fixed,</margin> *Sulphur*,
engendered with clear red *Sulphur*, well mixed in the earth,
and therefore he is without fault and lacks no perfection <note>original: "degree"</note>;
for he is nearly the hardest to melt and the heaviest in weight <note>original: "ponderosity"</note>.

29. *Venus* <note>the alchemical name for Copper</note> is a body more red, made in her substance of pure Mercury,
mostly of red and green *Sulphur*, and in this there is great variation:
engendered in the earth with corrosive and bitter substance,
well fixed and hard to melt, but crude <note>original: "rude"</note> in its management.

30. *Mercury* is a Body if he is moved with a Substance,
Mixing one kind with his own kind, so shall he be loved;
One Spirit received by another—whichever of them is the dominant one—
Is the cause of the generation of every metallic body.

31. *Luna* <note>the alchemical name for Silver</note> is a pure white Body born of clean *Mercury* and white *Sulphur*;
And she is a little difficult to melt <note>original: "hard of fusion"</note> and almost fully fixed <term>chemically stable and resistant to the effects of fire</term>.
And she is the next cleanest in the tincture <note>the color or essence</note> of whiteness,

33. Now I have declared the working of the Mineral Bodies,

So must the artificial Medicine <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> be, or else it is worthless.

34. Now I will declare the special worthiness of *Mercury*,

She is called the most principal matter of the three <note>The *Tria Prima* or Three Primes: Mercury, Sulphur, and Salt</note>.

35. Also, she is very subtle in many artificial operations;
She will both give and take the most special tincture <term>the substance or "stain" that changes the color and property of a metal</term>

Especially when she is warmed in her Nest <note>the alchemist's vessel or furnace</note>.

36. My Son, *Mercury* is called the mightiest *Flower of Flowers* <note>original: "Flos florum"</note>,
And most royal, and richest of all unique things <note>original: "Singulorum"</note>;
She is the true Patron and most royal Princess,
And she is the true Mother of every metal.

37. She is Vegetable, Animal, and Mineral;
She is Four in nature, and One in general:
She is Earth, Air, Water, and Fire;
Among all others, she has no equal <note>original: "Peere"</note>.

94. And if your work be thus well guided and led so forth,
Then you have succeeded in your work right well and skillfully;
For if you do otherwise than I have told you,
In the risk of your work, you may be too bold.

95. For if you work by good measure and perfect time,
You shall have very good gold and fine silver;
Then you shall be richer in yourself than any king,
Unless he labors in the *Science* <note>original: *Science*; here referring specifically to the art of alchemy</note> and possesses the same thing.

96. Now my dear *Son*, I shall teach you how to perform a *Projection* <term>The final stage of the alchemical process where the Philosopher's Stone is "cast" upon base metal to transmute it into gold or silver.</term>;
Therein lies all the great profit and the conclusion:
To lead an imperfect body to its great perfection,
By joining like to its like, you will stand in no distress.

97. For when you have joined the "milk" <note>likely referring to a liquid mercurial substance or "virgin milk"</note> to the dry bodies,
Then you truly have the White and Red *Elixir*;
Which is a marvelous and very precious Stone,
For in this *Science*, the whole work depends upon it.

98. In this *Science*, these Stones are in themselves so precious
That in their working and nature they are marvelous;
To show you their great virtue, I will further declare
That you may prosper well if you follow this method of working.

99. First, you must take that body <note>metal</note> which is closest to *Sol* <note>Latin: "Sun," representing gold</note> in perfection,
And in its color, weight <note>original: ponderosity</note>, and proportion;
Being soluble, as if it were clear running blood,
In the hot element, it is always lightest and most fluid <note>original: fleeting</note>.

100. Then take part of the Red *Elixir* that is the precious Stone,
And cast it immediately upon that body that runs like blood;
And when you have thus perfectly wrought this work,
It shall be turned into perfect *Sol* with little or no labor.

101. In the same way, do for *Luna* <note>Latin: "Moon," representing silver</note> that is so white in color,
By joining it with that body that is shining and somewhat light;
In the same proportion, cast the very white Stone upon it,
And then all your greatest work is both made and done.

# Pater Sapientiæ.

102. Then you have both the Red work and the White work, <note>These represent the two final stages of the Philosopher's Stone: the "White" for transmuting silver and the "Red" for transmuting gold.</note>
Therefore blessed be that time, both day and night:
For this work that stands by great virtue and love,
You must then thank Almighty God in heaven above.

103. *Son*, in the 21st Chapter there I wrote a very true rhyme,
That is to say, toward this work have no great disdain;
Until you have proven my words in deed and thought,
I know well this *Science* <note>original: *Science*; here referring to the art of alchemy</note> shall be set at nothing.

104. My *Son*, to these last precepts look that you take good heed,
For it is better to have than to wish for in time of need:
For whoever is so bold as to reveal secrets to a friend,
He that is your friend may become your foe and wreak his enmity upon you.

105. And therefore, my *Son*, I shall give you a great charge:
In uttering speech, be not too liberal;
To tell every man what you have in silver or gold,
For many men will be very bold to take it from you.

106. Also, do not indulge in revelry or riotous living that would exceed
Your bodily health; then the better shall you prosper;
Use a temperate diet and temperate labor,
For when a *Physician* fails you, this shall benefit you.

<margin>Conclusions</margin>
107. And leave all blind works <note>original: "blind warkes"; refers to false, fruitless, or misguided alchemical experiments</note> that you have seen or heard of,
Or proved by sublimations, preparations, distillations, or disso-
<margin>lutions;</margin>
Of such matters great books do greatly specify,
And all those contrary sayings in this craft I plainly deny.

108. Also, my *Son*, remember how you are mortal,
Abiding but a while in this *World* which is terrestrial:
You know not how long, nor how soon from hence,
That death shall visit you and come unto you.

109. And remember well at your departing,
Whomever you loved and trusted best, old and young:
Make him your *Heir* and the head of your *Council*,
And give him your *Cunning* <term>original: "Cunning"; meaning specialized knowledge, skill, or secret expertise</term> or your *Book* every part of it.

# Pater Sapientiæ.
<note>Latin: "Father of Wisdom"</note>

110. But beware of flattering and deceitful <note>original: "glofing" or "glozing"; fawning or using deceptive language</note> people,

And when they have achieved their intent, they will treat you with scorn.

111. Therefore, let no man of rude or unrefined <note>original: "rustie"; unpolished, ignorant, or untrustworthy</note> character be your counselor, 
But only him whom you know to be both true and trustworthy; 
In riding and walking, sleeping and waking, 
Both in word and deed, and in his conduct.

112. Also, ensure you are secret within your own chamber, 
See that your doors and windows are shut tight; 
For some will come and look in every corner, 
And soon they will ask what you are making there.

113. And therefore, a good excuse must be ready at hand, 
Or else you shall truly start to run mad; 
Say you are laboring hard, both sleeping and waking, 
Toward the perfect method of making strange colors.

114. Such as, for instance, Bice, Vermillion, *Aurum Musicum* <note>Latin: "musical gold" or "mosaic gold"; a pigment made of tin bisulfide used to imitate gold</note>, and others; 
Or else you shall never have peace <note>original: "have a doe"; have dealings or trouble</note> from some people; 
Also, you must have many samples of these to show, 
Otherwise, those who intend harm will say so <note>i.e., they will suspect your true work</note>.

115. Furthermore, I give you a very good warning: 
Beware of how you work and also how you speak <note>original: "uttering"; expressing yourself or distributing the product</note>, 
Regarding the scrutiny of people, whether they are high or low born, 
Before you have the money for your work in your purse.

116. Therefore, my *son*, take heed of these one hundred and twenty <note>original: "sixscore"</note> chapters, 
And all the things mentioned that should be done beforehand; 
For you must have a very good understanding of *astronomy*, 
Or else you will only have a superficial belief in this book.

# Pater Sapientiæ.
<note>Latin: "The Father of Wisdom"</note>

118. Now Son, to you who understand perfection and the sciences, 
Whether it be theoretical <note>original: "Speculative"</note> or practical <note>original: "Pracktick"</note> according to my teachings <note>original: "sentences"; maxims or instructional statements</note>: 
Regarding this science and labor, I think it a great pity <note>original: "ruthe"; a cause for sorrow or regret</note> [that it is so misunderstood], 
Therefore, I write the very truth to you.

119. But to you who understand neither perfection nor practice, 
And have proven no conclusion <note>i.e., completed no successful experiment</note> that resembles this work, 
I swear by Almighty God who has created all this world: 
I have said and performed absolutely nothing <note>original: "right nought"</note> for you.

120. Therefore, my *Son*, before you begin this book, 
Understand wisely what is written within it; 
For if you cannot find through this book either the Sun <note>original: "Sol"; representing Gold</note> or the Moon <note>original: "Moyne"; representing Silver</note>, 
Then go forth and seek further, as other fools have done.

->***Here ends the book called the Father of Wisdom.***<-
<note>original Latin: "Explicit Liber dictus Pater Sapientiæ"</note>

# THE HERMES BIRD.

1.
Problems of old likenesses and figures,
Which have proven to be fruitful in meaning <note>original: "sentens"; the inner meaning, wisdom, or moral authority of a text.</note>;
And have authority grounded in Scripture,
By resemblance of notable appearance;
Which moralities conclude in prudence:
Just as the Bible relates in writing,
How trees once chose for themselves a king.

2.
First, in their choice, they named the Olive
To reign among them, as the Book of Judges <note>original: "Judicum"</note> expresses;
But he quickly <note>original: "blyve"</note> excused himself,
[Saying] he could not forsake his fatness <note>In the biblical parable, the olive tree refuses to stop producing oil (its "fatness") to rule over others.</note>:
Nor the Fig tree its lovely sweetness:
Nor the Vine its wholesome, fresh flavor <term>Flavor</term> <note>original: "terrage"; the taste of the earth or soil in which a plant grows; terroir.</note>;
Which gives comfort to people of every age.

# Hermes Bird.

3.
And similarly, poets laureate,
By appropriate and dark <note>original: "derke"; obscure, symbolic, or allegorical.</note> parables,
Feign that birds and beasts of high status,
Such as royal eagles and lions, by common agreement,
Sent out summons to hold a Parliament;
->And established ranks, briefly to say,<-
->Some to have lordship and some to obey.<-

4.

The power of lions is seen upon the ground;

Flora is the Goddess and Queen of all flowers:
->Thus, in all things, there are diversities,<-
->Some of high status and some of lower degrees.<-

5.
Poets write wonderful likenesses,

They take beasts and birds as witnesses:
From whose invented fables first arose [wisdom],
And here I set out for my purpose,
->To translate a tale out of the French,<-

6.
This tale of which I make mention,
In its entirety <note>original: "In gros"</note> rehearses, to declare plainly,

Who was very desirous to escape from her trouble:
->Following the process of my author,<-
->I shall express it in the order that it happened.<-

7.
Once there was in a small village,
As my author recounts;
A churl <term>Churl</term> <note>original: "Chorle"; a person of low birth, often a peasant or commoner, sometimes implying a lack of refinement.</note> who had the desire and great spirit,

# Hermes' Bird.

8. All the alleys were made level with sand,
Benches covered with fresh green turf,
Planted herbs with conduits at the end;
That bubbled up against the bright sun,
Like silver streams as clear as any crystal:
    The bubbling waves boiled up there,
    Round as beryl, casting out their beams.

9. In the middle of the garden stood a fresh laurel <note>original: "Lawrer"</note>,
On which a *Bird* sang both day and night;
With shining feathers brighter than gold wire,
Which with her song made heavy hearts light;
To behold it was a heavenly sight:
    How toward evening and in the dawning,
    She did her best <note>original: "sche dyd her payne"</note> to sing most pleasantly.

10. Hesperus <note>The evening star.</note> strengthened her courage,
Toward evening when Phoebus <note>The sun.</note> went to his nest;
Among the branches to her advantage:

# Hermes' Bird.

13. I am now taken and stand in your power <term>original: "daunger"; in Middle English, this referred to the power or control held by a captor or lord.</term>,
Held so tightly that I may not flee;
Farewell my song and all my clear notes,
Now that I have lost my liberty.
Now I am enslaved <term>original: "thrall"</term>, though once I was free;
And believe well, I stand in such distress,
I cannot sing nor create any gladness.

14. And though my cage were forged of gold
And the pinnacles were of beryl and crystal,
I remember a proverb said of old:
*“He who loses his freedom is truly enslaved.”*
For I would rather, upon a small branch,
Sing like a blackbird <term>original: "Merle"</term> among the green woods,
Than in a cage of gold, bright and beautiful <term>original: "chene"; likely 'sheen'</term>.

15. Song and prison have no harmony <note>original: "acordaunce"</note>;
Do you believe <term>original: "Trowys"</term> that I will sing in prison?
Song proceeds from joy and pleasure,
And prison causes death and destruction.
The ringing of fetters makes no merry sound;
Or how should he be glad and cheerful <term>original: "jocownde"</term>,
Who lies bound in chains against his will?

16. What use is it for a lion to be a king of beasts
If he is shut fast alone in a tower of stone?
Or an eagle under tight chains,
Though he is also called the king of every bird <note>original: "Fowlys everichon"</note>?
Fie on lordship when liberty is gone!
Answer this, and do not dodge the point <note>original: "hit nat a start"</note>:
Who sings merrily if they do not sing from the heart?

17. If you want to rejoice in my singing,
Let me fly free from this captivity;
And every day in the morning,
I will return to your laurel tree <note>original: "Lawrer"</note>,
And sing freshly with clear notes;
Under your chamber or before your hall,
In every season when you wish to call me.

43. It causes **Love** and makes men **Gracious**,
And favorable in every man’s sight;
It brings agreement between two **Envious People**;
It **comforts the sorrowful** and makes heavy hearts light,
Like the shifting of bright **sunny** colors;
I am a fool to tell you all at once,
Or to teach a **Churl** <term>churl: a person of low birth, rude, or ignorant</term> the price of precious **stones**.

44. Men shall not put a precious **pearl** <note>original: "Margareyt"; from the Latin 'margarita'</note>,
Such as **rubies**, **sapphires**, and other **stones of India** <term>stones of India: gemstones believed to originate from the East, then considered the source of the finest jewels</term>;
**Emeralds**, nor round white **pearls**,
Before rude **swine** that naturally love pig-wash <term>draff: dregs, refuse, or swill fed to pigs</term>;
For a **sow** delights, as I find,
More in foul pig-wash to make her **piglets** glad,
Than all the **jewelry** <term>perry: jewelry or precious stones</term> that comes out of **Granada**.

45. Each thing is drawn to its like <note>original: "hys semblable"</note>,
**Fish** in the **sea**, **beasts** on the **shore**;
The **air** is commendable for **birds**,
The [earth] for the **plowman** to till his **land**,
And for a **churl**, a **manure-fork** in his hand.
I waste my time to tarry any longer
To tell you to beware of the **lapidary** <term>lapidary: a book or treatise describing the magical and medicinal properties of gemstones</term>.

46. What you once had, you shall get no more;
I defy your **lime-twigs** <term>lime-twigs: twigs smeared with sticky "birdlime" used to catch birds</term> and **snares** <term>panters: nets or traps for catching birds</term>;
You were very foolish to let me go,
To lose such riches only through folly.
I am now free to sing and to fly
Wherever I please; and he is a **fool** overall
Who goes at large and then makes himself a slave.

47. Your **ears** are half-deaf to hearing **wisdom**,
Like **an ass** <note>original: "a Nasse"</note> that listens to a **harp**;
You must go pipe on an **ivy leaf** <note>an idiom meaning to engage in a futile or trivial task</note>;
It is better for me to sing on sharp **thorns**
Than to chatter in a **cage** with a **churl**;
For it was said by **people** many years ago:
"A **churl’s churl** <note>This likely refers to someone who is a slave to a master who is himself unrefined or base</note> is often woebegone."

53. "In this teaching I wasted my labor,
To teach you such proverbs of substance;
Now you may see your ignorant <note>original: "lewd"; in this period, the word meant unlearned or foolish rather than its modern sexual connotation</note> and blind error;
For my whole body, weighed in the balance,
Does not weigh an ounce; your memory is poor;
Yet I have more weight enclosed in my entrails,
Than my whole body could ever counter-balance."

54. "My whole body does not weigh an ounce,
How could I then have a stone inside me
That weighs more than a great jacinth <note>original: "Jagounce"; a reddish-orange gemstone, likely a zircon or hyacinth, often associated with magical properties</note>?
Your brain is dull, your wits almost gone;
Of the three wisdoms, you have lost one;
You should not, according to my instruction <note>original: "sentence"</note>,
Give credit to every tale too hastily."

55. "I also told you to beware, both evening and morning,
Of things lost by sudden chance;
You should not make too much sorrow
When you see that you cannot recover them;
Here you fail, despite your diligent efforts;
In trying to catch me in the snare again,
You are a fool; your labor is in vain."

56. "In the third lesson also you rave;
I told you that in no way should you
Covet a thing which you cannot have;
In which you have forgotten my undertaking,
So that I may say plainly, to describe it,
In your madness, you have forgotten all three
Notable wisdoms that I taught you."

57. "It would be but folly to talk more with you,
Or to teach more or less of wisdom;
I consider him mad who brings out his harp
To teach a tune <note>original: "rode"; likely referring to music played by rote or a specific song</note> to a dull <note>original: "doilyd"</note> ass;
And mad is he who sings a Mass for a fool;
And he is most mad who makes it his business
To teach a Churl the terms of nobility <note>original: "Gentlenesse"; the virtues, refinement, and manners associated with a gentleman or the noble class</note>."

58. Similarly, in April and in May,
When gentle birds make the most melody,
The cuckoo can sing but one song;
In other tunes she has no interest.
Thus, as scholars specify, everything—
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Like fruit on the trees, and people of every age—
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Bears the mark of where they come from.
<note>original: "tallage" — historically a tax or tribute; here it refers to an inherent quality or natural characteristic inherited from one's origins.</note>

59. The Winter treats of his wholesome winds;
The gardener boasts of the gentle fruit;
The fisherman casts his hooks and his lines,
To catch fish in the fresh river;
The poor laborer speaks of tilling the land;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The gentleman speaks of nobility;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The <term>churl</term> delights to speak vulgarity.
<note>original: "rebawdry" — ribaldry; coarse or indecent talk.</note>

60. A falcon and a kite are treated as equals,
And an owl is as good as a parrot;
A dunghill duck is as precious as a <term>snipe</term>.
<note>original: "Snyte" — a snipe, a game bird considered a delicacy, contrasted here with a common duck.</note>
He who serves a churl has many a woeful day;
I resolve never hereafter to play with you anymore,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Nor to soar for a churl to sing any more,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Or to speak of wisdom during my life.

61. The people who shall see and read this fable,
I counsel them to flee from newly-invented lies;
For the loss of goods, do not take too great a concern;
Do not be too sorrowful for any adversity;
Do not covet the thing that cannot be;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;And remember wherever you go,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;A churl’s servant is often miserable.
<note>original: "A Chorlys Chorle" — literally "a churl's churl," meaning the servant or subordinate of a rude, low-born man.</note>

62. For this purpose, this proverb is very common,
Read and reported by old tradition:
"A child’s bird and a churl’s wife
Have often experienced sorrow and misfortune."
He who has freedom has enough;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Freedom with a little in happiness is better
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Than to be a churl with all the world’s riches.

# The Prologue of the Canon's Yeoman <page-num>230</page-num>

"Why is your Lord so slovenly <note>original: "slotlyche"</note>, I pray you,
And yet has the power to buy better clothes?
If his deeds match your speech,
Tell me that, I beseech you."

"Why," said this Yeoman, "why do you ask me?
As God may help me, he shall never thrive <note>original: "ythe"</note>;
But I will not admit what I say,
And therefore keep it secret, I pray you.

Therefore I consider him ignorant <note>original: "leude"</note> and foolish <note>original: "nyce"</note> in that;
For when a man has too much intelligence,
It very often happens that he misuses it.
So does my Lord, and that grieves me deeply;
May God amend it; I can say no more to you."

"No matter about that <note>original: "thereof no force"</note>, good Yeoman," said our Host,

Yet there is still something here, though we do not have it all;

You shall know that before I go away from you,
By the time I have finished my tale.

If shame or loss may cause any dread,

To such a man, I can never say no."

# The Canon's Yeoman

"What," said this *Canon*, "should I be dishonest?

Truth is something I will always keep
Until the day I crawl
Into my grave—or else God forbid!

I thank God—and may it be said at a good time—
That there was never yet a man poorly repaid <note>original: "yvel apayd"</note>

And Sir," said he, "now about my secret knowledge <note>original: "privyte"</note>,

And shown me such great courtesy,
To repay your kindness somewhat,
I will show you, if you want to learn it <note>original: "lere"</note>—
(I will show it to you right here, immediately)—
How I can work in alchemy <note>original: "Phylosophye"</note>.
Take good heed; you shall see it with your own eyes,
That I will perform a masterpiece <note>original: "Maistrye"</note> before I go."
"Yes, Sir," said the *priest*, "and will you really do so?
By Mary <note>original: "Marye"</note>, I pray you heartily for that!"
"At your command, Sir, truly,"
Said the *Canon*, "or else God forbid!"
Look how this thief knew how to offer his service <note>original: "con̄ the his servyce bede"</note>!
It is very true that such offered service
Stinks, as the old proverb witnesses;
And I will very soon verify it
In this *Canon*, the root of all treachery,
Who always has delight and gladness—
Such fiendish thoughts press into his heart—
In how he may bring Christ’s people to ruin.
God keep us from his false dissembling!
What did this *priest* know of whom he dealt with?

He felt nothing of the harm coming his way.

# The Tale, &c.

When it pleases Him, look, this is the end.
Therefore I conclude this: since the God of heaven
Does not wish the *Philosophers* to name <note>original: "nemen"; to name or tell.</note>:

# THE WORK OF
# *JOHN DASTIN.*

1. Not yet fully sleeping, nor yet fully awake,
But lying in a trance between the two;
My eyes half-closed in my slumber,
Like a man <note>The original "Mā" uses a macron/tilde to signify a missing 'n'.</note> enraptured, losing all normal expression and composure;
Through a kind of thinking and memory
Toward the dawn <note>original: "Aurora"</note>, before the sun <note>original: "Phœbus"</note> rose,
I dreamed someone came to me to give me pleasure
Who brought me a book sealed shut with seven seals.

2. Following this, I had a wonderful dream,
As it appeared to my inner thoughts;
The face of the one who brought this heavenly book
Shone like a sunbeam.
It contained such great riches that it cannot be bought;
Arranged in order by *Lady Philosophy* <note>original: "Dame Philosophie"; the personification of wisdom.</note>,
The capital letters and the decorative flourishes were created
By a wise prince called *Theology*.

3. This book was written with golden <note>original: "aureat"</note> letters,
To be kept in memory forever,
And the chapters were consecrated to *Apollo* <note>In alchemy, Apollo often represents the sun and the metal gold.</note>,
And to the seven gods in the heavenly assembly <note>original: "Consistory"; a council or gathering, here referring to the seven planetary deities.</note>.
And in *Mercury’s* <note>Mercury is the messenger god and the name for the liquid metal essential to alchemical transformation.</note> little chapel <note>original: "Oratory"</note>,
Grows the essence of all this science;
Whoever can explain these things and gain mastery <note>original: "Victory"</note> over them
May claim the triumph of his alchemical wisdom <note>original: "Minerall prudence"; skill and judgment in working with minerals and metals.</note>.

<summary>The poem begins with an allegorical dream-vision in which the narrator receives a sacred alchemical book sealed with seven seals. The text establishes alchemy as a divine science governed by Philosophy, Theology, and the planetary gods.</summary>

4. Regarding this matter mentioned above among the seven stars <note>The seven "stars" refer to the seven planets known to ancient and medieval astronomy, each associated with a specific metal in alchemy.</note>,
By the agreement of all the gods and goddesses,
*The Wand-Bearer* <note>original: "Caducifer"; an epithet for the god Mercury, who carries the caduceus wand.</note> was sent down from heaven to Earth;
*Saturn* acted as a *messenger* <note>original: "Bedell" (beadle); an officer who summons people or makes proclamations.</note> with great deliberation,
To summon a general Parliament
By the consensus of everyone, both old and young,
To briefly offer their most wise counsel:
For the common benefit, to arrange a marriage.

5. Between two born of imperial blood,
And descended from the lineage of *Jupiter*,
Whose natures are most pure and most good;
Their seed is most divine, without corruption <note>original: "infeccion."</note>,
So that no eclipse may prevent them from shining,
Provided that *Mercury* puts an end to all conflict,
And tempers their spirit <note>original: "Courage."</note>, inclining them toward humility;
So that they are not hardened by stubbornness <note>original: "frowardnes."</note>.

6. For the *Sun* who sits so high above,
Shall clearly rain down his golden dew-drops,
Through the agency of *Mercury*, whose motion was first made gentle;
Then there shall be a joyful conjunction <note>The "Alchemical Marriage" or union of opposing elements, usually represented as the King (Sun/Gold) and Queen (Moon/Silver).</note>,
Once a separation has been made;
And their two life-essences <note>original: "Spermes."</note> are made one by marriage,
And the aforementioned *Mercury*, through division,
Has taken flight and departed from them both.

7. These are the two "Mercuries" <note>In alchemy, "Mercury" can refer to the planet, the metal, or a philosophical principle of fluidity and transformation.</note> essential to philosophers,
Revived again with the spirit of life,
Richer than rubies or pearls locked in chests <note>original: "Cofeures."</note>;
Washed and baptized in life-giving <note>original: "vegitative."</note> waters,
The body separated by nourishing heat,
Through the moderate moisture of decay <note>original: "Putrefaccion"; a stage in the Great Work where the substance "dies" and blackens before its eventual purification.</note>;
So that there is no excess and no conflict
Between the four elements in their union <note>original: "Conjunccion."</note>.

8. The grain of wheat which falls on the ground,
Unless it dies, it cannot bear fruit <note>original: "fructifie"</note>;
If it remains whole, its power <note>original: "vertue"</note> fails <note>original: "appayle"</note>,
And it cannot multiply in any way.

From good grafts come fruits that last well <note>original: "lastage"</note>;
From crab-apples comes sour juice <note>original: "Verjuyce"</note>, and from ash is made lye;
From good grapes follows a good vintage.

9. He who sows good seed reaps good things again;
From sown weeds <note>original: "Cockles"</note> no good wheat can grow.
Just as such a plowman labors in vain,
Weeds are not suitable <note>original: "meete"</note> for fruitful land.
Gall is always bitter, and honey is always sweet;
False connections are made of things that are contrary.
Let the Male and Female always meet together,
But only if both are cleansed of their impurities <note>original: "Complexions," referring to the elemental makeup or "humors" of the substances</note>.

10. A man, by nature, produces only another man,
And every beast produces its own likeness <note>original: "semblable"</note>;
And as *philosophers* can well explain,
*Diana* and *Venus* are notable in marriage.
A horse does not join with a pig in a stable,
For where an unnatural <note>original: "unkindly"</note> generation is made,
What follows but abominable things?
Which is to say, a *monster* <note>original: "Monstrum"</note> in nature.

11. All this I find in the mentioned book,
Brought to me while I lay asleep;
And I took good heed of one thing:
The wolf is by nature <note>original: "in kinde"</note> the enemy of the sheep.
The rose is very different from the wild turnip <note>original: "Neepe"</note>;
For when contrary things are joined,
Lady Nature sits and weeps in complaint
Because of the false recipes found in her library.

13. Nevertheless, he who is seated so high in heaven,

14. And in that book, I found it well-written,

16. The said King rose up in his royal throne <note>original: "see"</note>,
