18. This liquid <note>original: "liquor"</note> is most wholesome and good
Against leprous fluids <note>original: "humors"</note> and false infections;

It cleanses every part from all corruptions.
This original substance is taken from the lineage <note>original: "generacions"</note>
Which is descended down from royal stock,
Nourished with milk of a pure constitution <note>original: "complexion"</note>
And with primary solvents <note>original: "menstrous"; in alchemy, the "menstruum" is a powerful solvent or the "blood" of the earth used in transmutation</note> that are not superficial.

# Dastin's Dream.

<page-num>262</page-num>

20. Of our birth and of our origin,
To make mention clearly and truly:
There is no excuse, in part or in whole;
Our conception was first in sin <note>In alchemical allegory, "sin" refers to the impurities or "original" flaws present in base metals like lead or iron compared to gold</note>.
Our bringing forth and generation
Were completed in sorrow and wickedness;
And our mother, in short,
Fostered us in distress with corrupt milk.

21. For who can make that seed clean
Which was first conceived in uncleanness?
For I mean that cankered rust can never,
By any craft, show forth perfect brightness.
Now let us all direct our course at once,
And go to our mother to ask immediately
The final cause of our corrupt sickness,
So that she may declare the cause and the "why" to us.

22. These children rose up in a fury
Of woeful rage, and went by common consent
To their mother, who was called *Mercury* <note>In alchemy, Mercury (quicksilver) is often described as the "mother" or the primary matter from which all other metals are born</note>.
Requiring her with great deliberation,
Before her *Goddesses* who were every one present,
To tell them truly and not to pretend in any part
Why their nature was corrupt and ruined <note>original: "shent"</note>,
Which caused them to weep and complain forevermore.

23. To whom the mother, with a face and complexion <note>original: "hew"</note> full of brightness,
Gave this answer recorded in scripture:
"First, when I was newly wedded,
I conceived by the process of true Nature
A child from seed that was most clean and pure,
Undefiled, most radiant <note>original: "orient"</note>, fair, and bright;
The chief of all the *PLANETS* in its generation,
Which now gives such a clear light in Heaven."

24. Whose complexion is most temperate,
In heat and cold and in humidity,
In Earth also, so that there is no debate,
Nor any repugnance from any quality:
Nor any occasion for any infirmity,
So that among them there may be no discord,
So well proportioned is each in its degree,
Every hour and moment they are in such true accord.

25. Whose Nature is so imperial,
That burning fire causes him no distress:
His royal kind is so celestial,
From corruption he takes no sickness;
Fire, Water, Air, nor Earth with its dryness,
None of them may alter his complexion,
He fixes spirits <note>original: "fixeth Spirits." In alchemy, to "fix" a spirit means to turn a volatile, evaporating substance into a stable solid that can withstand fire.</note> through his high nobility;
And saves infected bodies from their corruption.

26. Death may not assail his heavenly health,
He fears no venom, nor needs any medicine <note>original: "treacle." Historically, a "treacle" was a medicinal compound used as an antidote against poison or disease.</note>,
Wind, tempest, nor weather may prevail against him,
So high in Heaven is his dwelling place <note>original: "Tabernacle"</note>,
On Earth he works many a miracle:
He cures lepers and brings home the fugitive <note>In alchemical allegory, "lepers" are base metals and the "fugitive" is volatile mercury that escapes as vapor when heated.</note>,
And to gouty eyes gives clear sight:
Causing those who were lame all their lives to walk.

27. He is my son and I his mother dear,
Truly conceived by me in marriage;
As for your birth, the sickness appears,
Brought forth from menstruous blood in your tender age <note>Alchemists used "menstruous blood" as a metaphor for the impure "sulfur" or "earth" that they believed contaminated base metals during their formation in the earth.</note>,
Your leprosy is shown in body and in face,
To make your healing medicine there is no other
Drink or potion for your benefit,
But the pure blood of him who is your dear brother <note>The "brother" represents Gold or the Philosopher's Stone, whose "blood" (essence) was thought to possess the power to transmute or "heal" base metals into perfection.</note>.

28. A good shepherd must die for his sheep,
Without grumbling, to speak in plain words;
And likewise, take good care of this:
Your Brother must die and be born again anew.
Though he is old, be very certain of this:
He must be renewed to youth again,
And suffer passion <note>original: "paſſion." In both theology and alchemy, "passion" refers to suffering or a transformative ordeal.</note>, or else all would be in vain;
Then rising again, quite fresh and well-colored <note>original: "well hewd." In alchemy, the color ("hue") of the substance indicated its stage of perfection.</note>.

"Unless the Gospel means this:
To be renovated by Water and Spirit, hot and cold,

31. The King was sad <note>original: "triſty"</note> and heavy-hearted;

32. And to accomplish the meaning of his purpose,
By clear example, whoever looks correctly will see:
Heavy things from their circumference
Must ascend upward and afterward be made light,

33. Just as Jupiter, in a cloud of gold,

40. The King thus entered his royal bed,
The Queen conceived under a bright sun;
Under her feet was a mount like crystal,
Which had devoured her husband immediately,
Dead from desire and in the maidens' sight;
He lost all the color of his fresh face,
Thus he was dead; the maidens, feeble in their power,
Despaired and slept in the same place.

41. The bold serpent shed out his poison,
The Queen and maidens took flight out of fear,
Seven times ascending up and down <note>original: "Seaven tymes assending"; likely referring to the seven stages of distillation or the "seven gates" of alchemy</note>

Their generation <term>generation: the process of alchemical creation or transformation</term> was so strong in power,

42. The Queen took her full possession,
Reviving the soul of the dead King;
But from old hatred, the toxic poison

The Prince was buried, but concerning his rising,
The brethren <note>original: "Btethren"; likely an OCR error for "brethren," referring to the other base metals being transformed</note> were glad the truth was seen,

# PEARCE
## THE BLACK MONK
->*on the Elixir.*<-

<image-desc>A large ornamental woodcut initial "T" decorated with floral and foliate patterns inside a square frame.</image-desc>

Take Earth of Earth, Earth's Mother,
And Water of Earth, it is no other,
And Fire of Earth that bears the prize <note>original: "pryfe" meaning the prize or the highest value</note>,
But concerning that Earth, see that you be wise.
If you want to make the true Elixir,
See that you take Earth out of Earth,
Pure, subtle <term>subtle: refined, thin, or volatile, as opposed to "gross" or dense matter</term>, fair, and good;
And then take the Water of the Wood:
Clear as crystal, shining bright;
And join them together right away <note>original: "anon ryght"</note>.
Then let them lie for three days,
And then separate them privately and skillfully <term>slyly: here meaning with expert craft or cleverness</term>.
Then there shall be brought forth shining Water,
And in that Water is a soul <note>original: "foule," using the long 's' (∫), meaning the spiritual essence or "anima" of the material</note> reigning,
Invisible, hidden, and unseen—
It is a marvelous matter to imagine <term>ween: to think, suppose, or believe</term>.
Then separate them by distilling,
And you shall see an Earth appearing;
It shall be as heavy as metal,
In which is hidden a great secret <term>privity: a private mystery or secret knowledge</term>.
Distill that Earth in a green hue,
For three days, well and truly;
And put them in a vessel <note>original: "body" refers to the main glass flask or cucurbit used in distillation</note> of glass,
In which no work was ever done before.

In a furnace he must be set,
And on his head a good alembic <term>alembic: the cap or upper part of a distilling apparatus</term>;
And draw from him a water clear,
Which water has no peer <note>peer: equal</note>,
And after, make your fire stronger,
And there on your glass continue longer,
So shall you see a fire come;
Red as blood and of great ire <note>ire: intensity or heat; in alchemy, this refers to the "red" stage or Rubedo</note>,
And after that, an earth shall be left there,
Which is called the Mother of all;
Then into Purgatory she must be put <note>original: "doe," meaning placed or subjected to</note>,
And have the pains that belong to it,
Until she be brighter than the sun,
For then you have the mastery won;
And that shall be within three hours,
Which truly is a great marvel <term>ferly: a wonder, miracle, or extraordinary event</term>:
Then put her in a clean glass,
With some of the water that was hers.
And in a furnace put her again,
Until she has certainly drunk her water,
And after that water, give her blood,
That was her own, pure and good,
And when she has drunk all her fire,
She will grow strong and of great ire.
Then take meat and milk for it,
And feed the child as you should do,
Until he be grown to his full age,
Then shall he be of strong courage <note>courage: here meaning potency, vigor, or essential power</note>;
And turn all bodies that are lawful <note>lawful: likely referring to base metals that are "fit" or naturally capable of being transmuted</note> to be,
To his own power and dignity,
And this is the making of our Stone,
The truth here is told to every one of you.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;For all those who take any other way,
Much they lose and much they may <note>This sentence continues on the following page.</note>,

For truly there is no other way of right,
But Body of Body and Light of Light,
Man is begotten of Man,
And Beast of Beast after its likeness;
All the fools in the world seek
A thing that they may never find <note>original: "meeten"</note>;
They would have metal out of those things <note>referring to the non-metallic substances listed below</note>
That was never found by worldly men:
Nor was it ever found by God’s might,
That they should bear any such fruit <note>original: "fryghte," likely meaning productive essence or fruit</note>.
All salts and sulfurs far and near,
I forbid <term>interdite: to prohibit or forbid</term> them all together <note>original: "in fere"</note>,
All corrosive waters, blood and hair,
Urine <note>original: "Pyss"</note>, horns, worms, and glass gall <term>saudiver: the dross or scum that forms on the surface of molten glass</term>,
Alum, vitriol <term>atriment: atrament, a black substance or vitriol used in making ink</term>, I suspend them all;
Realgar <term>rasalger: red arsenic sulfide</term> and arsenic, I forbid <note>original: "defende"</note>,
Quicklime <term>calx vive: unslaked or "living" lime</term>, and slaked lime <term>calx mort: "dead" or slaked lime</term>, its brother,
I suspend them both, one and the other;
For of all things I want no more,
But four elements in general, I say so:
Sun and Moon, Earth and Water;
And here is all that men chatter about <note>original: "clatter"</note>.
Our Gold and Silver are no common metal <note>original: "plate"</note>,
But a seed <term>sperme: a life-giving essence or "seed" of the metals</term> that I take out of a body,
In which is all *Gold* <note>original: Sol</note>, *Silver* <note>original: Lune</note>, life, and light,
Water and Earth, Fire and fruit <note>original: "fryghte"</note>:
And all comes from one image,
But the "Water of the Wood" <note>an alchemical metaphor for a specific mercurial solvent</note> makes the marriage;
Therefore there is no other way,
But to take up your beads <note>rosary beads</note> and pray:
For greedy <note>original: "covetous"</note> men never find it,
Though they seek it forever and ever;
Set not your hearts on this thing,
But only on God and a good life.

ALL hail to the noble company
Of true students in holy *Alchemy*,
Whose noble practice teaches them
To veil their secrets with misty speech;

At his death he made me swear to him,
That I should never reveal <note>original: "undoe"</note> all the secrets
To any one man, but even spread a cloud
Over my words and writings, and shroud it so,
That those who desire this *Art*
Should first know well how to rule their Fire:

# The Green Lion

The *Lion* is the priest, the *Sun* and *Moon* the wedded couple,
Yet they were both born in the *Lion’s* bed;
And yet this King was begotten by none other
But by the *Sun* and *Moon*, his own sister and brother.

But they found nothing in their projection <term>projection: the final step of the Great Work, where the Stone is cast upon base metal to transmute it into gold</term>;
Therefore they marred what they had made before,
And would have no more to do with *alchemy*.
Thus do the old Fathers <note>The "Fathers" refers to previous master alchemists or "adepts" whose writings the author is interpreting.</note> hide it from a scholar <term>clerk: a learned person or scholar</term>,
Because in it consists the entire subtle work;
Which, if you wish to learn from me,
I shall not fail to show the truth.
When your pure matter is ready in the glass,
Before you shut your vessel,
A portion of your *lion's* sweat <note>original: "Lyons sweate" — This likely refers to a corrosive liquid, acid, or mercurial spirit used to dissolve and "feed" the solid matter.</note>
Must be given to it to eat.
And they must be ground so well together
That neither will flee from the other;
Then you must seal up your glass,
And in its furnace where it was,
You must set them there to dry.
When this is truly done,
You must prepare, like a good *physician*,
For another *imbibition*:

# The Green Lion

But always see that you dry
Up all his drink, so that none remains;
For if you make him drink too freely,
The longer your work will take.
And if you let him be too dry,
Then your Child <note>The "Child" is a common alchemical metaphor for the developing Stone or the substance within the vessel.</note> may die of thirst;
Therefore, it is best to keep to the middle ground <term>mean: the middle point or moderation</term>,
Between being over-moist and too scorched <note>original: "rost"</note>.
Perform your *imbibitions* <term>imbibition: the alchemical process of adding liquid to a dry substance until it is saturated</term> six times;
On the seventh, take that *Sabbath's* rest.
Allow eight days between each of those six days
To dry up the moisture and make the substance fixed <term>fix: to make a volatile substance solid or resistant to heat</term>;
Then, at the ninth stage, seal up your glass vessel,
And let him stand for six full weeks:
With his heat tempered so correctly
That, once the *Blackness* has passed, he may grow white;
And so, in the seventh week, keep him still,
Until you *ferment* <term>ferment: the addition of a specific substance (like gold or silver) to the alchemical matter to direct its transformation</term> according to your will.
If you choose to *ferment* for the *White* <note>The "White Stone" or "White Elixir," capable of transmuting metals into silver.</note>,
You will not gain a great profit from it;
For I assure you that you need not fear
To proceed with the fire until everything is *Red* <note>The "Red Stone," the final goal of alchemy, used to create gold and the Elixir of Life.</note>.
Then you must proceed as the *philosophers* of old did
To prepare your *ferment* of pure gold—
And though how to do this is a secret,
Yet I will truly teach it to you.
In the next *chapter*, as I said before,
So that you may find the truth;
Therefore, out of charity and for our Lord’s sake,
Let no man take from my writings
One word, nor add anything to them;
For certainly, if he does so,
He shall show malice, from which I am free—
Intending only truth and not deception <note>original: "subtilty"</note>.

## The Green Lion

So that your medicine may always increase;

If you are wicked, my heart is filled with pity <note>original: "reuth"</note>.
Remember that God can take away His blessing,
Even after He has given it, if you abuse it in any way.
For surely, if you are a scholar <note>original: "Clerke"</note>,

->Hunting of, &c.<-

You will find truth in this work:

And do not understand what I say,
Keep your own counsel then and leave your toy <note>original: "Toy" — here referring to alchemical experimentation viewed as a dangerous or trivial pastime for the unlearned</note>,
For it befits no idle rogue <term>Lymmer loy: a term for a scoundrel or a worthless person; "limmer" means a rogue or thief</term>,
To meddle with such great secrets:
As is this high Philosophy <note>original: "Phylosophye" — alchemy was often called the "Hermetic Philosophy"</note>.
Take my advice, for you shall find it true,
Cease seeking to pursue this *Lion* <note>original: "Lyon" — the "Green Lion," a central alchemical symbol often representing raw mineral ores or acidic solvents like vitriol</note>,
For to hunt him is a clever trick <note>original: "prety wyle"</note>,
Yet by his craftiness he deceives most people,
And devours them and leaves them full of sorrow <note>original: "care" — implying both mental distress and the financial ruin that often followed failed alchemical experiments</note>,

And I give you advice as my friend,
And so, I end my *Hunting* <note>original: "Hunting" — referring to the title of the work, "The Hunting of the Green Lion"</note> here.
Praying to God who made us that we may not fail
To dwell with Him in His heavenly bliss.

# THE BREVIARY OF NATURAL PHILOSOPHY.
## Compiled by the <term>unlettered: uneducated or lacking a formal university degree in Latin</term> Scholar THOMAS CHARNOCK.
### Student in the most worthy science of *Astronomy and Philosophy.*

->The first of January<-
->In the year of our Lord 1557<- <note>original: "Anno. Dom. 1557"</note>

->In the year of our Lord 1557, on the first day of the new year,<-
->This treatise was begun, as will later appear.<-

### The Book Speaks.

Come here, my children of this discipline,
Who have spent so much time in natural philosophy;
I am very willing to ease your painful study,
And by the grace of God, this shall be fulfilled;
If He will shed one drop of grace upon me (my *author*),
Then he shall finish me better and in a shorter time.
And if you wish to know for certain what I am,
I am named *The Breviary <note>A breviary is typically a book containing the service for each day, but here it refers to a concise summary or handbook</note> of Natural Philosophy.*
I explain all the *vessels* and *instruments*
Which serve our purposes in this science.
For more things belong to this art
Than any author has ever named;
This has caused many a person great doubt
Regarding what tools are needed for it;
Therefore, I will soon explain in the proper order
What *instruments* you need to prepare for our *art*.

<summary>This is the title page and introduction to Thomas Charnock's alchemical poem, "The Breviary of Natural Philosophy," written in 1557. Charnock, who styled himself an "unlettered scholar," introduces his book as a practical guide to the specific tools and vessels required for alchemical work.</summary>

## The Preface of the Author.

*Go forth, little book, small in volume,*
*Yet you have within you what is not in all the others,*
*To satisfy the minds of the students in this art;*
*You are worth as many books as would fill a cart.*
*Glad may he be who has you in his keeping,*
*For he may find through diligent seeking,*
*All things within you that shall be necessary,*
*Such as vessels and instruments belonging to alchemy;*
*Which would set many a man's heart on fire,*
*To have the same knowledge they so greatly desire.*
*And no wonder though they are glad and eager <note>original: "faine"</note>,*
*For they have spent many a pound in vain*
*In making vessels of many diverse sorts,*
*And having brought them from many strange ports,*
*Because they did not well understand*
*That all things we need, we have in England.*
*Now, do you not think this will save many a mark <note>A mark was a unit of currency worth two-thirds of a pound sterling</note>,*
*For those who have wrestled so long in our work?*
*Yes, some would spend all the money in their pouch*
*If they knew but this, or half as much.*
*Therefore, out of pity, I will no longer refrain*
*But declare all things to help them attain their purpose.*
*Therefore, if you happen upon my book,*
*Either by chance <note>original: "Casualty"</note>, or by hook or by crook:*
*Yet pray for my soul when I am dead and rotten,*
*For I have opened the door to the science of alchemy;*
*This is sufficient for you if you have any brains;*
*Now sharpen your wits so that you may attain it.*

<summary>In this poetic preface, Thomas Charnock emphasizes the practical value of his book, claiming it contains essential knowledge about alchemical vessels that can be found within England, potentially saving students from wasting money on imported equipment.</summary>

## The First Chapter.

Now I will explain everything in detail,
Concerning the tools <note>original: "Implements"</note> of this work and what the requirements <note>original: "charge"</note> are:
And first, I will begin with the *potter*,
Who cannot make what he has never seen;
Whether your vessels are made to your liking <note>original: "minde"</note>,
Stand by while he works to ensure they are correct <note>original: "more surety to finde"</note>,
And show him what to do by some sign or model <note>original: "similitude"</note>.
And if his wits are not too dull or unrefined <note>original: "rude"</note>,
He will understand what you mean,
For I think few potters within this *realm*
Have ever made such skillfully crafted items <note>original: "cunning ware"</note>,
As we fashion and prepare for our *science* <note>In this context, "science" refers specifically to the art of alchemy</note>;
And when he has formed them to suit your purpose,
You do not need to disclose the reason why.
But if he says to you, "My good master,
Tell me for what purpose or what device <note>original: "engine"</note>
Shall these vessels serve that you have me make?
For in all my life until now, I dare say,
I never formed such as these, nor anything like them;
Yet they are simple, without ridges or rims <note>original: "wrinkle or hem"</note>,
One within another—it is a clever design <note>original: "pretty feate"</note>,
The third on the outside <note>original: "without them"</note> to direct the heat upward."
Then say to him, to satisfy his curiosity <note>original: "minde"</note>,
That you have a father who is somewhat blind,
And, if it please God, you will endeavor
To distill <note>original: "stil"</note> a water to cure his blindness <note>original: "his blindnes to dissever"</note>;
Which is the *Elixir* of life, as wise men say,
And in doing this, may God send me my success <note>original: "pray"</note>;

Then he will say this or something similar:
"I pray God to send you that which you seek,"
And so you are finished with the *Potter*,
Unless you break your pots with the heat of the *Sun* <note>original: "Sun"; in alchemy, this refers to the intense heat of the furnace or the solar stage of the chemical process</note>:
Which, if it happens, will cause you grief <note>original: "paine"</note>,
And there is no way forward but to make them all over again.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As soon as you have finished with the *Potter*,

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;As for *Glassmakers*, they are scarce in this land,

His home is now in *Sussex*,

And ask him in the most humble way

It would be worth many an arm or a leg
If he could shape it like an egg;
To open and close as tightly as a hair—
If you have such a vessel, you need not fear.
Yet if you had many in reserve,
It would be even better, for *to have a supply is no disadvantage* <note>original: "Store is no fore"; a variation of the proverb "store is no sore," meaning it is better to have plenty of something than to run out</note>.

## The Second Chapter.

Now LORD, by your grace I beseech you to allow me
To finish my project <note>original: "pretence"; here meaning a formal undertaking or claim.</note> in this humble study:
For this, nor anything else, can be done without your help,
Just as neither the conjunction of the **Sun** nor **Moon**,
Nor yet other **Planets**, can move themselves for an hour
Without your providence and your divine power.
Therefore, in all things that we begin,
Let us call for his help with prayer,
That he may bring our actions to fruition;
Which must be done very carefully <note>original: "Circumspect."</note>.
Therefore, if you think to obtain your intent,
Fear God and keep his commandments:
And beware of pride—let it pass—
And never be looking too much in your glass <note>original: "Glasse"; a mirror, used here as a metaphor for vanity.</note>;
Deceive no man with false measures,
For truly, that is ill-gotten treasure.
But let your weights be true and just,
For every man must yield weight and measure
Uprightly to his neighbor,
And so must you in the work of **Philosophy**:
And also feed him who is hungry,
And give drink to him who is thirsty.
Give liberally, I say, as riches arise,
And do not turn away your eyes from a thirsty body.
What if two poor men come to you at one time
And say, "Master, for the love of God and our Lady <note>A reference to the Virgin Mary.</note>,
Give us your charity, whatever you please,
For we do not have one penny to provide us ease"?

I was never so troubled in all my life before,
As when attending to my *Fire* both *Midday, Evening*, and *Morning*:
And all to keep it at a steady state;
It has caused me more woe than I will say.
Yet one thing of truth I will tell you,
What great mishap befell my *Work*;
It was upon a *New Year's* day at *Noon*,
My *Tabernacle* <note>original: "Tabernacle"; here referring to the protective structure or furnace housing the alchemical vessel.</note> caught fire—it happened quickly:
For within an hour it had been quite well,
And suddenly I smelled fire.
I ran straight up to my work,
And when I came, it was all ablaze:
Then I was in such fear that I began to stagger,
As if I had been wounded to the heart with a dagger;

For if I had been a man of any wealth,
I would rather have given 100 Marks <note>original: "100 Markes"; a significant sum of money, with 100 marks being roughly £66 in the 16th century.</note> to the poor,

## The fourth Chapter.

When my man was gone, I began the work anew,
And old troubles then returned to my mind:
Such as frequently waking in the middle of the night,
For fear that my Work was not going correctly;
And I was often in great doubt,
Lest my fire should go out during the night,
Or that it should give off too much heat;
The anxiety of it caused me to lose sleep.

### The Fifth Chapter.

I am sorry I have nothing to repay my Master's gentleness,
But only this book, a little short treatise;
Which I dare say shall be as welcome to him,
As if I had sent him a couple of milk cows <note>original: "Milch Kine"</note>:
And here for his sake I will disclose to you,
A great secret which, by God and the Trinity,
Since our Lord first began this world,
Was never so revealed <note>original: "opened"</note>, I dare bet my hand <note>original: "lay my hand"</note>;
No, all the *philosophers* who lived before this day,
Never knew this secret, I dare boldly say.
And now, to obtain your purpose more quickly <note>original: "rathe"</note>,
Let your fire be as temperate as the Bath of the Bath <note>A reference to the natural hot springs in the city of Bath, England, used here as a metaphor for a consistent, gentle heat source—likely a "balneum Mariae" or water bath.</note>.
Oh, what a fine and profitable instrument,
Is the Bath of the Bath for our fiery intent!
To search the whole world throughout, I would not find,
For profit and freedom, a fire more fit for my purpose <note>original: "minde"</note>.
Go or ride where you please <note>original: "list"</note> for the space of a year,
You need not worry about maintaining <note>original: "mending"</note> your fire.
A monk of *Bath* who was the *Prior* of that house,
Told me in secret he used <note>original: "occupied"</note> no other fire;
To whom I gave credit even from the first,
Because it was based upon very good reason:
He had our *Stone*, our *Medicine*, our *Elixir*, and everything,
Which, when the *Abbey* was suppressed <note>Refers to the Dissolution of the Monasteries under Henry VIII (1536–1541), when monastic properties were seized by the Crown.</note>, he hid in a wall:
And ten days later he went to fetch it out,
And there he found nothing but the stopper made of a rag <note>original: "stopple of a Clout"; implying the alchemical treasure had evaporated, leaked, or been stolen, leaving only the worthless plug.</note>.
Then he told me he was in such an agony,
That for the loss of it, he thought he would go mad <note>original: "frenzie"</note>.

## Enigma of Alchemy <note>original: "Ænigma ad Alchimiam"</note>.

When seven times twenty-six <note>7 x 26 = 182. These numbers likely refer to the specific number of days required for certain stages of the alchemical process.</note> had run their race,
Then Nature revealed his black face: <note>The "black face" refers to *Nigredo*, the first stage of the alchemical process involving decomposition or "putrefaction."</note>
But when one hundred and fifty <note>original: "an C. and L."</note> had overcome him in fight,
He made him wash his face white and bright: <note>The "white face" refers to *Albedo*, the second stage where the matter is purified and washed.</note>
Then came thirty-six with great royalty,
And made Black and White flee away:
It seemed to me he was a Prince of honor,
For he was all in golden armor;
And on his head a crown of gold
That for no riches could it be sold:
Until I saw this, my heart was cold
Thinking at length who should win the field,
Until Black and White yielded to Red; <note>The "Red" refers to *Rubedo*, the final stage of the "Great Work" signifying the achievement of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>
Then heartily to God did I pray
That I ever saw that joyful day.

->1572. **T. Charnock.**<-

# Secreta Secretorum.
<note>original: "Secrets of Secrets"; a medieval treatise traditionally attributed to Aristotle as a guide for Alexander the Great.</note>

This Stone of color is sometimes citrine <note>original: "Citrynade"; a lemon-yellow or orange color associated with the gold-making stage of alchemy</note>,
Like the sun streaming in its nature;
Golden-tressed, it makes hearts very glad,
With more treasure than the King of India has,
Of precious stones created in their kind.
The citrine color represents the bright sun,
And white for the moon <note>original: "Morne"; likely a transcription error or variant for "Mone" (Moon), as white/silver represents the lunar stage in alchemy</note> that shines all the night.

This philosopher, educated in Paris,
Who wrote fully of the nature of these stones,
Set down all the classifications with great wisdom;
And thereupon he applied his diligent care,
So that the perfection should long endure,
Like the scope of Aristotle's findings <note>original: "fonde"</note>,
Which none but he could well bring to hand.

For though the matter was not told openly,
What the philosophers meant by these stones,
Aristotle, who was expert and old <note>Used here to mean wise and experienced</note>;
And he of Paris <note>Likely referring to the translator or a specific scholar like Philip of Tripoli</note> who sent forth this present work,
Was in all his promises faithful and true of intent:
With details from Arabia, India, and Persia,
Touching upon the stones that scholars <note>original: "Clerkys"</note> can describe.

Hermogenes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy</note> had by himself alone,
With the said Philip who was his confidant <note>original: "secre"</note>,
Knowledge of the power <note>original: "vertue"</note> of every secret stone;
As they were arranged by degree,
No strange secret <note>original: "uncouth prevyte"</note> was hidden from him.
This Hermogenes and he knew everything,
Of all such virtues as belong to a king.

# BLOOMFIELD'S
## BLOSSOMS:
->OR,<-
### *The Camp of PHILOSOPHY.*
<note>William Bloomfield was a 16th-century clergyman and alchemist. His "Blossoms" is a famous allegorical poem describing the journey to achieve the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

<image-desc>Large decorative initial capital W, entwined with floral patterns, begins the first paragraph.</image-desc>

1. When Phoebus <note>original: "Phœbus"; the sun personified</note> had entered the sign of the Ram <note>original: "Ramme"; the zodiac sign of Aries, marking the spring equinox</note>,
In the month of March when all things begin to grow;
As I lay in my bed, an old man came to me,
Laying his hand on my busy, slumbering head.
"I am," said he, "Time, the producer of all things.
Awake and rise; prepare yourself quickly,
My intent is to bring you to the Camp of Philosophy <term>Camp of Philosophy</term><note>An allegorical setting representing the gathered wisdom of alchemists and the search for the "Great Work."</note>."

2. Blooms and blossoms flourish plentifully in that field,
Pleasantly flourishing and adorned with gay colors;
There are also lively water fountains and beasts both tame and wild,
Overshadowed by trees that are fruitful on every branch <note>original: "ſpray"</note>.
Sitting there, the birds sing melodiously and say:
"Father, Son, and Holy Ghost—one God in three persons—
Dominion <note>original: "Impery"</note> and honor be to you, O Holy Trinity!"

3. Look, when he had said this, I arose quickly,
Putting on my clothes in haste and with agility.
We went toward the Camp of Philosophy,
To see the wonderful sights there.
Father Time brought me to a large, great gate,
Which was then closed; he said to me:
"Every thing has its time; do not be at all dismayed."

<summary>The author describes a vision in which Father Time appears to him in March and leads him to the "Camp of Philosophy," an allegorical landscape representing alchemical knowledge.</summary>

4. Then I was filled with great wonder,
With a painful and massive disturbance <term>perturbacion</term> of mind,
Seeing the gate fastened with twelve locks:
I imagined very little hope that Time would be my friend:
"Why do you study so hard, man?" said he, "Are you blind?"
He touched me with a rod, at which I fell down
Into a deep sleep, and in a dream he showed me everything.

1. Therefore, hear the dream which I saw. <note>original: "Igitur audite somnium meum quod vidi."</note>
In the year of Christ one thousand five hundred fifty-seven,
In the month of March, as I lay asleep,
Late in the night, about eleven o'clock,
I was suddenly wrapped in spirit into Heaven:
Where I saw sitting in most glorious majesty
Three beings I beheld; yet I adored but one Deity.

2. A Spirit without limits <term>incircumscript</term>, with burning heat that cannot be consumed <term>incombustible</term>,
Shining with brightness, as permanent as the fountain of all light.
Three joined in one with incomprehensible glory;
Which gave me great delight to behold:
Truly, to attain this is beyond my power:
But a voice from that glorious brightness said to me,
"I am one God of immeasurable majesty; do not be afraid."

3. In this clear vision, which revealed itself so widely,
A voice, most pleasant and being three in one,
Pierced my mind and taught me to comprehend
The dark sayings of every *philosopher*;
The *height* <note>original: "Altitude"</note>, *breadth* <note>original: "Latitude"</note>, and *depth* <note>original: "Profundity"</note> of the *Stone* <term>Stone</term>,
To be three in substance and one in essence;
A most heavenly treasure created by the Quintessence <term>Quintessence</term>.

4. Then I pondered what this quintessence should be,
Among the visible things apparent to the eye;
The fifth being a strange secret property <note>original: "privetie"</note>,
Resting invisibly in every substance;
I thought, the invisible Godhead is the same;
The primary cause of being and the primary essence:
And the most sovereign quintessence of the *Macrocosm* <term>Macrocosmy</term>.

10. Then I busily took the Key of Knowledge in my hand
And began to search the hollowness within the lock;
The words on it I scarcely understood,
So craftily were they set within its mechanism <term>stock</term>;

By bringing in great expenses for vile materials,
It is the very quickest way to bring a Prince to begging,
And to make a noble realm and commonwealth decay.
These are "Royal Philosophers" in exactly the opposite way!

35. Some also call it an overflowing *substance*,

# The second part of
# the Book.

*Saturn* <note>Lead</note> in all things has the most importance to this *Art*,
From whom we draw a most excellent *quintessence*;
He connects himself to our mastery <note>original: "Magistery"; the successful completion of the alchemical process</note>,
United in quality, and also made equal <note>original: "equipolent"</note>
In strength and in virtue; whoever chooses to be diligent
Shall find that we seek a heavenly treasure
And a precious jewel that shall endure forever.

2. **Jupiter** <note>Jupiter represents the metal Tin</note> the gentle, endowed with **Azure** blue,
The examiner who through Justice declares true Judgment,
Altering his colors, always fresh and new,

To *Philosophy* <note>In this context, "Philosophy" refers to alchemy, the "Hermetic Philosophy"</note> he is serviceable and also obedient,

3. **Mars** <note>Mars represents the metal Iron</note> who is martial in city and town,

A noble warrior, and famous of renown,
With fire and sword he defends his own life;
He stains with blood and slays with a knife
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;All spirits and bodies, his *Arts* are so bold;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;The hearts of all others he wins to him with **Gold**.

4. The **Sun** <note>The Sun represents Gold, the most perfect of metals</note> most glorious, shining with potent power,
Above all other seven fair *Planets*,
Shedding his light to them all impartially,
With his glorious beams and glistening shine,
He enlightens the Earth and the firmament of Heaven:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Whoever can dissolve him and draw out his **Quintessence** <note>original: "Quinteffence"; the "fifth essence" or purest spiritual core of a substance</note>,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Unto all other *Planets* he shall give influence.

5. Lady **Venus** <note>Venus represents the metal Copper</note> the fair goddess of love,
With her son *Cupid*, appertains to this *Art*;
When she addresses herself to the love of the *Sun*,
She strikes him to the heart with her darts of love;
Joined to his seed, she takes part in his substance:
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;She clothes herself in excellent fabric <note>original: "Tissue"</note>,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;When she renews her own corrupt nature.

With his rod of enchantment he prevails very little;
Often taken prisoner, he revives himself,
Until he is snared with the **Dragon's Tail**; <note>The "Dragon's Tail" (Cauda Draconis) is an astronomical point, but in alchemy, it often refers to the final stages of purification or the stabilizing of volatile Mercury</note>
Then he puts on a hard coat of mail,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Soldered <note>original: "Soudred"</note> together with the *Sun* and *Moon*;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Then he is mastered and his enchantment is done.

Follow their sayings, and wisely study them:
Then you shall not ignorantly delude yourself
In this excellent **Science** <note>The "Great Work" or alchemy</note>: Adieu, I conclude thus.

## The Theory Begins. <note>original: "Incipit Theorica"</note>

We intend now, through divine grace,
To write in a few words about **Chaos** <note>The "First Matter" (Materia Prima), the formless state of substance before the alchemist shapes it</note>,
To cause light to shine forth from **Darkness**,
Which was hidden long before, as I shall describe;
In every unknown thing, it is necessary
To search out a secret which is invisible:
The material of our Mastery, a substance beyond the senses.

2. Because I should not seem to enclose
Long-hidden secrets committed to me
By my Lord God, therefore, I will speak plainly of *Chaos* <note>original: "Chaos"; in alchemy, this refers to the "Prima Materia" or the raw, unformed matter from which the Philosopher's Stone is created</note>.
My purpose shall be to be acquitted of this duty,
For heavy burdens are not easily lightened.
In faith, therefore, I shall endeavor
To unburden myself before God forever.

3. Devoutly, therefore, I call unto you, O Lord:
Send me your grace to explain
*Chaos*; for you are the opener of all secrets,
Who are always ready to hear the *supplication*
Of your humble servants; with heartfelt *humility*
I apply to you: send me now your grace
To write of your *Secrets* in the proper order, time, and place.

4. *Chaos* is nothing more to say—this is doubtless—
(As *Ovid* writes in his *Metamorphoses*)
But a certain raw substance, *a shapeless heap* <note>original: "indigestaque moles"; a famous phrase from Ovid's description of the beginning of the universe</note>,
Having various natures resting within it,
Which we may untwine from their opposites
By the *Philosopher's Art* <note>The practice of alchemy</note>; whoever knows the technique
Can draw out the four *elements* from *Chaos*.

5. This *Chaos*, like all things, has three dimensions,
Which, if well considered, shall produce the result:
That is, *Altitude*, *Latitude*, and *Depth*.
By these three, all the "Water" <note>In an alchemical context, "Water" often refers to the "mercury of the philosophers" or the liquid state of the matter being worked upon</note> is directed;
Whoever has no respect for these dimensions
Shall never divide the *Chaos* into its kinds,
But after his labor, he shall find only failure <note>original: "fraud"; here meaning a deceptive or failed result rather than intentional trickery</note> in the end.

6. *Chaos* is to us the vine-tree, white and red <note>The "White" and "Red" refer to the two main stages of the alchemical Great Work: the "White Stone" which turns metals to silver, and the "Red Stone" which turns them to gold</note>,
*Chaos* is every beast, fish, and fowl of every kind,
*Chaos* is the ore and the mine of tin and lead,
Of gold and silver that we find,
Of iron and copper; these things bind
And hold our sights and wits captivated—
The secrets hidden in them which we do not understand.

7. Out of this misty *Chaos*, the expert *Philosophers*

I set before you the true figure of the *Tree*,
In which I will recite the *Art* in an orderly way.
Understand my meaning so that you may work correctly;
Consider what I said: that *Chaos* is everything
That we begin with—the true way of working.

10. Suppose your *Chaos* is *Animal*, *Vegetable*, or *Mineral* <note>The three "kingdoms" of nature from which alchemists believed the Prima Materia could be sourced</note>;
Let reason guide you to work according to the same.
If you work outside of its kind, you lose everything:
For Nature rejoices in nature and finds its true purpose there.
Work with the *Animal* kind and keep yourself from blame;
Treat the *Vegetable* and *Mineral* in their proper order,
And then you shall be counted a true *Philosopher*.

11. When you have found what it is indeed,
Then you will know by reason what its form must be.
Search it intelligently and draw the seed from it:
Then its surface *Altitude* will be visible to see,
And the *Latitude* shall soon appear, believe me.
When you have divided the elements from one another,
Then the *Depth* <note>original: "Profundity"</note> lies hidden beneath them.

17. This excellent work does not need great cost,
Nor many glasses or pots to be broken;
One glass, one furnace, and no more is necessary;

In this, the *Stone* is brought to its perfect creation.

This work is complete. Give glory to God <note>original: *Da gloriam Deo*</note>.

## The Practice Begins <note>original: *Incipit Practica*</note>.

We have sufficiently declared the *Theory*,
Making our declaration in mystical words.
Let us now proceed plainly with the *Practice*,
To make a full explanation of the Matter.
I desire, therefore, that you mark my narrative well,
And as true disciples, attend to my doctrine;
I commend my *Testament* and last *Will* to you.

2. Be holy, therefore, sober, honest, and meek;
Love God and your neighbor; do not be unkind to the poor;
Overcome Satan; see that you seek God's glory.
My *son*, be gentle to all men, as a friend;
Always keep the fatherless and the widow in your mind.
Love the innocent as brothers, and shun the wicked;
Let falsehood and flattery go, lest you regret it.

Next, the true proportion of that dust must be obtained,
Weighing them truly in a true balance;
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Mixing everything together with three times as much
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Of the fiery Dragon—then you have done well.

**8.** Once your substance is thus proportioned together,
Put it in a bed of glass with a bottom large and round.
There, in due time, it shall die and be reborn <note>original: "regenerate"</note>
Into a new nature, with three natures bound into one.
Then be glad that you ever found it,
For this is the jewel that shall serve you best:
The crown of glory and the diadem of your head.

**9.** When you have mixed your matter as described,
Seal the glass well so that the dragon <note>In alchemy, the "dragon" often symbolizes volatile substances or mercury that must be "tamed" and prevented from escaping as vapor.</note> does not get out;
For he is so subtle that if he is overwhelmed
With unnatural fire, I assure you <note>original: "put thee out of doubt"</note>,
He will search all over to escape.
Therefore, see that you keep him in with a gentle fire;
In this way, you shall win the whole mystery from him.

**10.** To duly fulfill the whole mystery of this work,
Set your glass and matter upon your athanor <note>original: "Athenor"; a self-feeding furnace designed to maintain a constant temperature for long periods.</note>;
Our furnace is called the *Philosophers' Dunghill* <note>An alchemical term for a furnace or heat source that provides steady, moist, and moderate heat, similar to the heat generated by decaying manure.</note>,
Working evermore with a temperate heat.
Continually keep fuel in store, night and day—
Whether of turf, sawdust, or dry chopped sedges <note>original: "segges"; grass-like water plants.</note>—
So that the heat is equal <note>original: "equipolent"</note> to a hen sitting upon her eggs.

**11.** See that you do not lack such continuous heat
For forty days, so that their perfect union
Is made within them. For first, it turns to black;
This color signifies the proper putrefaction <note>Known as "Nigredo," this is the stage of decomposition and purification through darkness.</note>.
This is the beginning of the perfect conception
Of your "infant" into a new generation—
A most precious jewel for our consolation.

**12.** For forty days more, the matter shall turn white
And clear as pearls, which is a declaration
Of the clearing away of its dark, cloudy night.
This shows our infant’s full formation <note>original: "organization"; the "infant" refers to the developing Philosopher's Stone.</note>:
Our **White Elixir**, most clear in its creation.
From white, it will transition into all colors without fail,
Like the rainbow or the peacock’s tail <note>original: "Peacocks Tayle"; the "Cauda Pavonis" stage, where a variety of colors appear before the final transformation.</note>.

## The Conclusion.

*Our Great Work <term>Magistery: The alchemical process or the resulting Philosopher's Stone</term> is Three, Two, and One:*
*The Animal, Vegetable, and Mineral Stone.*
*First, I say in the name of the Holy Trinity,*
*Ensure that you join Three Persons into One.*
*The Fixed, the Variable, and the Fugitive <note>These terms refer to the volatility of substances: 'Fixed' (stable under heat), 'Fugitive' (volatile/evaporating, usually mercury), and 'Variable' (intermediary).</note>,*
*Until they taste death and come to life together.*
*The first is the fierce <note>original: "fell"</note> Dragon,*
*Who shall both slay and conquer the other two:*
*The Sun and Moon <note>In alchemy, the Sun and Moon represent Gold and Silver, or the active and passive principles.</note> shall lose their light,*
*And they shall clothe <note>original: "dight"</note> themselves in mourning blacks <note>original: "Sables." This refers to the 'nigredo' stage, or the blackening of the matter during putrefaction.</note>,*
*For sixty days <note>original: "Threescore"</note> or nearly that long:*
*Then Phoebus <note>Latin: the sun god, representing the stage of the Red Stone or gold.</note> shall first appear,*
*With strange colors across the entire sky <note>original: "Firmament"</note>,*
*Then our joy is coming and is present at hand:*
*Then the rising <note>original: "Orient"</note> Phoebus in his hemisphere*
*Shall appear to us in full glory:*
*Thus, he who can work wisely*
*Shall attain our Great Work <note>original: "Maistery"</note>.*

# THE END. <note>original: "FINIS"</note>

# SIR EDWARD KELLY'S
## WORK.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A' featuring intertwined acanthus leaves and floral motifs.</image-desc>

All you who desire <note>original: "faine"</note> to be *Philosophers*,
And night and day broil in *Geber's* kitchen <note>Geber (Jabir ibn Hayyan) was a legendary 8th-century Arab alchemist whose writings were foundational to European alchemy.</note>,
Wasting the chips of ancient *Hermes' Tree* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the mythical founder of alchemy; his "tree" refers to the growth of alchemical knowledge or the "Tree of Philosophy."</note>,
Thinking <note>original: "Weening"</note> to turn them into a precious Oil,
The more you work, the more you lose and spoil.
To you I say, however learned you may be,
Go burn your books and come and learn from me.

Although you have read ten books for every one of mine,
That is not enough; for I have heard it said,
The greatest scholars <note>original: "Clarkes"</note> are not the wisest men;
A Lion once obeyed a lowly <note>original: "silly"</note> mouse.
In my goodwill, consider yourselves satisfied <note>original: "appaid"</note>:
And though I do not write half as sweetly as *Tully* <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman statesman and orator famous for his elegant Latin style.</note>,
Yet you shall find I follow the steps of *Lully* <note>Raymond Lully (Ramon Llull), a 13th-century philosopher and alchemist.</note>.

It does you good to think how your desire
And self-conceit guarantees your vain hope;
You spare no cost, you lack no coals for fire;
You know the virtues of the *Heliotrope* <note>original: "Elitrope." A gemstone or plant believed to have solar powers.</note>;
You think yourselves far richer than the Pope.
What thing has being, either high or low,
But you claim to know its *First Matter* <note>original: "Materia prima." In alchemy, the formless, original substance from which all things are created.</note>?

*The Elixir of Life* <note>original: "Elixir vitæ"</note> and the precious Stone—
You know how to make them as easily as an apple;
But if it comes to the actual work, then you should be left alone;
You know the colors—black, brown, reddish-brown <note>original: "bay"</note>, and dappled.
If someone challenges <note>original: "Controwle"</note> you once, then you begin to bicker <note>original: "fraple"</note>,
Swearing and saying, "What kind of fellow is this?"
Yet still you work, but you always work incorrectly.

<summary>In this opening to his poem, Sir Edward Kelly mocks amateur alchemists who waste resources on book-learning without achieving results. He positions himself as a practical authority, claiming to follow the tradition of Raymond Lully rather than mere rhetoric.</summary>

# Kelley's Work,

No, no, my friends, it is not boasting words,
Nor mighty oaths that gain that sacred skill;
It is obtained by grace and not by swords;
Nor by great reading, nor by sitting still for long,
Nor foolish conceit, nor working entirely by willpower.
But as I said, it is obtained by grace;
Seek grace, therefore, and let folly be restrained.

It is no costly thing, I assure you,
That begets *Magnesia* in her kind. <note>original: "Magnesia"; in alchemy, Magnesia refers to the "primitive matter" or the raw material of the Philosopher’s Stone, not the modern chemical element.</note>
Yet she herself is made pure through leprosy: <note>In alchemical symbolism, "leprosy" often refers to the impurities or the blackened state (*nigredo*) that must be cleansed from the base metal.</note>
Her eyes are clearer after being first made blind:
And he who can once unbind the Earth's firmness <note>original: "fastnes"</note>,
Shall quickly know that I have told the truth,
Of sweet *Magnesia*, Wife to purest Gold.

Now, what is meant by "Man and Wife" is this:
Agent and Patient, yet not two but one, <term>Agent and Patient</term> <note>In alchemy and Aristotelian philosophy, the "Agent" is the active force (associated with male/Sulfur) and the "Patient" is the receptive matter (associated with female/Mercury).</note>
Just as was Eve, Adam's wife, I know: <note>original: "I wisse"; an archaic term meaning "certainly" or "indeed."</note>
Flesh of his flesh and bone of his bone,
Such is the unity <note>original: "Unionhood"</note> of our precious Stone.
As Adam slept until his wife was made,
Even so does our Stone; there is nothing more to be said.

By this you see how it came to pass,
That first there was Man, and then Woman from him:
Thus Adam here was the first and foremost,
And still remained a man of perfect limb,
Then Man and Wife were joined together neatly. <note>original: "trimme"</note>
And each, in love for the other, immediately devoted themselves,
And increased their kind when God had blessed them.

Just so, the "Man" of our Stone is said to sleep,
Until such time as his Wife is fully formed; <note>original: "wrought"</note>
Then he awakes, and joyfully keeps
His new-made spouse, whom he bought so dearly;
And when they are brought to such perfection,
Rejoice in the beauty of so fair a bride,
Whose worth is more than half the rest of the world.

# Kelly’s Work.

I doubt as yet you hardly understand
What Man or Wife truly signifies;
And yet I know you believe <note>original: "bear yourselves in hand"; to persuade oneself or be under a certain impression.</note>,
That without doubt it is Sulphur and *Mercury*.
And so it is, but certainly not the common kind:
But essential *Mercury* is truly the true Wife,
Who kills herself to bring her Child to life.

For first and foremost she receives the Man;
Her perfect love makes her soon conceive.
Then she strives with all the force she can,
In spite of love, to deprive him of life;
Which being done, she will then never stop,
But labor naturally <note>original: "kindly"; meaning according to her "kind" or nature.</note> like a loving Wife,
Until she has brought him back to life again.

Then he, to requite her kindness in return,
Sets a Crown of glory upon her head,
And composes <note>original: "indite"</note> poems in her praise,
Whose poems make every poet write a story;
And she is not sorry that she slew him then,
For he, by the virtue <note>original: "vertue"; meaning power or efficacy.</note> of his loving Wife,
Not only lives, but also gives life.

But here I wish for you to rightly understand,
How he here makes his concubine his Wife;
Which if you do not know, do not take in hand
This work, which is not at all common <note>original: "rife"</note> to fools.
And see that you make reconciliation <note>original: "attonement"; literally "at-one-ment," the harmonizing of opposing elements.</note> where there is strife.
Then strip the Man to his shirt of tissue <note>original: "Tishew"; a rich fabric, often interwoven with gold or silver threads.</note>,
And her out of her smock <note>A woman's basic undergarment.</note> to engender offspring.

To tell you the truth, he lacks no wives
In Land or Sea, in Water, Air, or Fire;
Without their deaths, he does not spend their lives.
Unless they live, he lacks his chief desire.
He binds them apprentice to the most righteous Dyer <note>In alchemy, a "Dyer" refers to the process of "tincturing" or changing the color and quality of a metal.</note>,
And when they have once endured <note>original: "abidden"</note> all sorrows,
Then they find joys which at first were hidden from them.

# Kelley’s Work.

For then they find the joy of sweet increase,
They bring forth children beautiful to sight,
Who are able to release prisoners;
And give true light to the darkest bodies,
Their heavenly tincture <note>original: "Tincture"; in alchemy, a spiritualized substance capable of infusing its qualities into others, often used to describe the power of the Philosopher's Stone to transform base metals into gold.</note> is of such great might.
Oh! He who can but come across such a treasure,
Who would not think his joys were beyond measure?

Now by this question I shall quickly know
If you can tell who is his Wife indeed:
Is she quick-footed, fair-faced, yes or no,
Flying or fixed <note>original: "Flying or fixed"; referring to "volatile" substances that evaporate or "fixed" substances that resist the fire.</note> as you read in books?
Is she to be fed, or else does she feed?
In what does she rejoice? Where is her home?
Heavenly or earthly, or of a strange nation?

What, is she poor? Or is she of any wealth?
Splendid <note>original: "Bravely"</note> in her attire, or humble <note>original: "meane"</note> in her apparel?
Or is she sick? Or is she in perfect health?
Mild of her nature? Or is she given to quarrel?
Is she a glutton? Or does she love the barrel?
If you name her to be any one of these,
You do not know his Wife, nor did you ever see her.

And that I will prove to you with good reason,
That truly she is none of these;
This is a question for you that is rare <note>original: "geason"; uncommon or extraordinary.</note>:
And yet she must be some part of them all,
Why then, you may see that some part is not the whole.
Therefore the true Wife of whom I speak,
Is the middle point <note>original: "Meane"</note> between all these contraries.

As flour <note>original: "Meale"</note> and water joined together,
Are now neither flour nor water, but dough;
Which, being baked, is neither dough nor water:
Nor will they ever separate from each other again.
The balance <note>original: "meane"</note> between them is the Wife; our Wife is just like that:
And our secret lies in this hidden point;
It is enough; a few words satisfy the wise.

# Kelley’s Work.

Now by this simile here I reveal
A mighty secret, if you notice it well:
Call Mercury "Water," imagine Sulphur as "Meal" <note>original: "Meale"; flour or ground grain. Kelley uses the metaphor of baking bread to describe the mixing of alchemical ingredients.</note>;
What meal I mean, I hope the wise <note>original: "wife"; likely an OCR error for "wise," a common term for those initiated into alchemical secrets.</note> can tell.
Bake them with skill; make them live together,
And in your working, do not be in too much haste,
For she is not yet the "Wife" while she is in the form of paste.

Now that this lesson is learned, give me leave to play;
I shall be the better prepared to learn another.
My mind is turned completely awry <note>original: "cleane cam"; entirely crooked or in a different direction.</note> another way.
I do not love to smother sweet, secret thoughts;
It is a child, you know, that makes a woman a mother.
Since it is so, then we must have a child,
Or else we are cheated <note>original: "beguild"; beguiled or deprived.</note> of motherhood.

What will you say if I tell you a wonder,
And prove the Mother is both the Child and the Mother too?
Do you not think I am trying to play a prank on you <note>original: "sell you a bargaine in sport"; to trick or tease someone with a deceptive deal.</note>,
As some people are accustomed to do?
Is it possible for the Mother to wear her infant’s shoe?
In faith, it is so in our *Philosophy* <note>original: "Philosophy"; here referring to the "Hermetic Philosophy" or Alchemy.</note>,
As I will prove by logic very shortly.

George Ripley <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490) was a famous English alchemist. His "Twelve Gates" described the stages of the alchemical process.</note> tells you not to take it as an insult,
But with patience to wait for the true Conjunction <note>original: "Conjunccion"; the chemical union of the masculine (Sulphur) and feminine (Mercury) principles.</note>.
For, says he, our Child is born in the Air;
There he receives the holy unction <note>original: "Unction"; anointing with oil, referring here to the substance becoming "oily" or fixed during the process.</note>,
And with it, a heavenly function.
For after death, he is revived again to life;
This "all-in-all" is both Husband, Child, and Wife.

While all is solid, it is termed "Conception,"
And *Putrefaction* <note>original: "Putrefaction"; the stage where the substance turns black and decomposes, seen as a necessary death before spiritual rebirth.</note> is the time of "lying-in" <note>original: "lying in"; the period of bed rest for a woman leading up to and following childbirth.</note>.
Perfect Conjunction (as affirmed by alchemists <note>original: "artes-men"</note>)
Is the woman’s childbirth, where all joy begins.
Whoever does not know this has very thin wits.
When she is strong and shines fair and bright,
She is called the "Wife," most beautiful to the sight.

# Kelley’s Work.

Look, thus you see that you are not deceived;
For if you notice it, I have proved by reason
How both the Mother and the Child are one,
In conception, breeding, and childbirth, in every season.
I have declared this to you without any deception <note>original: "Treason"; here meaning trickery or betrayal of the truth.</note>,
Or any false, ambiguous words at all;
And having shown you the work, then you shall find it true.

This is that truly essential *Mercury*,
Which is the principle of the material *Stone*,
And not those raw amalgams that have newly begun;
These are but superficial *Mercuries*.
This is that *Menstruum* <note>original: "Menstrue"; a universal solvent in alchemy, believed to be capable of dissolving all bodies into their first matter.</note> of perfect tinting power:
This is most truly that One Thing,
Out of which all profit must spring.

If this does not satisfy you, then remain displeased with me,
For I have finished. If reason takes no hold,
What can be said, except that doubts will remain
Wherever folly wins the race, no matter what one does.
Let it suffice: this is the perfect Base,
Which is the *Stone* that must be dissolved.
How that is done, I will explain to you.

This is the *Stone* that *Ripley* <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), the famous English alchemist mentioned on the previous page.</note> tells you to take,
(For until it is in this state, it is no *Stone*).
Be ruled by me; do not forsake my advice,
And as he commands: let raw materials <note>original: "Crudities"; unprocessed or impure substances.</note> alone,
If you have the grace to keep yourself free from sorrow.
Then stick to this; do not let fancy overrule you,
Let reason rule, for fancy will betray you.

Take this *Stone*, this *Wife*, this *Child*, this *All*,
Which will be gummy, crumbling, and as soft as silk:
Grind it small upon a piece of glass or porphyry <note>original: "Porphire"; a very hard, reddish-purple rock used as a surface for grinding chemicals or pigments.</note>,
And as you grind, feed it often with *Mercury*,
But not so much that the *Mercury* swims on top.
Use equal parts, and seal them up <note>original: "nipt up"; to seal a glass vessel by heating and pinching the neck, creating an airtight "hermetic" seal.</note> to save their "seed";
Then each is buried within the other’s grave.

<meta>This page continues Edward Kelley’s alchemical poem. # Kelley’s Work.

When you have it thus and there as I have said,
Work in all ways just as Nature worked at first:
You need not be afraid of the blackness <note>In alchemy, *nigredo* (blackness) is the first stage of the Great Work, representing the dissolution or "death" of the matter.</note>,
It will become white; then you are past the worst stage,
Unless you break your glass vessel and are cursed;
But if you march through blackness toward whiteness,
Then it will be both white and as soft as starch.

This very stage is called by many names,
Such as *Imbibition* <note>The process of a solid absorbing a liquid until it is saturated.</note>, *Feeding*, *Sublimation*,
*Climbing high mountains*, and also *children’s games*;
And it is rightly termed *Exaltation* <note>The refinement or "uplifting" of a substance to a higher, more potent state.</note>,
When the whole process is nothing else but the *circulation*
Of the four elements, whatever fools may chatter,
Which is achieved by heat acting upon form and matter.

Earth is the lowest element of all,
Which, being black, is exalted into water;
Then we no longer call it earth, but water;
Although it seems like a black, earthy matter,
And will scatter all about as black dust,
Yet when it has climbed as high as the state of water,
Then is it truly said to be *sublimed*.

When this black mass becomes white again,
Both inside and out, like snow and shining fair,
Then this "child," this "wife," this "heaven" so bright—
This watery earth sublimed into air—
When it reaches that state, it will further prepare
Itself into the element of fire;
Then give God thanks for granting your desire.

This blackness and whiteness we call *separation*,
Which is not done by hand but is elemental;
It is no crude, physical sublimation of mercury,
But Nature’s true work, sharing the same substance <note>original: "consubstantial"; sharing the same essence.</note>.
The white stage is called *natural conjunction* <note>The alchemical union of opposites, such as the "King" and "Queen" or "Sulfur" and "Mercury."</note>,
A secret and perfect conjunction, not a coarse one;
Which brings profit, while all other methods lead to loss.

<summary>Kelley describes the alchemical stages of transmutation, detailing the transition from the black state (Earth) to the white state (Water/Air) and finally to Fire. He emphasizes that this is a natural, elemental process of circulation and conjunction rather than a manual chemical manipulation.</summary>

--- Page 355 ---
<meta>This page concludes Edward Kelley’s alchemical poem, moving from the philosophical stages of transformation to the practical application of the "Medicine"—the final Philosopher's Stone. It describes the process of "projection," where the elixir is used to transmute base metals like tin into gold or silver.</meta>

# Kelley’s Work.

When you have turned this wheel around three times,
Feeding and working it as I have described,
Then it will undoubtedly flow like wax:
Producing a tincture <note>original: "Tincture"; an alchemical substance or essence capable of transforming and coloring base metals into gold or silver.</note> that will not fade,
Enduring all the tests that can be performed.
If you can perform the projection <note>original: "Project"; the final stage of alchemy where the Philosopher's Stone is cast upon a base metal to achieve transmutation.</note> wisely and keep it pure,
It will bring you both profit and reputation.

Once your *medicine* <note>original: "Medicine"; a term for the Philosopher's Stone in its finished, curative, and transformative state.</note> is fixed and flowing perfectly,
You must realize that the White medicine will increase whiteness;
Just as Red medicine begets red, just as seed during sowing
Produces its own kind, or as animals do,
And fire must be the true peacemaker:
For white or red *ferment* increases your *medicine*,
And it perfectly colors the metal and quickly dissolves into it.

In other words, once your *medicine* is finished,
If it is the White medicine, melt down silver and project the medicine onto it;
If it is the Red, melt down *gold* <note>original: "Sol"; the alchemical name for gold, associated with the Sun.</note>, for that is the intention;
Do not reject the principle of "like unto like" in any way,
And make sure you choose the metal from the purest source.
Mix one part *medicine* with ten parts *ferment*,
Then one part of that mixture onto one thousand parts of *tin* <note>original: "Jupiter"; the alchemical name for tin, associated with the planet Jupiter.</note>.

When your *tin* is standing red-hot on the fire,
As soon as your *medicine* is cast upon it,
It immediately becomes as hard as a wire,
For then it is "fixed" and will only melt by a furnace blast <note>original: "melteth by blast"; refers to the high heat of a bellows-driven furnace, indicating the metal has achieved a higher melting point like gold or silver.</note>;
And of all your working, this is the last step.
Then let it be tested by a cupel or nitric acid <note>original: "strong water" or aqua fortis; a corrosive acid used by alchemists to test the purity of precious metals.</note>,
The finest gold or silver will endure no better than this.

Raw mercury heated in a crucible,
Immediately hardens like annealed silver;
And is seated on the high throne of *silver* <note>original: "Luna"; the alchemical name for silver, associated with the Moon.</note>,
Becoming silver or gold, as the *medicine* has determined:
And thus I have revealed our great *secret*.
Which many people have seen, and I myself have performed,
And I prize it dearly, yet I give it to you for nothing.

->THE END.<-

# SIR EDWARD KELLEY
## *CONCERNING*
### the Philosophers' Stone, written to
->*his especially good friend, G. S. Gentleman.*<-

The heavenly vault <note>original: 'Cope'; referring to the sky or the overarching canopy of heaven.</note> has in it nature's four elements, <note>original: 'Natures fower'; Earth, Air, Fire, and Water.</note>
Two are hidden, but the rest appear to sight:
Wherein are the seeds <note>original: 'Spermes'; the vital principles or "seeds" from which metals and minerals were thought to grow.</note> of all the lower bodies;
They are most secret, yet they spring forth once a year,
And as the Earth and Water are the creators, <note>original: 'Authors'</note>
So on his part, Dryness is the end of care. <note>In alchemy, reaching the state of "dryness" or "fixation" often represents the successful completion of a stage.</note>

No flood is so great as that which flows constantly,
Nothing is more fixed than Earth digested three times:
No wind is so fresh as when it serves one's will;
There is no more profit than to keep it in and be wise,
No better fortune <note>original: 'happ'</note> than to dry up Air into dust,
For then you may leave off, and satisfy your desires. <note>original: 'sleepe thy lust'; meaning you have achieved your goal and can rest easy.</note>

Yet I will warn you lest you chance to fail:
Sublimate your Earth with stinking water <note>original: 'stinkeing Water'; likely a reference to a strong acid or mercurial solvent used to break down materials.</note> first,
Then in a place where only the tail of the Sun <note>original: 'Phæbus'; the Greek sun god, representing the alchemical principle of Gold or the Sun.</note>
Is seen at midday, see that you mingle them best:
For nothing shines that lacks its light,
Nor doubles its beams, unless it is first bright.

# Sir Edward Kelley to G. S. Gentleman

Let no man lead, unless he knows the way
That wise men teach, or *Adrop* <note>original: 'Adrop'; a technical alchemical term for the "body" or raw material of the Stone, often associated with lead or antimony.</note> leads in,
Of which the first is a large and easiest prey;
The other is hard, and meant only to begin.
->For surely these and no others are found,<-
->Wherein *Apollo* <note>Apollo, the sun god, frequently represents Gold or the "Solar" principle in alchemy.</note> will sound his harp-strings.<-

Learn from the example of GOD who placed the skies,
Reflecting virtues <note>In this context, 'virtues' refers to the inherent powers or astrological influences of the stars and planets.</note> from and to every point,
In which the prime mover <note>Referring to the 'Primum Mobile' or the original source of motion in the universe.</note> in whom all things lie,
Does hold the virtues of every joint:
->And therefore the *Fifth Essence* <note>original: 'Essence fift'; the Quintessence, the pure, celestial element beyond the four earthly ones.</note> may well be said,<-
->To contain all and yet remain a virgin <note>original: 'a Maid'; implying something that is pure, uncorrupted, and capable of generating new life.</note>.<-

Remember also how the *Gods* began,
And by descent who was the father <note>original: 'Syre'</note> to each,
Then learn their lives and kingdoms if you can,
Their manners also, with all their full attire; <note>Alchemists used the stories and descriptions of Roman gods as allegorical codes for the properties and "behaviors" of metals.</note>
->If you do this, and know to what effect,<-
->The learned *Sages* <note>original: 'Sopheis'; likely a variant of the Greek 'sophoi', meaning wise men.</note> will not reject you.<-

If this my doctrine does not suit your mind <note>original: 'bend not with thy brayne'</note>,
Then I say nothing, though I have said too much:
Truly, it was goodwill that moved me, not profit,
To write these lines: yet I do not write for those
->Who reach for crab-apples, when better fruits appear,<-
->And fail to choose at the fittest time of year.<-

You may say, my friend, "What kind of teaching <note>original: 'lore'</note> is this?"
I answer: it is such as ancient *medicine* <note>original: 'Phyſicke'; here referring broadly to natural philosophy and the study of nature’s laws.</note> taught:
And though you have read a thousand books before,
Yet compared to this, they teach you nothing:
->You may likewise be blind, and call me a fool,<-
->Yet these rules shall forever bring praise to their school.<-

# THE TESTAMENT OF JOHN DEE, GREATEST PHILOSOPHER
<note>original: *Testamentum Johannis Dee Philosophi Summi*</note>
## ->Sent to John Gwynn, 1568.<-
<note>original: *ad Johannem Gwynn, transmissum 1568*</note>

> This third and last letter I intend to write,
> At your request for the sake of true virtue;
> Set aside your written anxieties <note>original: "panges"; likely referring to the struggles or "pains" of study</note> and methods,
> And ensure that you never stray from what I command <note>original: "byd"</note>.
> Divide into three that which Nature has made one,
> Then strengthen it, even by itself alone,
> With which you should then cut the powdered Sun <note>In alchemy, the "Sun" (Sol) represents gold or the masculine, solar principle of the work.</note> in two,
> Through the passage of time, and heal the wound again.
> You must wound that same Sun twice more,
> Always with new knives of the same kind and sharpness <note>original: "grounde"</note>;
> Use our true <term>Monas</term> <note>The *Monas Hieroglyphica* is John Dee's unique symbol and philosophical concept representing the unity of all creation through alchemical and mathematical principles.</note> in this way by nature's law,
> Both bind and loosen <note>original: "lewse"; a reference to the alchemical maxim *solve et coagula* (dissolve and congeal)</note>, using only the ripe and the raw,
> And always <note>original: "ay"</note> thank God, who alone is our guide,
> All is sufficient; no more for now <note>original: "at this Tyde"</note>.

# THOMAS ROBINSON
<note>original: *Thomas Robinsonus*</note>
## *ON THE PHILOSOPHER'S STONE.*
<note>original: *De Lapide Philosophorum*</note>

The heavens, the earth, and all that is in them,
Were in six days perfected from the abyss:
From one sprang four; from four, a second one;
This last a grit <note>original: "Gritt"; a small particle or stone, representing the physical result of the work</note>; that first, the corner stone.
Without the first, the last may not be had;
Yet compared to the first, the last is far too base <note>original: "too too bad"</note>.
When the heavens were separated from the earth,
Were the heavens not first cohobated <term>cohobated</term> <note>An alchemical process where a liquid is repeatedly distilled and poured back over its solid residue to concentrate its essence.</note> with the earth?
And when the heavens, and earth, and all things did not exist;
Were only the heavens created, and the earth forgotten?
No: heavens and earth all sprang from one at first:
Then who can say whether heavens or earth is worse?
Is the earth not the mother of them all?
And what are the heavens, but the earth's essence?
Although they have no earthly residence in heaven,
Yet their heavenly influence rests in the earth:
If the earth did not exist, what would the other three <note>The other three classical elements: Air, Fire, and Water.</note> be?
If the heavens did not exist, what could be on the earth?
Thus, as they came, so shall they pass together;
But it is not known to man from where they come, or where they go.
And during the time of the earth’s purification by heaven,
They live and die for six thousand years:
Then all shall rest eternal and divine,
And shine by the beauty of the Godhead.
I swear there is no other truth but this
Regarding that great Stone, which many seek and miss.

->THE END.<-
<note>original: *FINIS*</note>

<note>In alchemical literature, Experience and Philosophy are often personified as guides or divine figures who lead the seeker toward the truth of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>

Have you not heard, you great princes, and you lords and ladies all,

In the arts in which they excelled,
No earthly tongue can do it well.
