# THE MAGISTERY <note>original: "Magistery"; in alchemy, this refers to the "Great Work" or the process of creating the Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

Through lack of skill and the light of reason,
*Men stumble at noonday;*
While they busily seek our Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold and granting long life.</note>,
That lies right in their path.

Those who thus seek they know not what,
Is it likely they should find it?
Or hit the mark they aim at
Any better than a blind man can?

No, sons of Hermes <note>original: "Hermes Sonns"; alchemists, who considered themselves the spiritual descendants of the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus.</note>, ask for Wisdom;
She will direct your footsteps:
She will reveal Nature's way, the secret cave,
And the Tree of Life.

*Sun and Moon in Hermes' vessel <note>The "Sun and Moon" represent Gold and Silver, or the male (Sulfur) and female (Mercury) principles; "Hermes' vessel" is the alchemical flask or sealed glass container.</note>,*
*Learn how the colors show,*
The nature of the elements,
And how the daisies grow.

How great *Apollo* slew *Python <note>In alchemical allegory, Apollo killing the serpent Python often represents the "fixation" of volatile spirits or the process of putrefaction (the black stage of the work).</note>,*
*Cadmus* and his *hollow oak:*
His new-raised army, and how *Jason*
Yoked the *fiery steers <note>Jason’s quest for the Golden Fleece was a common allegory for the alchemist's quest for the Stone; the "fiery steers" and "new-raised army" (from dragon teeth) represent the volatile and dangerous chemical reactions that must be controlled.</note>.*

The eagle which flies aloft,
See that you bring it to the ground;
And give wings to the snake,
Which is found in the earth <note>This is a classic alchemical instruction: the "eagle" (volatile substances that evaporate) must be "fixed" or made solid, while the "snake" (solid, "earthy" matter) must be made "volatile" or spiritualized.</note>.

# ANONYMOUS <note>original Latin: *Anonymi*</note>
## OR, SEVERAL WORKS OF
### *Unknown Authors.*

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop-cap 'N' set in a square border, depicting a classical urn or vase containing various flowers and foliage.</image-desc>

Now I shall here begin,
To teach you a <term>conclusion</term><note>In alchemy, a "conclusion" refers to the final result or a specific experiment.</note>;
In the name of the Trinity
Send us grace that it may be well;
Now take two ounces and as much of another,
And dissolve one there with the other,
I tell you the truth as my brother,
Put into a glass without anything else:
Then take three ounces of the bitter,
And mix it with the sweeter;
And put them then into a glass,
Even just as the other was:
Then take an ounce of the best,
And do with it as you did before <note>original: "erst"</note>,
In a glass then you put it,
And see that the mouth is well shut;
Now you have three glasses here,
Even like unto the Trinity <note>Alchemists often used the concept of the Trinity to represent the three primary substances: sulfur, mercury, and salt.</note>,
Then seal every one of them,
Even as surely as you have one:
Around your glasses make a wall,
Lest the wind makes them all crack,

Then your glasses, now all three,
Within that grave <note>In alchemy, a "grave" often refers to a warm sand bath or a pit of manure used to provide steady, low heat for incubation.</note> they shall be,
Now this I feed with moist heat,
To make those glasses toil and sweat <note>original: "swynke and swete"; an alchemical metaphor for the process of condensation and evaporation within a sealed vessel.</note>,

# Anonymous Author <note>original Latin: "Anonymi"</note>

I show you here a short conclusion,
To understand it, if you have grace,
Written without any delusion;
Contained within a little space.
All that is written in this book,
Is contained in this place:
How Nature works in her own way;
Keep this lesson well in your mind.

I have declared many things, <note>original: "micle thing" (meaning great or many things)</note>
If you have the grace to keep them in mind,
How our Principle <note>The fundamental substance or "First Matter" of the alchemical work.</note> is one thing,
Many in number and one in nature;
For there are seven things
That dwell within a Principle,
Most precious under Heaven—
I have sworn such an oath that I may not tell.

In this book, I show you in writing,
As my brothers each do,
A likeness of every similar thing,
From which we make our <term>Stone</term> <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of transmuting metals and granting long life.</note>.
Our <term>Stone</term> is made of one simple thing,
That has within it both soul and life;
He is two and yet one in nature,
Married together as man and wife.

Our <term>Sulphur</term> <note>In alchemy, Sulphur represents the active, masculine, and hot principle.</note> is our masculine,
Our <term>Mercury</term> <note>In alchemy, Mercury represents the passive, feminine, and fluid principle.</note> is our feminine,
Our Earth is our clear water,
Our <term>Sulphur</term> is also our fire;
And as Earth is in our clear water,
So is Air in our fire.
Now you have the four powerful elements,
And yet only two appear to the sight;
Water and Earth you may clearly see,
While fire and air exist within them as a quality <note>According to classical physics, the four elements were defined by their qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note>.

# Anonymous <note>original Latin: "Anonymi"</note>

This *Science* may not be taught to everyone;
He would be accursed who would do so:
How would you have servants then?
For then none would do anything for another,
To till the land or drive the plow,
For every man would be proud enough;
The learned and the unlearned <note>original: "leude" (meaning ignorant or common people)</note> would push themselves forward,
And be very busy in their works,
But yet they have very little success <note>original: "increse"</note>,
Because the writings are so mysterious <note>original: "misty"</note> to them.
It is very hard to find this *Science*,
For fools who labor against nature <note>original: "kinde" (meaning the natural order)</note>;
I pray you to conceal this *Science*,
Or else do not meddle <note>original: "meale"</note> with it,
For if you cannot prevail in it,
Then you may speak of much sorrow:
By the sudden movement of *Elements*, *Nature* may be hindered <note>original: "letted"</note>,
And where *Decoction* <term>Decoction</term> <note>The process of heating or boiling a substance to extract its essence or "cook" it to perfection.</note> is lacking, no perfection can be,

Raw watery humors cause an excess <note>original: "superfluity"</note>:
Therefore the *Philosopher* in his wisdom <note>original: "reason"</note> has devised
A perfect *Medicine* for bodies that are sick,
To be relieved of all infirmities;
This heals *Nature* and also <note>original: "eak" (eke)</note> prolongs life;
This *Medicine* of *Elements* being perfectly created,
We do not need to buy prescriptions from the *Apothecary*,
We value their *drugs* and *drams* <note>original: "dragms", a unit of weight for medicine</note> as nothing,
For with their substitutions <note>original: "quid pro quo" (referring to the practice of substituting one drug for another)</note> they tell many a lie.
Our *Drinkable Gold* <note>original Latin: "Aurum potabile" (a legendary alchemical medicine made of dissolved gold)</note> will increase *Nature*,

The *physicians* push themselves forward with *minerals*:
But it avails little or even nothing at all.
You shall find this *Science* in the old book of *Turba* <note>Referring to the *Turba Philosophorum* (The Assembly of the Philosophers), one of the oldest and most famous Latin alchemical texts.</note>;
How perfectly the *Philosophers* have created this *Medicine*,

# Anonymous <note>original Latin: "Anonymi"</note>

The *Rosary* <note>original: "Rosary," likely referring to the *Rosarium Philosophorum*, a famous 16th-century alchemical treatise</note> also records with him,
That we use nothing more than the four elements;
We use no common mercury or gold,
Until we have perfectly made our *Stone*;
Then with those two, we multiply our Medicine,
Truly, we have no other recipes from the apothecary.
You may well take a hundred ounces of *Saturn* <note>The alchemical name for lead.</note>;
Boil <note>original: "Seeth"</note> them on the fire and melt it in a mold,
Perform a projection <term>Projection</term> <note>The final stage of the alchemical process where a small amount of the Philosopher's Stone is cast upon a molten base metal to transform it into gold or silver.</note> with your medicine upon them,
And immediately <note>original: "anon"</note> you shall change it into fine gold;
One ounce for a hundred ounces is sufficient,
And it is just as effective on a thousand ounces perfectly worked,
Without dissolution or thinning <note>original: "Subtillant"</note>;
Otherwise, we have no way of increasing our medicine.
Eternal joy and everlasting bliss,
Be to Almighty God, who shall never fail.

### *In some copies, I found these following*
### *verses placed before this work.*

Earth cleansed pure out of earth,
By Earth itself through its nature,

Evermore drowned in the bottom of his well,
Until all his leprosy will no longer remain,
In his own nature, he changes completely
Into a pure substance—you know <note>original: "wat"</note> what I mean.
*I show you here a short conclusion, etc.*

Why are you so poor and I so rich?
In me you may [find] an abundance of treasure;
In all the world I am like nothing else,
Except Man, who is so akin <note>original: "proginitous"; meaning sharing a common origin or nature</note> to my kind.
The rich man has no pity for the poor;
In me, therefore, have trust <note>original: "affiance"</note>.
It is often seen in town and city:
He who has no craft or science <note>original: "Scyence"; meaning knowledge or skill</note> is ill at ease.
The rich men now have great contempt for the poor,
[Fearing] that they should win any good thing with their cunning <note>original: "cunyng"; knowledge or skill</note>;
And they have no delight in giving alms to the poor;
There is little charity within them.
And the example of *Dives* <note>Latin for "rich man," used as a proper name in the parable of the rich man and Lazarus from Luke 16</note> as the Scripture tells:
Poor *Lazarus* died at his gate for lack [of help].
Had he given him alms, he would not have gone to hell;
Now it is truly too late for him to repent.
Man, you have no goods except those God sends;
Share <note>original: "Departe"</note> with your brother as God commands you.
This will better amend your life;
Death will deal with you with a sudden hand.
You shall forsake your worldly goods:
Give every beast back its due <note>A common moral trope: man's luxuries belong to the animals they came from—silk from the worm, wool from the sheep—leaving the soul naked at death</note>,
And then your body shall be completely naked:
Death will feel no pity <note>original: "rue"</note> for you.
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Why so far away and I so near?
Have you no grace, Man, to meet me,
As often as I appear to you?
And yet you take no notice <note>original: "keepe"</note> of me.
You seek me in common mercury:
In alkali and in sal alebroth <note>original: "Alembroke"; a double salt of corrosive sublimate and sal ammoniac used in alchemical experiments</note>,
In common sulfur and arsenic also <note>original: "eke"</note>,
Which makes many a man lose his mind <note>original: "dote"</note>.
Common mercury is not good;
It brings many a man to sorrow <note>original: "care"</note>.

# Dialogue between the FATHER and the SON,
## Concerning the two Principles of the BLESSED STONE.

<margin>Father.</margin>
<image-desc>A decorative drop cap "M" featuring a figure amidst ornate scrolling foliage.</image-desc>My son, if that *sulphur* is absent,
Our work is rejected <note>original: "reproved"</note>, whatever they may say;
And it is water and fire, as true as your Creed,
Which constrains a body until it is dead.
From it, you shall never have your desire,
Until it becomes as blue as lead through its own fire.
I liken our *sulphur* to the lodestone <note>original: "Magnet Stone"</note>,
Which naturally and constantly draws things to itself;
So it is with our *sulphur* and the fiery woman, Mercury,
When she would otherwise flee from her husband.

<margin>Son.</margin>
Father, I pray you out of charity,
Where shall I find this *sulphur*?
For I have never seen it with my eyes,
Nor have I ever known its true nature <note>original: "kinde"</note>.

<margin>Father.</margin>
Keep it in your mind, my son: it is in our water,
Where it will appear as white as any snow.

<margin>Son.</margin>

<meta>This page transitions from John Gower’s *Confessio Amantis* to a famous alchemical poem by Sir George Ripley (c. 1415–1490), an English Augustinian canon and renowned alchemist. This short, allegorical work describes the process of creating the Philosophers' Stone through the metaphor of a toad.</meta>

<image-desc>A decorative horizontal band of fleurons (stylized floral ornaments) spans the width of the page at the top, featuring a central star-shaped flower. Below the title, a large ornate woodcut initial letter 'W' begins the poem, featuring floral and scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

# THE VISION OF
## Sir George Ripley:
### CANON OF BRIDLINGTON.

**W**hen I was busy with my book upon a certain night,
This vision expressed here appeared unto my dimmed sight:
I saw a toad, bright red <note>original: "rudde"</note>, drink the juice of grapes so fast,
Until, overcharged with the broth, his bowels all burst apart;
And after that, from his poisoned bulk, he cast out his cruel <note>original: "fell"</note> venom,
For grief and pain of which his limbs <note>original: "Members"</note> all began to swell.
Approaching his secret den with drops of poisoned sweat,
He then turned his cave all white with blasts of smoky <note>original: "fumous"</note> air;
And from which, in time, a golden fluid <note>original: "humour"</note> followed,
Whose falling drops from above stained the ground with a reddish color.
And when this corpse began to lack the force of vital breath,
This dying **toad** immediately became as black as **coal** in color.
Thus drowned in his own veins of poisoned flood,
For a term of eighty-four days, he stood rotting.
I then desired to expel this venom by trial,
For which I committed his carcass to a gentle fire.
This done—a wonder to see, but even more to describe—
The **toad** was pierced through every side with rare **colors**,
And **white** appeared when all the various hues were past,
Which, after being tinted **red** <note>original: "Rudde"</note>, lasted forevermore.
Then, from the venom handled in this way, I made a medicine,
**Which** venom kills, and yet saves those who happen to take poison.
Glory be to Him, the granter of such secret ways,
Dominion and honor, both with worship and with praise.
->AMEN.<-

<meta>catchword: THE</meta>

<summary>In this alchemical allegory, Sir George Ripley describes the chemical process of putrefaction and transformation (the Great Work) through the metaphor of a toad that drinks too much, bursts, rots, and eventually changes colors through fire to become a universal medicine.</summary>

# THE MYSTERY
## OF ALCHEMISTS,
->Composed by **Sir George Ripley,**<-
->Canon of Bridlington.<- <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490) was an English Augustinian canon and alchemist whose works remained foundational in the field for centuries.</note>

<image-desc>Two circular woodcut illustrations are positioned in the margins alongside the text. In the left margin is a crescent moon (Luna) featuring a profile of a human face. In the right margin is a radiant sun (Sol) with a full human face. Decorative, wavy cloud-like lines extend from both celestial figures across the margin space.</image-desc>

When the Sun is in Aries <note>original: "☉ in ♈"; this refers to the spring equinox, the traditional beginning of the alchemical work</note> and Phoebus <note>original: "Phœbus"; a poetic name for the Sun</note> shines bright,
Reviving the elements as the new year springs forth,
The Sun by his virtue gives Nature and Light,
And moisture refreshes all growing things.
In the season of the year when the Sun grows warm,
The flowers grow fresh and fragrant;
We cannot discern Nature’s subtle workings,
Nor can we understand it through our own reason.
Within the four elements <term>earth, air, fire, and water</term> are three things comprised:
Animals, Vegetables, and Minerals must be.
From these we derive the principle by which we make our Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note>,
Though its quality and quantity are unknown to many.

<margin>Son.</margin> Father, I would gladly know its quality:
Of what nature it is, and what properties it possesses.
<margin>Father.</margin> It is like the diverse colors that grow upon the ground;
Keep this secret well, my son, and mark it in your mind.
<margin>Son.</margin> Without knowing the proportions, Father, how should I understand it?
This process is currently beyond my comprehension.
<margin>Father.</margin> Nature and its kind grow together, my son;
You shall never find its quality through weight alone.
<margin>Son.</margin> To separate the elements, Father, I must know
Their proportions—which are more and which are less.

This child is both King and Emperor

All the world honors him
Because of the power he has received from the fire.

# The Mystery

<margin>Son.</margin> I wonder greatly, Father, and marvel in my mind,
Of what this *Stone* is generated <note>original: "engendered"</note>,
And also of what manner of kind;
For I have traveled through many a country,
In low valleys and on high hills,
And asked <note>original: "spurred"; to inquire or ask</note> both foes and friends about it,
Yet I could never see that Sulphur,
Nor do I know <note>original: "wat"; to know or perceive</note> in any place where to find him.

<margin>Father.</margin> *Son*, he is made of the Elements,
To which God has given both soul and life;
From Metal he may never be absent,
For he rules both man and wife. <note>In alchemy, "man and wife" often refers to the union of opposite principles, such as Sulphur and Mercury.</note>

<margin>Son.</margin> *Father*, I pray you for charity,
Where shall I find this Sulphur?
For I do not know his quality perfectly,
Nor do I yet know him by his nature <note>original: "kinde"</note>.

<margin>Father.</margin> In our Water, *Son*, keep this in mind,
For there he will appear as white as snow.

<margin>Son.</margin> Great thanks <note>original: "Gramarcy"; from the French "grand merci"</note>, *Father*, you are very kind to me,
For through your teaching, I know it full well.
Now *Father*, I pray you for charity,
While it is in your mind,
To teach me to know the red Sulphur,
And then I trust to understand your doctrine.

<margin>Father.</margin> White and Red, *Son*, are both one in kind;
Now you have all your desire.
Keep this secret well and close it in your mind:
His coloration <term>original: "tincture"; the property of a substance to change the color or nature of another, or the final medicine</term> and growth is by the power of our Fire.
For in our Fire, our *Stone* will grow,
And there his riches increase;
And no other stone that I know does so—
That in the fire will be put to the test <note>original: "put him in prease"; to put into a state of pressure, heat, or trial</note>.
We liken him, therefore, unto the Sun,
That gives light to all Elements.

## The Preface prefixed to Sir George Ripley's
# *M A R R O W <note>original: Medulla</note>;*
### Which he wrote in the year of our Lord <note>original: Ann. Dom.</note> 1476 and Dedicated to George Nevell, then Archbishop of York.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'R' featuring floral patterns and scrollwork.</image-desc>
RIGHT noble Lord, and dear Prelate,
Deign to accept these verses from me,
Which I present unto you here,
That make mention of the Stone,
Put into meter by wise men for your sake.
*For which I crave this much from you:*
*To have your gentle favor.*

2. This divine Stone of which I write,
*Is known as One, and it is Three;*
Which though it has its force and might,
*By being of a triple nature,*
Yet they judge and test <note>original: "try"</note> metals.
*And it is called by all wise men,*
*The mighty Stone that shall conquer.*

3. Do not disdain nor yet refuse,
*To learn their virtues now,*
By which you may, if you use them,
*Preserve yourself and also know how*
To hide old age, and show forth youth.
*And brass is transmuted by them,*
*And sharp <note>original: "eger," meaning acidic or corrosive</note> bodies are certainly <note>original: "I wis"</note> cleansed.*

4. Refined also and made fully pure,
*And turned into gold <note>original: "Aurified"</note> at the last.*
The first of these, I assure you,
*Is very hurtful for a man to taste,*
For it will dissolve and waste away life.
*Made of corrosives that corrupt everything,*
*And it is named the Mineral.*

# The Preface

5. But Animal is the second,
   The third, indeed, is the Vegetable;
   Their virtue is to cure all things,
   In every case, whatever might happen;
   They shall preserve mankind in health:
   It renews youth and keeps it sound,
   As is found to be true by proof.

6. And here I will teach you plainly,
   How to make their mixtures pure,
   In fair order, without disdain.
   I will tell you no dream, be sure;
   Believe me while my life endures.
   Observe what I say to you with my mouth;
   My deeds shall always prove it true.

7. Yet some figure <note>a metaphor or symbolic illustration</note> shall hide my meter <note>original: Meeter; the rhythm and structure of the verse</note>,
   Lest the Art should fly awry with wings,
   And so slide abroad as something worthless;
   Its sense or truth cannot decay,
   And without fraud, I will display
   The matter plainly on every side,
   And likewise true, whatever happens.

8. Although before this you have heard it said,
   That those who practice this Art
   Always seek their prosperity in ashes <note>A reference to failed alchemists, often called "puffers," who spent their fortunes on coal and bellows only to end up with nothing but ash</note>;
   And learn at length with a heavy heart,
   To make their share not more, but less;
   Yet do not be dismayed because of that,
   Nor fear nor shrink from it any more.

9. But trust the words which I tell you,
   For truly, I say plainly,
   I have both seen and known it well,
   And will always witness to the same;
   This is called the Marrow <note>original: Marrow; referring to the "Medulla Alchimiae" or the essential core of the alchemical secret</note>, I say;
   A truer text, I know <note>original: wote</note> full well,
   You shall not find in all this world.

10. Then as this working of our wine <note>original: "Working of our Wine"; a metaphor for the alchemical solvent or "mercury" of the philosophers</note>,
Of which I bring you here a taste;
Whose heavenly water, pure and fine,
Does work all things without any waste,
According to your desire, the solid bodies
It does dissolve, making them light and open
With other things not yet spoken of.

11. Yet it is not against nature,
But natural, as men may believe <note>original: trow</note>,
Which, being cleansed from its spots,
There Phoebus' <note>Phoebus is the Greco-Roman sun god, representing the "Sulfur" or the golden, masculine principle in alchemy</note> splendor shall show forth,
And cause it to grow fragrantly;
For the more fragrant it shall be,
So much more of value is he.

12. For Phoebus' nature does surpass
Both pure bodies and even the sky;
It shines upon both corn and grass,
The sun renews from on high,
And causes things to bear fruit.
It mixes, and fixes, and endows with nature <note>original: natureth; to imbue with natural properties or life</note>,
Drives plagues away and nourishes.

13. It banishes, draws, and cleanses the air,

Makes things soft, hard, sweet, and fair;
And purifies the Natures <note>the four elements or the fundamental qualities of matter</note> perfectly,
By its incessant working;
It makes all things grow, I say,
And chases ugly things away.

14. In the laurel tree, it is fully green,
In gold, it lodges glitteringly;
It decks stones with bright luster <note>original: sheene</note>,
The shining bodies are made by it;
But if you wish more certainly
To have knowledge of Phoebus' virtue,
Then Saturn's child <note>original: "Saturns Chyld"; Saturn represents lead. His "child" refers to the secret substance or the "Philosophical Mercury" extracted from base metals like lead or antimony</note> must bring forth the issue.

# Lydgate out of Aristotle's

The power <note>original: "Powder"; likely a variant of "Power" or "Pouer," referring to the celestial forces.</note> of the **Planets** and the moving of all **Stars**,
And of every heavenly **Intelligence**;
The **disposition** of **Peace** and also of **Wars**,
And of each other strange, hidden **Science**,
As the seven **Gods** <note>The "seven gods" refers to the seven classical planets: the Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> by their **Influence**
**Dispose** the orders of **Incantations**,
Or the **Transmutations** of the seven **Metals**.

With other **Crafts** which are secret,
**Calculation** and **Geomancy** <term>A method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or the patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand.</term>,
The **transformations** of **Circe** and **Medea** <note>original: "Dyfformacions of Circes and Meed"; referencing the famous sorceresses of Greek mythology known for changing forms and using magic.</note>:
The reading of **Faces** <term>Physiognomy, or the art of judging character from facial features.</term> and **Pyromancy** <term>Divination by means of fire.</term>,
On **Land** and **Water**, the **Craft** of **Geometry**.
**Height** and **Depth** with all **Experience**,
Therefore the **King** desires his presence,

But for all this, within himself there was 
A **Secret** he chose not to disclose;
Nor to publish openly to the **King**,
Taking an example from two things in a **Rose**:
First, how the **Flower** provides great sweetness:
Yet in the **Thorn**, men find great sharpness,
And thus in **Knowledge** <note>original: "Konnyng"; skill, craft, or wisdom.</note> there may be a likeness.

In **Herb** and **Flower**, in **Writing**, **Word**, and **Stone**,
Each has its virtue from God and from **Nature**,
But the knowledge is hidden from many a person:
And not declared to every **Creature**,
Therefore he deliberated <note>original: "cast"; to calculate or consider.</note> between **Reason** and **Moderation**:
To find a way to please the **King**,
And somewhat to reveal <note>original: "unclose"</note> his secrets and set his heart at ease.

# The Secrets of Secrets

There is by right a great difference,
Between a Prince's royal dignity,
And the common people's crude intelligence,
To whom it does not belong to meddle in any way,
With branches of knowledge <note>original: "Konnynges"</note> that should be kept secret;
For it belongs to a King’s famous magnificence,
And to scholars <note>original: "Clerkys"</note> who have experience.

It is appropriate <note>original: "cordeth," meaning it accords or agrees</note> to search out scriptures,
Hidden mysteries of birds, beasts, and trees,
And of angels, most subtle of nature;
Of minerals, and fish in the sea,
And of stones—especially of three:
One *Mineral*, another *Vegetative*,
Divided into four parts to lengthen a man’s life.

Of which I once read among other stones,
There was one called *Animal*;
Four elements worked out for the purpose <term>original: "for the noonys"; specifically for this occasion or task</term>:
Earth, water, and air, and especially,
Joined with fire in equal proportion.
I dare say briefly and without delay,
No such stone is found in the *Lapidary* <term>A treatise or book describing the properties of gemstones and minerals.</term>.

I read once of a *Philosopher*,
[Who] against each sickness is of the most value to cure,
More than all the treasure and gold in *Croesus’* coffer;
Or all the stones that grow by nature,
Created by craft or forged by depiction.
*Stone and not a Stone* <note>original Latin: "Lapis & non Lapis"</note>, stone of greatest fame,
*Aristotle* gave it that very name.

And because I have but little read or seen,
To write or meddle in such high matters,
Some would feel disdain for my presumption;
To be so bold or climb in my desires:

Of philosophers, to *King Alexander*,
[He] wrote of this *Stone*, the marvel of all workings.

To rectify <term>To purify or set right a substance through a chemical process.</term> every one of them.
And after this, according to his opinion,

But false error has confounded many a one;

For lack of brain they were made so mad <note>original: "wood," meaning insane or crazed</note>,
To begin a thing which they did not understand.

## How *Aristotle* Declares to King *Alexander* About the Stones.

Touching the Stone of the Philosophers of old,
Of which they make most sovereign mention;
But there is one, as *Aristotle* told,
Which excels all others in comparison,
The Stone of Stones, most sovereign of renown;
Touching the power <term>original: "vertue"</term> of this rich thing,
Thus he wrote to the most sovereign King.

"O *Alexander*, greatest in dignity,
Monarch and Regent of all this world,
Who has the sovereignty of all nations;
Each one is to obey and be obedient to you,
And to conclude the goal <term>original: "fyn"</term> of our intent,
All worldly treasure, briefly compressed into one,
Is declared in the power of this *Stone*.

You must first conceive of it in substance,
By a kind of strange <term>original: "uncouth"</term> division:
Water from Air by a separation,
And Fire from Air by a partitioning,
Each one preserved from all corruption;
As philosophers have specified a form,
Which by reason may not be denied.

Water separated prudently from Air,
Air from Fire, and Fire from Earth;
When the craft is understood and divided truly,
Without error or deception,
Every element is pure in its own nature <term>original: "complexion," referring to the specific balance of qualities in an element</term>.
As it pertains plainly to its part,
And as is perfectly remembered in this art."

### THE
# FIRST CHAPTER.

In the name of the holy Trinity,
I will write of this work briefly;
Leaving aside matters of detail <term>original: "circumstance"</term>,
And I promise to promote the truth:
I will not write figuratively,
But declare the matter plainly,
And how things must be made to agree <note>original: "accord"</note>,
By Nature’s true work and the help of our Lord:
The world is but one, enclosed by the roundness of the heavens,
Though diverse <note>original: "divers"</note> matters and forms are found within it:
The Earth, this world’s center, is held up by the air,
In its nature <term>original: "kinde"</term> it has nothing more than bare existence,
And is nearest to non-existence, as philosophers have told;
In its natural constitution <term>original: "complexion"</term>, it is completely dry and cold;
And now, regarding my figure of roundness <term>original: "rotundity"</term>,
I will show how elements agree and disagree:
And though the elements are so contrary,
Yet by heaven's influence, they are brought to unite,
And when they once bind a body together,
Nothing may loosen them without destroying the nature <term>original: "wrecke to the kinde"</term> of that thing.
First, fire in nature is hot and dry;
Air differs from fire only in moisture:
Earth differs from fire only in its coldness;
This harmony <note>original: "concord"</note> and discord every person sees:
Air is hot and moist in constitution and nature;
Water differs from air only in heat, we find:

So <note>This is the catchword "Soe" from the bottom of the original page, indicating the first word of the next page.</note>

So that in moisture we find them both one;

Now, of all things, blood is the noblest,

# CHAPTER II.
## *Of the procedure of the Work.*

Now, after the Matter, calculate the Manner
Of how to bring this work of ours about:
First, take the Matter in its crude state as it is,
Which will cost you little or nothing, I believe <note>original: "I wis" — certainly or truly</note>:
Sieve <note>original: "Searce" — to sift or strain through a fine cloth</note> it as clean as it can be,
Until it is entirely free from filth,
Which will be done in three or four hours;
Then it will be clear of its "ill humor" <note>In alchemy and early medicine, "humors" were fluids or qualities that needed to be balanced; an "ill humor" refers to impurities or unwanted qualities in the substance.</note>:
Then take the dregs <note>original: "Faces" (faeces) — the solid remains or sediment left after a liquid is poured off</note> which you shall find
In the same which the Matter left behind:
Purge them also with the noblest Element <note>Likely referring to Fire, the element used for purification and calcination.</note>,
Until they are burned <note>original: "brent"</note> to Earth:
Then you have a *Stone* of wonderful might,
A true secret obtained at small cost.
Take this Stone and use the "miller's craft" <note>The practice of grinding or milling the substance into a very fine powder.</note>,
Until it is a fine powder and made very soft:
Then give it the moisture which you took from it,
Then use it as you shall find described in this book.
But give it no other drink except its own kind,
For otherwise you do not follow my instructions.
Let it drink no more than will suffice;
Beware of "floods," I advise you: <note>In alchemy, "flooding" occurs when too much solvent (moisture) is added, which can "drown" the material and stop the chemical reaction.</note>
Then sieve <note>original: "search"</note> it twice again as you did before,
And continue to add its own liquor:
Thus, the first Order is brought to completion,
And your "foulest work" <note>The "foulest work" refers to the initial, messy stages of the alchemical process, often associated with the "Nigredo" or blackening stage, where the matter is broken down.</note> is fully performed.

## CHAPTER III.
### Of the Second Order.

Now I will clearly show the second method,
How you shall perform it with little difficulty: <note>original: "paine"</note>
When your three siftings <term>searsings: the process of sifting or straining to refine a substance</term> are completed according to my teaching, <note>original: "lore"</note>
Then break the Stone as you did before.
Then you must have a vessel,
Which must be shaped like an eggshell,
Into which vessel you must put the Matter,
Then ensure that it is well sealed up.
Divide the vessel into three parts,
Of which two parts must remain empty.
This vessel must be placed in a gentle <note>original: "kinde"</note> heat,
So that the Matter may naturally sweat;
The spirits must not be overwhelmed <note>original: "opprest"</note> by the fire,
For then you shall never achieve your desire,
Nor must your vessel be exposed to cold,
For then it will be ruined, as the *Philosophers* <note>Refers to the ancient alchemists and natural philosophers who established these traditions</note> have told;
But keep it in a temperate heat always,
For a period of forty days.
Then Blackness will appear to the sight;
That Blackness you must transform into Whiteness.
Take out the glass at the end of the forty days,
And see that you protect it from the cold;
And place it in a furnace with dry fire,
Until it becomes White, according to your desire,
Which will be accomplished in three weeks,
And dried completely of its moisture.

If you want to have both the Red and the White elixirs,
To make the Red, you must follow this order,
And for the White, do the same;
It must be fermented with *Lune* <note>original: "Lune" — Latin for "Moon," the alchemical symbol for Silver.</note> by name.

## CHAPTER 5.
### *How to Multiply.*

Now in this chapter I mean to show
How to multiply, so that you may know:
If iron is not regularly applied to the lodestone <note>original: "Load-stone" — a naturally magnetized mineral. The author uses this as an analogy: just as a magnet's power must be maintained, the Stone's power must be increased.</note>,
Its power will decrease wonderfully;
The species of all things, both great and small,
Are maintained by means of multiplication;
For if they are not multiplied, they decay,
But multiplication allows them to last forever.
After conception, all things receive natural food
To maintain their kind, as Nature sees fit:
So likewise, our *Stone* must certainly multiply,
Or else the species of that *Stone* will die.
And multiplication must involve a substance
That the thing being multiplied is most compatible with.
Fire, which burns perpetually,
Will die out if it lacks fuel <note>original: "Matter" — the physical substance, such as wood or oil, required to sustain the flame.</note>;

And for every bit you add in quantity,
Your medicine will truly increase by that same amount.
Yet you must use reason so as not to choke <note>original: "cloye" — to overfill or saturate until the process is stifled.</note>
The natural <note>original: "kind" — innate or life-giving.</note> heat with too much cooling.

### THE
## HERMIT’S TALE.

In pilgrimage only one thing I found
Of worth in *Lemnos* <note>original: "Lemnes"; an island in the Aegean Sea, traditionally the location of Vulcan's forge</note> near to *Vulcan’s* shop:
A crystal fountain running underground,
Between a valley and a mountain top.
Pleased with this sight, I bid a *hermit* tell
The story of the place, who there did dwell.

Within this vale a hollow, dusky cave
There is (he said) of great antiquity,
Where plumes of *Mars*—blue, green, and red—you have,
Torn from his crest for his iniquity.
The troop of smiths, as he with *Venus* lay,
Surprised and took him, yet he got away.

For as the *Cyclops* <note>The one-eyed giants who served as Vulcan's assistants</note> him in triumph brought
To limping *Vulcan* to receive his doom,
They lifted up his visor <term>original: "beaver"; the movable part of a helmet</term> and found naught
But vacant space and armor in the room.
Of the armor then they thought they had a good prize,
But working it, they found it disintegrate <term>original: "scyndarize"; to turn into cinders or dross, likely an alchemical term for the breakdown of a substance</term>.

The smiths, amazed at finding themselves deluded,
Sat all in council in their master's den;
Deliberating well, at length they concluded:
There is no equal war between gods and men.
Let’s find the angry god and crave pardon;
Let’s give him *Venus* to save our poor selves.

### The Hermit's Tale.

They fought in Heaven; *Mars* knew his deed <note>original: "fact"; from the Latin *factum*, meaning a deed or crime</note> was so bad,
He came out from there; then one began to tell:
*Saturn*, turned from his throne, had a place
Not far from there, right by this crystal well.
They went there and found two gods alone,
Sitting within a dark but glittering throne.

Down fell old *Vulcan* on his crooked knee,
And said, "Forgive, O mighty God of War,
My servants and myself (once a god like you);
Then use your will with *Venus*, my fair star."
"*Saturn*," said *Mars*, "and I must not yet part,
Though she for whom you are pardoned has my heart."

With this, the cuckold <note>A man whose wife is unfaithful; here referring to Vulcan, whose wife Venus was famously involved with Mars</note> with his sweaty troop
Went to his forge and seemed to bow <term>original: "make a leg"; to bow by drawing one leg back while bending the other</term>,
At every step where limping made him stoop,
In thanks to *Mars* for granting what he begged for;
In whose remembrance you shall always have
Cinders <term>original: "syndars"; ashes or dross left after smelting metal</term> and fetters in that hollow cave.

But let me tell you all that then happened:
*Jove* <note>Jupiter, the king of the gods</note>, seeing this and intending to do right by the smith,
Sent down a winged god <note>Mercury, the messenger of the gods</note> he trusted well,
Disguised in the form of a shining light,
Which, coming to the valley from the hill's high top,
Frightened all the smiths in *Vulcan's* shop.

A voice was heard from *Jove's* ambassador,
Summoning *Mars* to appear before the gods.
With *Saturn*, *Venus's* lover <term>original: "paramour"</term> came forth,
Thinking with might to gain the advantage over right.
Downward he came nine miles, and they upward four;
All met in mist; he fled, and they never went lower.

# The Hermit’s Tale.

*Vulcan* came hobbling up to see what was done;
He finds neither light, nor gods, but another shape.
To witness this deed <note>original: "fact"; from the Latin *factum*, meaning a deed or crime</note>, he calls the *Sun* <note>original: "Sonne"</note>,
Who immediately cries "Murder!" and hurried to escape.
   Some dying soul groaned out, "*Apollo*, stay!
   Help, wise *Apollo*, before you go away."

With this, *Apollo*, looking all around,
Espies this fountain and knows the voice was here;
And bowing down to find the person <note>original: "party"</note> out,
Himself immediately appears to himself <note>He sees his own reflection in the water</note>.
   He gazed there until a heavy shower of rain
   Took wise *Apollo* away from himself again.

"Farewell, *Apollo*," then *Apollo* said,
"Tomorrow, when this storm has fully passed,
I will return and bring some comforting aid,
By which I will free you before the final throw <term>original: "latter cast"; the final stage of a process or a final stroke of fortune</term>."
   Then it cried out as if its voice were spent,
   "Come, sweet *Apollo*!" and so it went downwards.

*Vulcan* went to his forge, the *Sun* to bed,
But both were up early <term>original: "betimes"</term> to meet again;
The next morning after the storm, a pale, dead soul
Was found at the bottom of this fair *fountain*.
   "Smith," said *Apollo*, "help to drain <term>original: "lade"; to bail or empty out liquid</term> this spring,
   That I may raise that dead thing yonder back to life."

Then *Vulcan* held *Apollo* by the heel,
While he drains the waters of the well;
Bowing and straining made *Apollo* feel
Blood from his nose, which fell into the fountain.
   "*Vulcan*," he said, "this occurrence <note>original: "accident"; in alchemical philosophy, a non-essential property or an unexpected event</note> of blood
   Is the only thing that will do this creature any good."

# Prolegomena

...over the room; and that with so great splendor, that it overcame the light that was kindled therein. Besides, the hermit refused to project it upon metal (as being unworthy of it) but made his experiment upon veronica and rue <note>original: "Veronica and Rue"; these are common herbs (speedwell and herb-of-grace), used here to show the stone's power over living plants rather than just base metals.</note>.

By the Magical or Prospective Stone, it is possible to discover any person in what part of the world soever, although never so secretly concealed or hidden—whether in chambers, closets, or caverns of the earth—for there it makes a strict investigation. In a word, it fairly presents to your view even the whole world, wherein to behold, hear, or see your desire. Nay more, it enables man to understand the language of the creatures, such as the chirping of birds, the lowing of beasts, and so on. It can convey a spirit into an image which, by observing the influence of heavenly bodies, shall become a true oracle; and yet this, as E.A. <note>Elias Ashmole (1617–1692), the celebrated antiquarian and compiler of this collection of alchemical texts.</note> assures you, is not in any way necromantic <note>original: "Necromanticall"; referring to black magic or the conjuring of the dead.</note> or devilish, but easy—wondrously easy—natural, and honest.

Lastly, as touching the Angelical Stone, it is so subtle, says the aforesaid author, that it can neither be seen, felt, nor weighed, but tasted only. The voice of man (which bears some proportion to these subtle properties) comes short in comparison; nay, the air itself is not so penetrable, and yet (O mysterious wonder!) it is a stone that will lodge in the fire to eternity without being prejudiced <note>meaning: without being harmed or diminished.</note>. It has a divine power, celestial and invisible, above the rest, and endows the possessor with divine gifts. It affords the apparition of angels and gives a power of conversing with them by dreams and revelations; nor dare any evil spirit approach the place where it lodges. Because it is a quintessence <term>quintessence</term> <note>In alchemy, the "fifth essence" or purest substance, which remains after the four elements (earth, air, fire, water) have been purified.</note> wherein there is no corruptible thing; and where the elements are not corrupt, no devil can stay or abide.

Saint Dunstan <note>A 10th-century Archbishop of Canterbury who was later associated with alchemical legends.</note> calls it the "Food of Angels," and by others it is termed the "Heavenly Viaticum" <note>original: "Viaticum"; usually refers to the Eucharist given to someone near death to sustain them on their journey to the afterlife.</note>, the "Tree of Life," and is undoubtedly (next under God) the true Alchochodon <term>Alchochodon</term> <note>original: Alchochodon; an astrological term referring to the planet that determines the length of a person's life.</note>, or Giver of Years. For by it, man's body is preserved from corruption, being thereby enabled to live a long time without food; nay, it is made a question whether any man who uses it can die. I do not wonder at this so much as I wonder why the possessors of it should desire to live—those who have those manifestations of glory and eternity presented to their fleshly eyes—but would rather desire to be dissolved and to enjoy the full fruition <note>meaning: the complete enjoyment or possession of a thing, here referring to the afterlife.</note>, rather than live where they must be content with the bare speculation <note>meaning: mere observation or contemplation.</note>.

### The Hermit’s Tale

He laid this down at *Apollo's* <note>original: "Apollo"; the Greek god of healing and light, frequently used in alchemy to symbolize the Sun or the perfected state of gold.</note> feet,
And said, "By curing one, you have saved three:

Offering themselves to you, as they are already yours.
Be our *physician*, and as we grow old,
We will bring enough to make new worlds of gold."

With that, this *hermit* took me by the hand
And led me to his cell; "Look here," he said,
"If you could but stay and truly understand
What you now see, you would know this mystery."
*I stayed, I saw, I tried, and understood:*
*A heaven on earth, an everlasting good.*

### A
# DESCRIPTION
## of the STONE.

Though *Daphne* <note>original: "Daphne"; in alchemical allegory, Daphne usually represents the "volatile" or feminine principle, often associated with Mercury or silver.</note> flies from bright *Phoebus* <note>original: "Phœbus"; a name for Apollo, the sun god, representing the "fixed" or masculine principle, heat, and gold.</note>,
    Yet they shall both be one,
    And if you understand this right,
You have our hidden *Stone* <note>original: "Stone"; the Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance said to transmute base metals into gold and grant long life.</note>.
For *Daphne* is fair and white:
    But *volatile* <term>original: "Volatile"; a substance that easily evaporates or changes state when heated; in alchemy, it represents the spirit that must be captured.</term> is she;
*Phoebus* is a *fixed* <term>original: "fixed"; a substance that remains stable and does not evaporate when exposed to heat; it represents the body or "sulfur" that anchors the spirit.</term> god of might,
    And he is red as blood.
*Daphne* is a *water nymph*,

Until they flow like wax,
    And you can see no smoke <note>original: "fume"; the absence of smoke or vapor indicates that the substance has become completely "fixed" and stable under heat.</note>,
Then you have all you need to ask for,
    Praise God and be thankful.

# The Placement of the *Glass* for the Time of the Putrefaction and Congelation of the MEDICINE.

> **The** *glass* <note>original: "Glasse"; the hermetically sealed vessel used in alchemical experiments.</note> with the *medicine* <note>original: "Medicine"; a common term for the substance of the Philosopher's Stone during its development.</note> must stand in the fire
> Forty days until it is black to the sight; (as you desire),
> It will remain in that blackness for forty days <note>In alchemy, the "black" stage is known as *Nigredo*, symbolizing the death or putrefaction of the base matter before it can be reborn.</note>
> And then forty days more, until it is white,
> And thirty more in the drying, if you wish to do it correctly;
> And then is the sulfur perfectly calcined <term>original: "Calcinate"; reduced to a powder or purified through prolonged heating.</term>,
> Prepared to drink up its own moisture.
>
> During this time, neither open nor shut the *glass*,
> But let it still remain for all the aforementioned days,
> Do not take it up from the furnace even once:
> For by cooling the matter, the medicine is ruined,
> Therefore, you must continue the fire always,
> In one consistent and moderate degree of heat,
> Until everything is white and the sulfur is complete.
>
> This heat is sufficient for this first principle,
> Which is the chief foundation of all our secrets,
> Without which knowledge, you must not attempt to make the Stone,
> If you labor your whole lifetime, you shall not prosper,
> Therefore, take care <note>original: "merry"; likely a scribal variant or shorthand for "marry," an interjection meaning "indeed" or "listen," or potentially "merely" in the sense of "be very careful."</note> that you do not fail.
> But first learn truly before you begin,
> And so you shall be better able to achieve success in the true working.

## A Philosophical Riddle. <note>original: "Ænigma Philosophicum"</note>

There is no light, but what lives in the *Sun*;
There is no *Sun*, but that which is twice begotten;
*Nature* and *Art* were the parents who first began:
By *Nature* it was, but *Nature* does not perfect it.
*Art* then takes what *Nature* left behind,
And out of *One* it makes a *twofold* work.

A *twofold* work it makes, but such a work
As admits no *division* at all
(See here where the *Secret* most of all lurks)
Unless it be a *mathematical* one. <note>This likely refers to a conceptual or symbolic division rather than a physical separation of the substance.</note>
It must be *two*, yet make it *one* and *one*,
And if you separate them, you take the way to make it *nothing*.

Look here at the *primary secret* of this *Art*,
Do not despise it but understand it correctly;
Whoever fails to attain this first part,
Shall never know *Art's* force nor *Nature's* might.
Nor yet have the power of *One* and *One* so mixed,
To make, by the *one* that is fixed, the *unfixed one* fixed. <note>In alchemy, "fixing" <term>fixation</term> is the process of transforming a volatile or liquid substance into a solid state that can endure fire without evaporating.</note>

->**D. D. W. Bedman.**<-

<summary>This page presents an alchemical riddle explaining that the "Sun" (the goal of the work) is produced by both Nature and Art working together. It emphasizes the paradoxical "Primary Secret": the alchemist must unite two substances into one "fixed" state that cannot be divided.</summary>

<keywords>Ænigma Philosophicum, alchemy, Nature, Art, Sun, Secret, fixed, unfixed, D. D. W. Bedman, paradox</keywords>

# Another Conclusion.

First calcine <term>heat to high temperatures to drive off volatile substances</term> and after putrefy <term>allow to rot or decompose as part of the purification process</term>,
Dissolve, distill, sublime <term>purify by turning into vapor and back to solid</term>, descend, and fix <term>solidify or make non-volatile</term>;
With *Aqua Vitae* <note>original: "Aquavitæ"; literally "Water of Life," usually referring to concentrated alcohol or a specialized alchemical solvent</note> wash and dry many times;
And make a marriage between the Body and Soul, with the Spirit in between.
If you cannot naturally mix them together in this way,
Then the Body shall utterly die in the flux <term>the state of being liquid or flowing</term>.
Bleeding and changing colors as you shall see;
He shall rise up and descend in the clouds <note>original: "In nubibus"</note>;
First up to the Moon <note>representing the stage of the White Stone or Silver</note> and after up to the Sun <note>representing the stage of the Red Stone or Gold</note>,
Only transported within a little glass tun <term>a large cask or vessel; here, the alchemical flask</term>.
When he arrives there, then the entire mastery <term>the successful completion of the Great Work</term> is won,
On which journey you shall not spend great wealth,
And you shall be glad that it was ever begun,
If you choose to attend to your work patiently.
Whoever shall make our Pearl and our Ruby <note>The Pearl represents the White Stone (transmuting to silver) and the Ruby represents the Red Stone (transmuting to gold)</note>,
Let him not forsake our starting principle:
For if his principle is true at the beginning,
And if he can skillfully bake it so,
Truly, at the end, he shall not regret his work.

<summary>This alchemical poem outlines the chemical and allegorical steps—calcination, distillation, and the "marriage" of elements—required to create the Philosopher's Stone. It emphasizes that a correct starting material and patient labor will lead to the "Pearl" and "Ruby" of alchemy.</summary>
<keywords>Alchemy, Calcination, Putrefaction, Aqua Vitae, Chemical Marriage, Moon and Sun, White Stone, Red Stone, Mastery</keywords>

## The Whole Science.

There is a body of a body,
And a soul and a spirit,
With two bodies they must be joined <note>original: "knete"</note>.

There are two earths, as I tell you,
And two waters dwell with them;
The one <note>original: "ton"</note> is white, the other is red,
To quicken <term>to bring to life</term> the bodies that are dead.

And one fire hidden in Nature,
And one air with them that performs the deed.
And all of it comes out of one kind <note>original: "kynde"; meaning one nature or substance</note>,
Mark this well, man, and keep it in mind.

---

Take *Mercury* from *Mercury* which is his wife,
For *Mercury’s* wife to *Mercury* makes great strife:
But *Mercury’s* wife’s wife,
To *Mercury* makes no strife.

---

And if you wed *Mercury* to *Mercury* with her wife,
Then shall *Mercury* and *Mercury* be merry with-
->out strife:<-
For *Mercury’s* wife to *Mercury* makes great strife,
But *Mercury’s* wife’s wife to *Mercury* makes no strife.

I will propose a riddle to you,
Of a common thing which most men know,
Which now in the Earth grows very rife <term>abundant</term>,
But is of small price, as all men know;
And that without root, stalk, or seed,
Wherewith to breed another of its kind:
Yet of that nature, that it cannot cease,
To increase itself if you plant it by pieces;
Right heavy by nature, yet forced to fly <note>This refers to "volatility"—the ability of a solid substance to be vaporized by heat.</note>,
Completely worthless <note>original: "Starke nought"</note> in the purse, yet good in the eye,
This "something" is "nothing," which seems very strange,
Having tasted the fire which makes the change:
And has many colors, yet shows but one,
This is the material of our *STONE* <note>The Philosopher's Stone, the legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold.</note>.

---

I asked Philosophy how I should
Have from her the thing I would,
She answered me when I was able,
To make the water malleable <note>Capable of being hammered or pressed into shape; a paradox, as liquids cannot be hammered.</note>,
Or else the way if I could find,
To measure out a yard of wind:
Then shall you have your own desire,
When you can weigh an ounce of fire:
Unless you can do these three,
Content yourself, you will not get me.

Let the old man drink wine until he urinates:
The means to the blessed Stone <term>the Philosopher's Stone</term> is:
And in that menstrual water <note>original: "menstrous water"; in alchemy, this usually refers to a potent solvent or the "mercurial" starting liquid.</note> drown,
The radiant brightness of the Moon <term>symbolic of silver</term>,

If you will apply yourself to his Medicine <note>the alchemical elixir or the process of transformation</note>,
Make first heavy, hard, hot, and dry:

If you can dissolve the Fixed <note>turning a solid substance into a liquid or gas</note>,
And cause that which is Dissolved to fly <note>to vaporize or become volatile</note>,
Then bring that which is Flying to Fixing <note>to solidify a vapor back into a stable, non-volatile state</note>,
Then may you live most happily.

<margin>Page 6. line 1.</margin> **TO the honor of God---**

<image-desc>A large ornamental drop cap letter 'F' depicting a landscape with a building and a vessel in the foreground.</image-desc>

From the first word of this *Introduction* <note>original: "Proeme"</note>, and the *initial letters* of the six following *chapters* (discovered by *acromonosyllabics* and *syllabic acrostics* <term>literary devices where the first syllables or words of sections form a hidden message</term>), we may collect the *author's name* and place of *residence*. For those letters (together with the first line of the *seventh chapter*) speak thus:

->**Thomas Norton of Bristol;**<-
->**A perfect Master you may him trust.**<-

Such like *fancies* <note>imaginative or clever devices</note> were the results of the wisdom and humility of the *ancient philosophers* (who, when they intended not an absolute concealment of *persons, names, mysteries, etc.*), were accustomed to hide them by *transpositions, acrostics, isogrammatics, symphoniacs*, and the like. These the searching *Sons of Art* <term>a traditional name for alchemists</term> might possibly unriddle, but they were designed to remain concealed things to others. Furthermore, if questioned, no other answer should be returned than that of the (a) Angel to Manoah: *His name was Peli, that is to say, admirable and secret.* <note>original Latin/Hebrew reference: "His name was Peli, to wit, admirable and secret." From Judges 13:18.</note>
<margin>(a) Judges 13:18.</margin>

In imitation of whom, it is probable our *author* (not so much seeking the vanity of a name as wanting to assist the lovers of *wisdom*) thus modestly and ingeniously unveils himself; although to the generality of the world he meant to pass unknown, as appears by his own words:

<margin>(b) Norton's Ordinal, page 6.</margin>
> (b) **For that I desire not worldly fame,**
> **But your good prayers; unknown shall be my name.**

<margin>(c) On the Illustrious Writers of England, page 666.</margin>
<margin>(d) On the Writers of Britain, Century 11, folio 67.</margin>
(c) *John Pitts* (drawing from *John Bale*, (d) who in turn drew from *Robert Record*) relates that this *Thomas Norton* was the most skilled alchemist of his time <note>original: "Alchymista suo tempore peritissimus"</note> and much more curious in the studies of *philosophy* than others. Yet they pass some indecent and abusive censures upon him, regarding this "vain and frivolous" science,

Science, as they are pleased to term it—and I find they had no better opinion even of Hermetic learning <term>Hermetic learning: the mystical and alchemical traditions attributed to the legendary figure Hermes Trismegistus</term> itself. Indeed, not every man who is educated as a scholar is born to enjoy or be successful in every art; some love one, some another, but few love all. This arises from the various influences of the stars, which create different inclinations and interests in men according to the different constitutions and temperatures <note>original: "Temperatures"; referring to the balance of the four bodily humors</note> of their bodies. Thus, commonly, what a man does not enjoy or does not know, he despises or condemns, yet seldom with any show of reason. But it is no good conclusion for blind men to affirm the sun has no light simply because they were never so happy as to see it. For though you yourself (says Conwrath) are ignorant of a matter, it is not denied to others to know the same. However, our author was so happy as to <margin>e) Ordinal p. 33.</margin> become a master of this science very early: which he learned in (e) forty days, and when he was

<margin>f) Ordinal p. 88.</margin>
-> **(f) Scarcely at the age of twenty-eight years,** <-

He earnestly moved his master (who is generally thought to be George Ripley <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490) was a famous English alchemist and author of "The Compound of Alchymy."</note>) to communicate the Red Medicine <term>Red Medicine: the final stage of the Philosopher's Stone, capable of transmuting base metals into gold</term> to him; after some time (finding him capable of it), his master accordingly did so.

Much more might be said in honor of this author, but I refer the reader to the *Ordinal* itself, which will abundantly satisfy.

Besides this work—which is called by both Pitts and Bale <note>John Pits and John Bale were 16th/17th-century biographers and bibliographers.</note> *A Summary of Alchemy* <note>original: "Epitomen Alchymie"</note>, but by himself

In the time of Henry VIII, there flourished nine brothers of the family of the Nortons, and all were knights. One of them, namely Sir Sampson Norton, Master of the Ordnance <note>Master of the Ordnance: a high-ranking military official responsible for artillery and supplies.</note> to the said King (an office of great honor, and not usually con-<margin>i) Weever's Funeral Monuments folio 526.</margin> ferred but upon men who were very eminent), lies buried in (i) *Fulham Church near London*. **D**oubtless Norton was truly sensible of the high injuries done to learned men through the erroneous transcriptions of their books, and had shared in the unimaginable misfortune which thereby befell the students in philosophy at that time. --- Page 463 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Thomas Norton's "Ordinal of Alchemy," specifically addressing the challenges of transmitting secret knowledge before the age of printing and the importance of oral tradition between master and student.</meta>

<page-num>439</page-num>

<margin>k) The first printing press was set up in Westminster Abbey by Simon Islip in the year 1471, and William Caxton was the first to practice it there. See Stowes Survey, page 525.</margin>
Books were only manuscripts (printing had not yet served an apprenticeship in England (k) when he wrote this *Ordinal*), and in that regard, he lays this weighty charge upon unfaithful *scribes* who negligently or willfully alter their *copy*. By doing so, even the most cautious *students* are encumbered with doubts and misled, or plunged into unhappy *errors*.

How common a fault this was among the *transcribers* of former times may appear by *Chaucer*, who (I am confident) took as great care as any man to be served by the best and most heedful *scribes*, and yet we find him complaining against *Adam*, his scrivener, for the very same thing:

<margin>l) Chaucer to his Scrivener.</margin>
> (l) So often a day I must your work renew,
> To correct it and also to rub and scrape;
> And all is through your negligence and haste. <note>original: "rape"; in Middle English, this meant haste or speed.</note>

But as in other *arts* and *sciences* the fault is scarcely pardonable, it is especially so in *Hermetic learning* <term>Hermetic learning: the study of alchemy and occult philosophy attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</term>, where the *injury* may prove irreparable.

<margin>m) Ordinal page 11.</margin>
> (m) And changing even one single syllable,
> May make this book unprofitable.

---

Page 33, line 13: 
> If I should write, I should my fealty break,
> Therefore mouth to mouth I must needs speak.

This is part of the letter which *Norton's Master* wrote when he invited him to come and receive the *secret* by word of mouth; for without a breach of his *oath*, he dared not commit it to writing, lest he might "cast the *children's bread to dogs*" <note>A biblical reference (Matthew 15:26) often used by alchemists to mean giving sacred knowledge to the unworthy or uninitiated.</note>.

In like manner, *Aristotle* refused to communicate to *Alexander* by letter things appertaining to this *mystery*, until a personal meeting might allow him to do it *by word of mouth* <note>original: "viva voce"</note>. For thus writes *Lydgate* <note>John Lydgate (c. 1370–1451), an English poet and monk.</note> in his translation of *Aristotle's Secrets of Secrets* <note>original: "Secreta secretorum"; a popular medieval treatise purportedly containing Aristotle's advice to Alexander the Great.</note>:

> There are secrets of matters high and low,
> Hidden in nature, concealed and secret,
> Which Alexander desired to know;
> By Aristotle a certain privacy,
> Not specified, was kept close within himself,
> Which was delayed by great foresight,
> Until he himself came into his presence.

<margin>Chapter 2.</margin>
And this was for fear his *writings* should come to the view of those whose eyes were not worthy of reading such sublime *secrets*, and thereby suffer the contempt of the profane *vulgar* <note>The "common people" or the uneducated masses.</note>, or be abused by wicked men for wicked uses. (For a *secret* discovered will not fail to do *injury* to one party or another), which (if it should happen by his means) might render him *criminal* before *God*, and a presumptuous violator of the *Celestial Seals*.

<margin>G. br.</margin>
However, the ancient *philosophers* have used writings, both obscure and obvious, so that the *ignorant* might be more *ignorant*, but the *wise* understand and profit—one being deceived, the other allured. And like *Aristotle* who (publishing his *Acroamatic Discipline* <note>original: "Acromaticall Discipline"; referring to Aristotle's esoteric teachings intended only for his closest students</note> and) being therefore criticized by *Alexander* (because he alone had learned them from him) answered *that he had written them, and* <note>original: "Se scripsisse, &"; the full historical quote is "I have written them, and yet not written them," meaning they were written in such a way that only those already taught could understand them.</note>

<summary>This page explains the necessity of oral transmission in alchemy to prevent errors by scribes and to keep secrets from the "unworthy." It cites Chaucer’s frustration with poor copying and Aristotle’s refusal to write down his deepest mysteries for Alexander the Great.</summary>
<keywords>printing press, William Caxton, scribes, Geoffrey Chaucer, Hermetic learning, Thomas Norton, Aristotle, Alexander the Great, secrecy, Secreta Secretorum, John Lydgate</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the commentary on the secretive nature of alchemical transmission, contrasting the errors of physical manuscripts (discussed on the previous page) with the intentional obscurity used by alchemical authors to protect their "Great Work."</meta>

<page-num>(440)</page-num>

<margin>Anonymous authors.</margin>
[They claim] not to have written; they have published indeed, but for readers who do not understand. <note>original Latin: "non scripsisse; edidisse quidem sed legentibus non intelligentibus."</note> They have taken much pains through *enigmatic* and *metaphorical* revelations (according to their preferred idioms) to point out the *Philosopher's Mercury*. With a unanimous consent, they have asserted the wondrous operations of an *agent* and *patient* <term>Agent and Patient: in alchemy, the active and passive principles—often symbolized as male and female—that react together to produce the philosopher's stone</term> united; but *we must not look for the name of that thing in plain words which, until now, no man has ever dared to name*. For they have locked that up *within the cabinet of the heart* <note>original Latin: "in scrinio pectoris"</note> and intentionally deprived it of light.

Their chief study was to wrap up their secrets in *fables* and spin out their fancies in *veils* and *shadows*. These *rays* <note>original: "Radii"</note> seem to extend in every direction, yet they all meet at a common center and point only at one thing.

<margin>o) Chaucer, Prologue to his own Tale.</margin>
> (o) And thus you know that every Evangelist
> Who tells us of the pains of Jesus Christ,
> Does not say everything exactly as his fellow does,
> But nonetheless, their meaning is all true.
> And all agree in their meaning,
> Even if there is a difference in their telling.
> For some of them say more and some say less
> When they express his piteous passion.
> I mean Mark, Matthew, Luke, and John,
> But doubtless their meaning is all one.

<margin>p) *On the Wonders of Alchemy*, second part, page 28.</margin>
And to this effect is the statement of *Count Trevisan* <note>Bernard Trevisan (1406–1490): a famous Italian alchemist known for his long search for the philosopher's stone.</note>: (p) He who well understands the philosophers shall find they agree in all things, but those who are not the *Sons of Art will think they clash most foully*.

---

->Page 33, line 15: —— My heir unto this art<-
->I will you make ——<-

There has always been a continuous *succession* of philosophers in all ages, although the heedless world has seldom taken notice of them. For the ancients usually (before they died) *adopted* one person or another as their "sons," whom they knew to be well-fitted with qualities like those set down in the letter that *Norton's* master wrote to him when he sent to make him his heir to this science. And let no man expect to attain it for any reason other than pure virtue's sake, as was seen in the case of *Tonfile* <note>Tonfile: a character in Thomas Norton's "Ordinal" who unsuccessfully attempted to learn alchemy through bribery and greed rather than merit.</note>.

<margin>q) *The Ordinal*, page 41.</margin>
> (q) —— For money <note>original: "Almes"</note> I will not provide it;
> To disclose it plainly has never been done before.

<margin>r) Ibid., page 35.</margin>
Neither rewards nor terrors (be they ever so generous or dreadful) can wrench this secret out of the heart of a *philosopher*; among others, witness (r) *Thomas Dalton* <note>Thomas Dalton: a 15th-century English alchemist who was reportedly imprisoned and threatened with death by nobles who wanted his secret, yet he refused to reveal it.</note>.

Now, under what ties and commitments this secret is usually delivered (when bestowed by word of mouth) may appear in the weighty obligations of that oath which *Charnock* <note>Thomas Charnock (c. 1524–1581): an alchemist who recorded his apprenticeship under a master who taught him the secret of the "Stone."</note> took before he obtained it; for his master spoke to him thus:

And if it so happened that they did not meet with anyone whom they conceived in all respects worthy of their *adoption*, (s) they then resigned the secret into the hands of *God*, who best knew where to bestow it. However, they seldom left the world before they left some written *legacy* behind them, which (being the offspring of their *brain*) stood in the room and place of *children*, and becomes to us both *parent* and *schoolmaster*. In these writings, they were so universally kind as to call all *students* by the dear and affectionate title of *sons* (t)—*Hermes* <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy.</note> setting the first precedent—wishing all were such who take the pains to tread their fathers' steps and industriously follow the rules and dictates they passed over to posterity, in which they faithfully revealed the whole *mystery*;

<margin>u) Ordinal, page 10.</margin>
> u) **As lawfully as they may by their loyalty,**
> **By the permission of the terrifying Judge on Doomsday.**

In these *legitimate children* (their books) they lived longer than in their *adopted sons* (their students); for though the students certainly perished in a single *lifetime* <note>original: "Age"</note>, yet their *writings* (as if when they died their souls had been *transmigrated* into them) seemed *immortal*—enough, at least, to perpetuate their memories until *time* should be no more. And to be the *father* of such *sons* is (in my *opinion*) a most noble happiness.

<margin>w) Randolph's Poems, page 63.</margin>
> w) *Let commoners* <term>original: "clownes"; here meaning unlearned or rustic men</term> *produce heirs and wealth; when I am gone,*
> *And the great bugbear, grisly death,*
> *Shall snatch this idle breath,*
> *If I leave a poem, that poem is my son.*

Judicial Astrology <note>The branch of astrology used to predict earthly events and human fate.</note> is the key to natural magic, and natural magic is the door that leads to this blessed Stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

For if there is anything in (what we call) magic other than a searching into those hidden virtues which God has been pleased to bestow upon created things (though closely locked away by the general Curse <note>Refers to the biblical Fall of Man, which was believed to have hidden the true nature and power of the natural world.</note>) whereby we may aptly and naturally apply active causes to passive subjects <note>original: "Agents to Patients"</note>—I say, if there is anything else in it, they are only subtle falsehoods that shelter and shroud themselves under that title. Being in league with the Devil, they make use of his assistance in their works to counterfeit and corrupt the admirable wisdom of the *Magi*, between whom there is as large a difference as between angels and devils.

*What has been said so far will not (I presume) offend the ears of the most pious, for here are no* incantations, *no* words, *no* circles, *no* charms, *nor other fragments of invented fooleries; nor is there any need for them.* Nature *(with whom true* magicians *only deal) can work without them; she finds the* matter, *and they provide the* art *to help and assist her, and that is* all.

(*h*) As a learned gentleman said (whose *Defense of Judicial Astrology*, published long ago, remains firm and unrefuted despite the weak attacks of any opponent): *The heavenly influences never cease to flow into us. In that regard, she is properly called (m) *An instrument of the armies from above*: things are steered according to her current *condition*. The reason is because the *moisture* and *sap* that should feed them is exceedingly diminished. Yet, this is the fittest time for cutting down *timber*, or whatever else we would preserve from decaying.

In a word, by *Elections* we may *govern*, *order*, and *produce* things as we please: *Every man is the architect of his own fortune* <note>original: "Faber quisq; Fortunæ propriæ"</note>.
