Page 100, line 1. **Is a direct and airy Ascendant.**

In this line and the first ten that follow, the author’s rules for framing an <term>Election</term> <note>original: "Election"; the practice of selecting an auspicious astrological time to begin a task</note> are laid down. Agreeable to these rules, he constructs for you <term>Schemes</term> <note>original: "Scheames"; astrological charts or diagrams</note> (calculated for a latitude of about 51 degrees) which are placed before the sixth chapter. I have caused these to be exactly copied from the original, although I must acknowledge that some <term>Planets</term> are not placed in the exact order (regarding <term>houses</term> and <term>signs</term>) that astronomical rules direct and the doctrine of astrology requires. 

For example, in the first house of the first figure, you have Mercury at 7 degrees of Sagittarius, the <term>Ascendant</term> <note>original: "Ascendent"; the sign and degree rising on the eastern horizon</note> at 2 degrees of Sagittarius, and then the Sun at 18 degrees of the same sign. However, since 2 degrees of Sagittarius is fewer degrees than the 7 degrees where Mercury is placed, it should precede it. Again, in the second figure, you have both Mercury and the Moon in the 11th house, though they should rightly be positioned in the 10th. This is because the 20th degree of Aquarius is the <term>Cusp</term> <note>original: "Cuspe"; the boundary line between two houses in a chart</note> of the 11th, and therefore all planets in fewer degrees of that sign fall into the 10th house. Besides, you see Venus placed in every figure so far from the Sun that astronomers must consider it absurd, since she is never more than 48 degrees away from him. Yet, in the third figure, she does not even come within the range of a <term>Trine</term> <note>original: "△ Aspect"; a favorable astrological angle of 120 degrees</note> aspect; indeed, in the second, she is almost in <term>Opposition</term> <note>original: "☍"; an aspect of 180 degrees</note> to him.

Regarding their position: I could have placed them in houses according to the rules of the art, but I chose instead to let them stand as I found them in the original. I am well-assured they were positioned this way by design, and not through ignorance or mistake; for our author shows himself to be a learned astrologer and too careful a writer to be guilty of either. And though it may seem contrary to the art for Venus to be so far distant from the Sun, it is consistent with his rule of <term>Election</term> that she is so often placed in the 4th house (especially since the sign she is <term>exalted</term> <note>original: "exalted"; a sign where a planet's influence is particularly strong</note> in falls there), because he requires the ruler of that house to be fortunate.

<margin>o) Norton's *Ordinal*, page 100.</margin>
->(o) **For this is the <term>hidden treasure</term> <note>original: "Thesaurum absconditum"</note> of old scholars.**<-

Furthermore, the planets as they stand here in their signs and houses are not arranged as if these figures were the actual chosen times for the author’s own alchemical operations (or anyone else's in that profession). Instead, they are probably fictional and invented only to demonstrate his rules. To satisfy myself in this matter, I have taken some pains to calculate the positions of the planets for several years around the author’s time, but I cannot find the three <term>superior planets</term> <note>original: "Superiors"; Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars</note> and the position of the Sun in those signs where he has placed them.

<margin>p) Aristotle.</margin>
It is also worth our observation to see how the author continues to use "veils and shadows"—as he does in other parts of the <term>Mystery</term> <note>original: "Mistery"; here referring to the secret art of alchemy</note>—even in the very symbols of some of the planets. He does not show them using the characters commonly used now (or then), but hieroglyphically, in figures that match their natures. Yet, (p) a diversity of names (or figures) makes no difference in the things they signify. For Saturn is represented by a spade, Jupiter by a <term>miter</term> <note>original: "Miter"; a bishop's tall, pointed hat</note>, Mars by an arrow, Venus by a beautiful face, and Mercury by the figure (in those days) usually stamped upon the back of English coins. Only the Sun and the Moon are left in the style that the ancients gave them.

->**Trust not to all Astrologers, I say why:**<-
->**For that Art is as secret as Alchemy.**<-

Astrology is a profound *Science*: The depth this *Art* lies obscured in is not to be reached by every common plummet <note>original: "vulgar Plumet"; a lead weight used by sailors to measure the depth of water.</note> that attempts to sound it. Never was any *Age* so pestered with a multitude of *Pretenders* who would be accounted (and do not hesitate to style themselves) *Masters*, yet are not worthy to wear the Badge of illustrious *Urania* <note>The Muse of Astronomy and Astrology in Greek mythology.</note>. And (oh, it is to be lamented!) the swarm is likely to increase until, through their ignorance, they become the ridiculous object of the *Enemies* of *Astrology*; (would that that were all,) and *eclipse* the glory of that *light* which, if judiciously dispensed to the *World*, would cause *admiration*; but when unskillfully exposed, becomes the scorn and contempt of the *common people*.

He that understands no more of *Astrology* (nor will make a further use of it) than to boast with a few *Terms* in a *Horary Question* <term>Horary Question</term> <note>A branch of astrology where a chart is cast to answer a specific question based on the moment the question is asked.</note> is no more worthy to be esteemed an *Astrologer* than he who has only learned *Hebrew* may be accounted a *Cabalistic Rabbi* <note>A teacher of Jewish mysticism; the author suggests that knowing the language is not the same as knowing the deep spiritual secrets.</note>. It is true, he may be so full of words as to amuse the unlearned with the *canting* noise of them, but what is that if compared to the full and entire knowledge of the *Language*? Yet of this sort at present have started up various illiterate *Professors* (and *Women* are among the number) who even make *Astrology* the go-between and pander to all manner of iniquity, prostituting chaste *Urania* to be abused by every corrupt *Interest*. And what will be the issue? (I wish it may prove no *prophecy*.) Before long, *Astrology* shall be denounced as an *Impostor* because it is made use of as a decoy <note>original: "Stale"</note> for all bad *practices*, and a laudable *Faculty* is used to support the trickery <note>original: "legerdimane"; sleight of hand or deception.</note> of a *cheat*. And besides, having now grown famous by the true *predictions* of some of her able and honest *Sons*, she shall grow into as much disgrace and infamy by the unskillful *prognostics* of ignorant, *illegitimate bastards*. Rather than accusing themselves when they fail to find the truth in their *judgments*, they will not hesitate to condemn *Astrology* itself as defective and lame in what their slothful negligence or ignorant blindness was not able to find out. And therefore *Norton* <note>Thomas Norton, the 15th-century author of the *Ordinal of Alchemy*.</note> here speaks truly: that *Astrology* (take it with all its complexities) is as *secret* or *mysterious* as *Alchemy*, and as difficult to be thoroughly and perfectly understood.

There are in *Astrology* (I confess) shallow *brooks* through which young *beginners* <note>original: "Tyroes"</note> may wade; but withal, there are deep *fords* over which even the *giants* themselves must swim. Such is the *Doctrine* of *Nativities* <term>Nativities</term> <note>The study of an individual's birth chart to determine their character and destiny.</note>, *Directions* <term>Directions</term> <note>Predictive techniques used to determine the timing of events in a person's life.</note>, *Annual Revolutions* <term>Annual Revolutions</term> <note>Also known as Solar Returns; a chart calculated for the exact moment the Sun returns to its position at birth to predict the year ahead.</note> and whatever else depends upon them belonging to *Man*, the little *world* <note>The Microcosm.</note>. Regarding the violent nature of the Medicine <note>In alchemy, the "Medicine" often refers to the Philosopher's Stone or the substance in its final stages of transformation.</note>, which is indeed deadly because its *Nature* is so infinitely stronger than *man's* that it overcomes his *spirits* and poisons him; *Norton* therefore drops a hint about which parts an operator ought to *protect* <note>original: "Arme"</note>, and from where to *draw breath*. He means by this that the orifices of the body should be tightly closed (through which there is such an open passage that a *strong vapor* would fly as quickly as lightning into the *inmost parts*) while the *vessel* is being opened. But how to breathe in the meantime is the *difficulty*. We have *practices* somewhat similar to it, such as those who attempt to stay long under *water*, etc.

And therefore, let this be a sufficient *warning* to young *practitioners* in this *science*: when they work upon a *matter* and bring it (as they suppose) to some perfection, if they can endure the opening of their *vessel* without being *protected*, they may rest satisfied that nothing is more certain than that their *matter* is not the *Philosophers' Mercury* <note>A key alchemical substance, the "universal solvent" or the base for the Stone; it was said to be highly volatile and dangerous.</note>, and their *practice* is erroneous.

## In the year of Christ 1477, this work was begun ———

<margin>a) Isaacson's *Chronology*, folio 468.</margin>
<margin>b) Stow's *Annals*, folio 426.</margin>
In the search I have made for *authentic manuscripts* to complete this *work*, a private *gentleman* lent me a very fine one of *Norton's Ordinal* <term>Ordinal</term> <note>The *Ordinal of Alchemy* is Thomas Norton's most famous poem, written in 1477.</note>, which I chiefly followed; yet I did not neglect to compare it with fourteen other *copies*. It was written on *vellum* and in an ancient formal hand <note>original: "sett Hand"</note>, very exact and exceedingly neat. The *figures* (from which I caused those printed here to be *engraved*) were also most neatly and exquisitely limned <note>original: "lym'd"; meaning painted or illuminated by hand.</note>, and were better work than those in *King Henry* the Seventh’s own *book* (as I am informed by those who have seen both). It had placed in the middle and bottom of the *decorative borders* <note>original: "Compartiments"</note> of *flowers*, *birds*, and *beasts*, the *Neville coat of arms*, along with others which that family quartered. This induced me to believe it to be the *original* (or one exactly copied from it) presented by the *author* to *George Neville*, then *Archbishop* of *York*, who was a most wealthy and *magnificent bishop*. This is apparent not only by the rich *(a)* *jewel* he offered at *Becket's tomb*, but also for the great and stately *entertainment* <note>A massive feast or banquet.</note> he provided at *More* in *Hertfordshire* for *King Edward* IV. To make that event more magnificent, he brought forth a *(b)* vast *treasure* of *silver plate* that he had hidden during the distractions of former years. All of this the *King* seized, along with his *money* and *goods* then valued at £20,000 (a far more considerable sum of *money* in those days than now); the King even made a *crown* for himself out of the *Archbishop's miter*, which was set with precious stones.

<margin>c) See the Preface.</margin>
<margin>d) Godwin’s *Successors*, page 482.</margin>
<margin>e) Godwin, same page.</margin>
I have been informed that there was great *correspondence* between this *Archbishop* and the *Hermetic philosophers* of his time. This is partly confirmed to me by *Ripley's (c) dedication* of his *Medulla* <note>George Ripley's *Medulla Alchimiae* (The Marrow of Alchemy), written in 1476.</note> to him in the year *1476*, as well as the presentation of this *Ordinal* by *Norton*. Although I find the said *Archbishop* died the same year this *Ordinal* was begun to be written, I cannot yet learn the certain time of that year. However, it was towards the end of it when his successor (*Lawrence Booth*) was *consecrated*, namely on *(d) September 25*. Besides, in all probability, he did not lie sick for long, because he died (at *Blyth*) while on a *(e) journey* from *York*. So the *book* might have been finished and presented (or if not presented, at least intended) before he died, even though it was begun that same year.

<meta>This page continues Elias Ashmole's commentary on the English alchemist George Ripley and his seminal work, the *Twelve Gates*. It focuses on the validity of Ripley’s later writings compared to his earlier, failed experiments.</meta>

->*Happy is the man who is made cautious by the dangers of others.*<- <note>original: "Felix quem faciunt aliena pericula cautum."</note>

In this work, he beseeches all men, wherever they shall meet with any of his experiments written by him or that go under his name (from the year 1450 to the year 1470), either to burn them or give them no credit. They were written according to his own estimation at the time, not based on proof; and (after testing them) he found them false and vain. For that is how long he was seeking the Stone, but in the truth of practice, he had not found it until toward the end of that year. And then, he says, "I found him whom my soul loves" <note>original: "Inveni quem diligit anima mea," a quote from the Song of Solomon often used by alchemists to signify the successful discovery of the Philosopher's Stone.</note>.

So this *Treatise of the 12 Gates*, being written the year after, is unquestionably to be relied upon because it was penned from grounded experimental practice, as he himself testifies in his *Admonition*:

<margin>h) Ripley’s *Admonition*.</margin>
> h) **I never saw the work truly but once,**
> **Of which in this treatise the truth I have told.**

In this (for the student’s safeguard), he gives an account of his own erroneous experiments, following the examples of Chaucer, Richardus Anglicus, Dionisius, Zacharius, the noble Bernard of Trevisan, and various other honest and conscientious philosophers.

<margin>
i) The year 1649.
k) Preface to the *Works of G. Ripley*.
</margin>
Ludovicus Combachius (who has (i) lately published several of Ripley's works in Latin) tells us (k) that he then had in his hands these *Twelve Gates* rendered in most pure elegiac verse <term>elegiac verse</term> <note>A poetic form consisting of couplets, traditionally used for serious or meditative subjects.</note> by one Nicholas May at the command of the Emperor Rudolph II. He says he would have willingly added it to what he published (which was translated out of English into Latin verse by Sir Edward Kelley) for a better understanding of the work, but the copy was not his own.

<margin>l) Printed at Toulouse.</margin>
The learned Faber (1646) bestowed much pains and cost in publishing to the world (l) Basil Valentine’s *Triumphal Chariot of Antimony* and others in one volume. In the argument of that book, "George Ripley, a most learned and wonderful English Canon, in whom there is nothing false or superfluous regarding the manifestation of the properties and natures of all metals" <note>original: "Georgius Riplæus Canonicus Anglus doctissimus & mirandus in quo nihil falsi & supervacui ad metallorum omnium proprietates, & naturas manifestandas."</note>, is thus ingeniously acknowledged. He further assures us that Ripley’s works are worthy to keep pace with the best philosophers. He knows that policy in printing is surest, and appeals well to the judicious reader, to begin with a good work and end with the best—to which final place he refers our Ripley. 

But I must tell the reader that on page 338, and so to the end, he is by mistake called "Triplanus" instead of "Riplæus." There are other similar notorious faults for which the printer (most likely) is guilty, such as giving Isaac Holland the name of "Irfacus." Cornelius Drebbel he prints as "Tornelius" (and sometimes "Fornelius") "Prebellianus." 

Besides these, there are further causes for objection to other parts of the work (too many to be mentioned here). Among the rest, Faber says they were all rendered into Latin out of Dutch, and that this piece of Ripley's, which he there calls *Triplanus on the Philosopher’s Stone* (but is indeed an epitome <term>epitome</term> <note>A summary or condensed version of a larger work.</note> of these *12 Gates*), was translated out of Dutch into Latin by one Nicholas Barnard, a philosopher. He implies it was originally written in the German tongue, which is very false, injurious to our author, and dishonorable to our nation.

So much for the work; and now to say something regarding our author. Philemon Holland, in his translation of Camden’s *Britannia* printed in 1636...

In the *progress* this *science* has made throughout the *world*, we may find that *God* has always been pleased to bring certain select and eminent *men* onto the stage in various ages. ...parts of *Art* <note>original: "Art," referring to the various branches of science, medicine, and alchemy</note> asunder, which *Nature* has joined in a harmonious *agreement*, and whose wide breaches honest-hearted *philosophers* endeavor to mend through a friendly *reconciliation*. <meta>This page continues Elias Ashmole’s defense of sigils and talismans, explaining the theory of "Signatures"—the belief that physical objects bear the marks and qualities of the celestial bodies that govern them.</meta>

Roots, seeds, fruits, and even crude stones, *flints*, and other inferior *bodies* [bear these marks].

Nor are these remarkable *Signatures* <note>original: "Signatures," the theory that plants and objects have physical features that reveal their medicinal or magical properties</note> made and described by *chance* (for there is a certain *Providence* which leads all things to their end, and which makes nothing except for some purpose). Rather, they are the *characters* and *figures* of those *stars* by which they are principally governed. Along with these particular *stamps*, they also have peculiar and different virtues bestowed upon them. What *artists* <note>In this context, "artists" refers to practitioners of alchemy or natural magic</note> do regarding these *characters* is only to pursue the track that is beaten out by *Nature*. And the more the *matter* upon which such *impressions* are made is suitable to the *qualities* of those *stars* whose *characters* it is signed with, the more apt and inclined it will be to receive those virtues that shall empower it to produce an *effect* in the things to which it is applied.

Nevertheless, this is not all, for this body must have a soul, as it were, infused into it, and be impregnated with a *celestial* vitality; otherwise, it remains *ineffectual* and *dead*. In this respect, other means must be found before we can obtain that *effect*. Therefore, we are to consider that the soul of the world is not confined, nor are the *celestial influences* limited. Instead, they emit and communicate their *virtues* indifferently to all—to things *artificially* made as well as to those that are *naturally* generated—though sometimes they are more vigorous and powerful, and at other times less, according to the different *aspects* <note>original: "Aspects," the angular positions of planets relative to each other in astrology</note> under which they are wrought. 

In this regard, a fit *election* <note>term: "election" refers to the astrological practice of choosing the most auspicious time to begin an action or create an object</note> must be built up from the foundation of *astrology*, suitable to the *nature* of the *operation* proposed. When this is achieved, and the *stars* find a *figure* aptly disposed for receiving them, they immediately *impress* their virtue. Retaining this virtue, the objects afterward operate upon things they find to be similar. And this is not strange if we reflect upon common experiments with the *loadstone* <note>original: "Loadestone," a naturally magnetized mineral (magnetite)</note>. When it communicates its virtue to a piece of *iron* (a thing made fit by *nature* to attract and retain it), that *piece* thereby becomes strong enough to communicate this virtue to a third. But if we should consider the *operations* of this *magnet* thoroughly (which proceed only from a *natural principle*), there is no other *mystery*—whether *celestial*, *elemental*, or *earthly*—which can be too hard for our *belief*.

Moreover, these *celestial virtues* and peculiar *gifts* are not infused into *individual* and particular things by the *Idea* and by means of the *soul* of the *world* alone. They are also invited there through the *obedientiality* <note>original: "Obedientiality," meaning the receptive capacity or readiness of matter to obey a higher spiritual form</note> of their *matter*, and a certain aptitude and likeness that these *inferior* things bear to their *superiors*. Once these virtues are taken in, the objects then contract and retain them (besides those they receive from their own *species*). They also retain those natural *virtues* and roots of the *stars* with which they arouse and stir up the *influences* of the *celestial bodies*. These celestial bodies are (as if by a compact when *united*) *obliged* to operate in and for that purpose which the *artist* appoints for them—and especially so if the mind of the *operator* is vehemently inclined toward the same. 

For through the strength and efficacy of the *imagination* and *passion* (being seriously intent upon any *operation*), the operator’s mind is joined with the *mind* of the *stars* and *Intelligences* <note>term: "Intelligences" refers to the spiritual beings or angels believed to govern the planets</note>. It is as suddenly fitted with *virtues* as if it were the proper *receptacle* of their *influences*, and consequently helps more effectually to infuse their *virtues* into our *works*. And the reason is *because there is an apprehension and power of all things in the mind*; whereupon all things...

having a natural obedience to it, also necessarily have an efficacy; and even more so to that which desires them with a strong and intent desire.

Notwithstanding, all these wonders are not performed except by the cooperation of second causes <note>original: "second Causes," referring to the natural laws or physical agents that God uses to enact His will</note> disposing of the *physical matter*. God (the first cause of all things) has variously distributed these virtues to everyone as He pleases; by His command and appointment, they are compelled to produce their *effects*. This *matter* (by reason of its purity or inequality) may cause the *celestial virtues* to fail in their *actions*; for certainly *influences* may be hindered and prove ineffectual through the indisposition or insufficiency of the *matter*. 

Therefore, it is no ordinary contemplation to awaken the sleeping *spirit* which lies bound up in the narrow prison of the *body*; to invite and allure that propitious *spirit* to descend from *heaven* and unite itself with that which is *internal*; and therewith to convey a *bond* <note>original: "Vinculum," a Latin term for a link or chain used in magic to bind celestial forces to an object</note> into it, which has the power to hold fast and fix the *celestial influences* from recoiling back into their united centers.

This is the *series* and *order* of *nature* conjoined with *art*; and all of this must be accomplished before one true *magical operation* can be performed.

## The Book of the Father of Wisdom <note>original title: "Liber patris Sapientiæ"</note>

<margin>Page 194.</margin>
**Though** I cannot yet satisfy the reader as to who the *author* of this was, and therefore must **register** it (together with **Experience** and **Philosophy**, and the **Hermit's Tale**) among the *anonymous authors* <note>original: "Anonymi"</note>, I can nevertheless assure him that he gives exceedingly good advice to the *student* in this *science*. He bids the student be *secret* in the carrying on of his *studies* and *operations*, and not to let anyone know of his *undertakings* but his good *angel* and *himself*. Such a closed and private heart <note>original: "retyred Breft"</note> had *Norton's Master*, who:

<margin>w) Ordin. p. 32</margin>
> w) **When men disputed of the colors of the rose,**
> **He would not speak but keep himself very hidden.**

*Privacy* will (unquestionably) prove an unimaginable benefit to him, whereas, on the contrary, *openness* <note>original: "Apertness"</note> exposes a true *philosopher* to a multitude of misfortunes. Witness Sir *Edward Kelley*, whose immoderate *ambition* to spread his name lifted him up even to a *madness* of public *conduct*; which, not correcting in time, led to his miserable fall through the fatal *vertigo* of imprudent *glory*. To such people, therefore, I shall only add *Chaucer's counsel*, which may prove of no little advantage if they remember it:

<margin>x) Ten Commandments of Love</margin>
> x) **Make privy to your dealings as few as you may,**
> **For three may keep a secret if two are away.**

## **Hermes' Bird**

This piece (as it is thought) was written originally by *Raymond Lully* (or at least translated into *English* by the aforementioned *Cremer*) and under these circumstances:

<margin>a) See Cremer's Testament.</margin>
*Cremer*, traveling into *Italy*, became acquainted with *Lully*. He so greatly influenced him with his persuasion that he (a) brought him over to *England*, where within two years (but after thirty years of failed *experiments*), he obtained the *Secret* from him. Afterward, bringing *Lully* to meet *Edward III*, the *King* entered into deep *engagements* and *promises* to personally lead a *war* against the *Turks*, and to donate to the *House* of *God*, but to spend nothing out of *pride* or for *warring* against other *Christians*. Because of this, Lully was content "by Divine permission to make the King wealthy through his Art" <note>original: "permissione Divina Regem sua Arte divitem facere"</note>. However, once the *King* had obtained the gold, he broke his *promise*. He turned his *plans* against *France* (the first expedition being (b) in the *year* 1337). <margin>b) Stow's Annals, folio 234.</margin> Finding that *Lully*—after seeing the King violate his faith by destroying *Christians* instead of *Muslims* <note>original: "Mahumetans"</note>—refused to support his *ambition* with a new supply of *gold*, the King locked him up in the *Tower* of London. He lay there a long time; seeing no possibility of release, he began to plan his *freedom*. To that end, he made himself look like a *leper* <note>a person with leprosy; Lully likely used chemicals to simulate the disease to gain more freedom from his guards</note>, by which means he gained more *liberty* and eventually an *opportunity* to escape into *France*, where in all probability he wrote this *piece*.

The whole work is *parabolic* and *allusive*, yet truly *philosophical*. The *Bird* (for which it is titled) is the *Mercury* of the *Philosophers* (whose virtues and properties are extensively described therein). By the word *Churl* <note>original: "Chorle"; a rude, low-born, or selfish person</note>, he means the *covetous* and *ignorant artist*. The *garden* is the *vessel* or *glass*, and the *hedge* is the *furnace*.

## **The Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale**

One reason why I selected the *Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale* from *Chaucer's Canterbury Tales* was to let the *world* see the notorious *cheating* that has always been practiced under the pretense of this true (though slandered) *science*. Another is to show that *Chaucer* himself was a *master* of it.

For in this tale, *Chaucer* vividly exposes the deceptions in *alchemy* and notably speaks out against all such villainous *pretenders* who, being completely ignorant of the *Art*, have nonetheless learned the *cunning* to deceive the *world*. He took this effort (as he himself declares) purely:

<margin>c) Canon’s Yeoman’s Tale.</margin>
> **c) To the intent that men may beware thereby,**
> **And for no other cause truly.**

In this, he followed the *example* <note>original: "President"</note> of all sincere and conscientious *philosophers*; the injured world cannot condemn the abuses of these *impostors* more than the philosophers themselves do.

Now, concerning *Chaucer* (the author of this tale), he is ranked among the *Hermetic Philosophers* <note>Philosophers following the tradition of Hermes Trismegistus, often associated with alchemy and secret wisdom</note>, and his master in this *science* was Sir *John Gower*. Their close and familiar acquaintance began at the *Inner Temple* <note>One of the four "Inns of Court" in London, where lawyers were trained</note> upon *Chaucer's* return to *England*. The troubles of the *times* toward the latter end of *Richard II’s reign* had caused him to retreat from danger into *Holland*, *Zeeland*, and *France*.

He is cited by *Norton* as an *authentic author* in these words:

<margin>p) Ordinal, page 42.</margin>
**p) And Chaucer rehearses how Titan <note>original: "Tytans"; in alchemy, Titan often refers to the sun or the metallic principle of gold/sulfur</note> is the same.**

Besides this, he who reads the latter part of the *Canon's Yeoman's Tale* will easily perceive him to be a *judicious philosopher* and one who fully knew the *mystery* <note>original: "Mistery"; refers to the secret knowledge or "trade" of alchemy</note>.

Master *Speght* (in that commendable account he gives of *Chaucer's* life) is persuaded he was born in *London*, based on something suggested in his *Testament of Love*. But *Bale* says he was (q) born of a noble rank <note>original: "Nobili loco natus"</note> and near *Oxford*; for (he says) *Leland* had *arguments* which made him believe he was born in either *Oxfordshire* or *Berkshire*. But what those *arguments* were, we do not know now; yet we may believe them to be of considerable weight because they were undoubtedly those he gathered in his six years of laborious searching through the libraries of our *English monasteries* and *colleges*, aided by the liberal encouragement and commission of *Henry VIII*. Had it not been for his tireless efforts, all that was notable in this nation (r) would, in all likelihood, have been perpetually obscured or, at best, only lightly remembered as uncertain shadows. Nevertheless, the fruits of this famous *antiquary's* labors are nowhere to be seen in their entirety now, unless they are dispersed through the works of other men who have most arrogantly and unworthily claimed them as their own. Among the rest, I perceive that *Polydore Virgil* stole much "timber" from this worthy *structure* [Leland's research], using part of it to build up his own *work*; the rest he enviously burned, for thus I find *Leland's Ghost* complaining:

<margin>q) Bale, Century 7, folio 525.</margin>
<margin>r) See his New Year's gift to Henry VIII.</margin>
<margin>s) Leland's Ghost.</margin>

> **s) Am I deceived? Or does not Leland’s spirit**
> **Complain with the ghosts of English chroniclers <note>original: "Notaries"</note>,**
> **Whom Polydore Virgil robbed of merit,**
> **Deprived of fame, and ransacked of histories,**
> **While (wretch!) he ravaged English libraries.**
> **Ah, wicked book-thief, whoever did it:**
> **Should one burn everything just to get a single bit of credit?**

> **Am I deceived? Or does not Leland’s spirit**

> **Rifling his works and erasing his name and merit;**

> **Along with a learned writer's labor, wits, and health.**
> **All these he spent to do his country pleasure;**
> **Oh, save his name, so the world may know his treasure.**

But begging pardon for this digression (being on behalf of so deserving a scholar), I return to *Chaucer*. *Pits* <note>John Pits (1560–1616), a Catholic biographer</note> positively says he was born in *Woodstock* of noble parents, and that "he had a father of the knightly order" <note>original: *Patrem habuit Equestris Ordinis Virum*</note>; his father was a knight. And this may not be unlikely if we consider that not only is the name as ancient as (t) *William the Conqueror’s* time, but that some of the family have been of both large fortunes and good status. For we find (u) that *Edward I* heard the complaint of *John Chaucer* regarding damages of 1,000 pounds <note>An enormous sum in the 13th century, equivalent to millions today</note>. And also that there was, in the reigns of Henry III and *Edward I*, one *Elias Chaucer*, of whom it is written (w): "Edward, by the grace of God, etc., pay from our treasury to Elias Chaucer ten shillings" <note>original: *Edwardus dei gratia, &c. liberate de Thesauro nostro Eliæ Chaufecir’ decem Solid:*</note>. With which spelling <note>original: "Characters"</note> our *Geoffrey Chaucer* is written in the records of *Edward III and Richard II*.
<margin>x) Speght in the life of Chaucer.</margin>

<margin>y) Stow's Annals, folio 957.</margin>
But wherever he was born, his education was chiefly in the *University* of *Oxford* at *Canterbury College* (y) (suppressed by Henry VIII and now joined to *Christ Church*), though for some time he studied at *Cambridge*.

<margin>z) The Court of Love, Chapter 1.</margin>
### z) **Of the Cambridge Clerk.** <note>A reference to Chaucer's own description of himself in "The Court of Love"</note>

<margin>a) Bale, folio 525.</margin>
He quickly became a witty *logician*, a sweet *rhetorician*, a pleasant poet, a grave *philosopher*, a holy *theologian* <note>original: "Divine"</note>, and a skillful *mathematician*. His tutors in these subjects were **Friar John Somer** and **Friar Nicholas of Lynn** (a) (*Carmelite Friars of Lynn* remembered with honor in his *Treatise on the Astrolabe*), and moreover (I may safely add) an able astrologer, for in almost every work he interweaves most sound and perfect astrology. In brief, he was universally learned, as his student *Thomas Hoccleve* <note>original: "Occleve"</note> affirms:

<margin>b) Prologue to Henry V while he was Prince.</margin>
### b) **O universal father of science.**

<margin>c) Page 472.</margin>
*Pits* styles him (c) "a man wonderfully flourishing in the arts of both war and peace" <note>original: *Vir Belli Pacisq; Artibus mirè Florens*</note>. He was a man who excelled in the arts of both *war* and *peace*, and a little later: "For even before he had reached manhood, he was an elegant poet, and one who so illustrated English poetry that he might deservedly be considered the **English Homer**" <note>original: *Nam jam antequam virilem ætatem attigisset, erat Poeta Elegans, Et qui Poesim Anglicam ita illustravit, ut Anglicus Homerus merito haberetur*</note>. *Lydgate*, the monk of *Bury*, calls him the (d) *lodestar* <note>A guiding star used for navigation</note> of our language and tells us that it was he who:

</margin>

> e) **First caused to distill and rain**
> **The gold dew-drops of speech and eloquence**
> **Into our tongue through his excellence.**
> **And first found the flowers of rhetoric,**
> **To illuminate our rude speech thoroughly** <note>original: "or’e-ly"</note>,

For indeed, in his time, all good literature <note>original: "Letters"</note> was laid to sleep in most parts of the *world*, and in *England* our tongue was exceedingly wild and rude; yet (through his refining and polishing) it became more sweet and pleasant, in which regard he is styled:

<margin>

He spent many of his years in *France* and *Flanders*. He held several appointments at Court, for he was (g) *King's Squire* <note>original: *Armiger Regis*; a position of very high status</note> to *Edward III*, (h) *Groom of the Palace* <note>original: *Valectus Hospitii*</note>, and later, in the time of *Richard II* (i), Controller of the Custom House in *London*. Along with these roles, he was granted several annual pensions during his life by *Richard II* and *Henry IV*. His abilities for foreign service were so well regarded that he was sent abroad to other countries two or three times. He was also considered fit to be one of the ambassadors to *France* to negotiate a marriage between *Richard II* (while he was still Prince of *Wales*) and the Lady *Mary*, daughter of the *French* King. His annual income was 1,000 pounds—a very large estate, considering the times.

He died in *London* on October 25, 1400, as appears by the inscription upon his tomb at Saint *Peter's* in *Westminster Abbey*, in an aisle on the *south* side of the church.

Mr. *Nicholas Brigham* built this *marble monument* to his memory. I have had the true portrait of it exactly engraved in brass and placed on page 226. Formerly, these following *verses* were written around the ledge of the *tomb*, but now no trace of them remains.

->If you ask who I was, perhaps fame will tell you;<-
->But if fame denies it, because the world's glory passes away,<-
->Read these monuments.<-
<note>original Latin: *Si rogites quis eram, forsan te fama docebit: Quod si fama negat, mundi quia gloria transit, Hæc monumenta lege.*</note>

The portrait of *Chaucer* is now somewhat decayed, but the engraver has restored it based on an original left to posterity by his worthy student *Thomas Occleve*, who also wrote these *verses* about it:

> Of his person, I have here had this likeness
> Created, to this end in truthfulness,
> That those who have lost thought and memory of him,
> By this painting, may find him again.

->*Geoffrey Chaucer, poet and the pride of poetry,*<-

### Page 298. line 25. Charnock is his name, of the Isle of Thanet. <note>original: "Tenet"</note>

<margin>i) Chapter 5.</margin>
Thanet or Tainet is an island that lies in the eastern part of Kent and was the birthplace of Charnock. However, though he may have been born there, he lived near (i) Salisbury when he first met his master, Bird. He calls himself the "Unlettered Scholar," and from several fragments and notes I have seen in his own writing, it does not appear that he understood much Latin or knew how to write correct English. Yet, though he lacked the "shell" <note>referring to formal education</note>, he obtained the "kernel" <note>referring to the essential secret of alchemy</note> and had the good fortune to encounter in plain English what many—who have the help of other languages—go without. Thus we see through him that God has not excluded those who master no language other than their own from the happiness of understanding many abstruse and subtle secrets. I could cite several examples in this science. This very consideration prompted that noble fraternity of the Rosy Cross <note>original: "R.C."</note> to publish their *Fama* and *Confessio* <note>The *Fama Fraternitatis* and *Confessio Fraternitatis* are the founding manifestos of the Rosicrucian order, originally published in German and Latin.</note> in five different languages, so that the unlearned might not be deprived and cheated of that knowledge. Nor was the process of teaching Charnock—which all students should note—tedious or long. For he says:

<margin>k) His Master Bird.</margin>
> ->Within three or four words (k) he revealed to me<-
> ->The great mystery of mineral wisdom.<-
<note>original: "Minerall Prudence"</note>

He lived as an ordinary man; otherwise, I assume his social status <note>original: "Quality"</note> might have exempted him from being pressed into service as a common soldier. And from a memorandum in his own hand, it can be gathered that he practiced surgery <note>original: "Chirurgery"</note>; for it appears he negotiated a fee of five marks <note>A mark was a unit of currency worth two-thirds of a pound sterling, or 13 shillings and 4 pence.</note> for healing the leg of one Richard Deane. For the payment of this fee, John Boden and William Lawly acted as guarantors.

...forcing him to be drafted as a **soldier** <note>original: "prest for a Souldier"</note> for the mission of relieving Calais (which was at the (o) beginning of January in the year 1558, almost six months after he had finished the *Breviary of Philosophy*). Because of this, in a fit of frustration <note>original: "Discontent"</note>, he destroyed **everything**.

### Page 303, line 6. **And if God spares my life, I will amend this another day.**

The *Breviary of Natural Philosophy* was started within two or three years after he became a **Master of the Secret** <note>One who has successfully achieved the "Great Work" of alchemy, the creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. Although he seems to promise another work, I could never find that he wrote anything afterward, except for his two *Enigmas* (which I have arranged after his *Breviary*) and the fragments inserted on page 424. It is uncertain when he died, but I have found nothing written in his own hand after the year 1577, even though his pen was active for several years before that. In various blank spaces in his books, he inserted many notes, usually including a date; I have published some of those in this *Theatrum* <note>The *Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum*, the 1652 collection of alchemical texts by Elias Ashmole from which this commentary comes</note>.

---

### Page 305. **Bloomfield's Blossoms.**

The author himself also calls this work the *Camp of Philosophy*, and he titles the practical section <note>original: "Practick"</note> of it his *Last Will and Testament*. It was written by **William Bloomfield** (some copies have called him *Sir William Bloomfield*), a Bachelor of Medicine <note>original: "Physick"</note> licensed during the reign of Henry VIII.

I have seen a fine manuscript of *Norton's Ordinal*, where (at the top of the leaf that begins every chapter and other prominent places) there is a scroll. In the first fold of the scroll is written [**Myles**], in the middle is the chapter number, and in the third fold is [**Bloomfield**]. I assume this **Myles Bloomfield** was the owner of the book (and perhaps a brother or relative of our William Bloomfield). However, according to a note in that book (written in a fairly old hand), I later found that this Myles is identified as the author of:

->**Bloomfield's Blossoms.**<-

### Page 324. **Sir Edward Kelley's Work.**

I cannot provide the reader with an account of **Sir Edward Kelley** without also mentioning that famous expert <note>original: "Artist"</note>, **Doctor John Dee** (whose *Last Will and Testament* follows Sir Edward Kelley's work). Dee was for a time Kelley's intimate friend and long-time companion in philosophical studies and chemical experiments. Eventually, the worthy Doctor (leaving Kelley in Germany) returned to England and so, by God's providence, escaped from being his companion any longer during the strict imprisonment <note>Kelley was imprisoned after failing to produce gold for the Emperor</note> that Sir Edward Kelley suffered at Prague by the command of **Rudolph II, Emperor of Germany** <note>original: "Radulph the 2"</note>.

Mercury is the ruler of the Ninth House—the house of knowledge, wisdom, and science—and is placed upon the "cusp" <note>the border or entrance of an astrological house</note> of that house in Virgo. In that position, Mercury is exceedingly strong and fortunate in his "dignities" <note>the relative strength of a planet's influence based on its zodiacal position</note>, both "essential" and "accidental."

**Venus** is also "angular" <note>located in one of the four most powerful houses of a chart</note> and aspects the cusp of the Ninth House with a sextile. Kelley was at all times ready to further and promote [the work], and from whose position the nature of those abusive slanders may be (generally) gathered. As for **Doctor Dee**, he chiefly focused his studies on **mathematics**, in all parts of which he was an absolute and perfect master. Witness his *Mathematical Preface* to *Euclid's Elements*, in which many arts are enumerated that were wholly invented by him (by **name, definition, property,** and **use**) — more than either the Greek or Roman mathematicians have left to our knowledge. His epistle prefixed to John Field's *Ephemerides* (1557); his work *On the Use of the Celestial Globe* <note>original: "De usu Globi Coelestis"</note> dedicated to Edward VI; his book *On the Distances of the Clouds, Sun, Moon, and the Rest of the Planets, etc.* <note>original: "De Nubium solis lunae ac reliquorum Planetarum, &c. And lastly, that he was a good **astrologer** and a studious **philosopher**, his *300 Astrological Aphorisms*; his *120 Aphorisms on Certain More Excellent Virtues of Nature* <note>original: "De praestantioribus quibusdam naturae virtutibus"</note>; his *Hieroglyphic Monad* <note>original: "Monas Hieroglyphica"</note>; his *Mirror of Unity* <note>original: "Speculum unitatis"</note> (being an apology <note>A formal defense.</note> for our famous Friar Roger Bacon); and his *Concise Table of the Hebrew Cabala* <note>original: "Cabala Hebraica compendiosa Tabula"</note>, along with many others, afford no small evidence to the world.

All of these and many more (in several other kinds of learning, such as history, heraldry, etc.) were written by him before the year 1583. For some time, he devoted himself to <margin>p) December 28, 1579.</margin> common chemistry <note>original: "vulgar Chemistry"</note> and was a master of various secrets within it. His great ability in astrology and the more secret parts of learning (to which he had a strong inclination and unwearied imagination) drew many rash, vile, and lying scandals from the envious and common people upon his most honest and justifiable philosophical studies. For that there was some great and wonderful unkindness from *Sir Edward Kelley* appears by his sending for *Doctor Dee* at the beginning of *January 1588*, under a show of reconciliation and discovering more than an ordinary intimacy and compliance about that time. The good *Doctor* notes these fair shows with this prayer: *God lead his heart to all charity and brotherly love.* It also appears by letters sent from *Doctor Dee* to *Sir Edward Kelley* and his wife at the end of March following, requiring mutual charity at their hands. <margin>z) May 9.</margin> (z) Afterward, upon *Mistress Kelley* receiving the Sacrament, she gave her hand to *Doctor Dee* and his *wife* as a token of charity. But it seems these things were not heartfelt <note>original: "cordiall"</note> but only outward; for on the 9th of *September* following (the Lord Chancellor coming to *Trebona*), the rancor and dissimulation were more evident to him, and it seems grew to a greater height than he could bear. On the ninth of *April*, he came to *Bremen* and had not stayed there three days before the *Landgrave of Hesse* <note>Maurice, Landgrave of Hesse-Kassel, a prominent patron of the arts and occult sciences.</note> sent letters of civil compliments to him; and within three days after, *Doctor Dee* presented him with his *Twelve Hungarian Horses*.

Being settled again at *Mortlake*, the *Queen* used to call at his *house* to visit him, and she showed herself very *courteous* to him on all *occasions*. Toward *Christmas* 1590, she sent him *two hundred Angels* <term>Angel: a gold coin worth about 10 shillings, named for the image of the Archangel Michael on its face.</term> with which to keep his *Christmas*, and a hundred *marks* <term>Mark: a unit of currency worth two-thirds of a pound.</term> toward *Christmas* 1592. She likewise sent him word by *Mr. Thomas Cavendish* <note>A famous English explorer and circumnavigator.</note> to do whatever he wished in *alchemy* and *philosophy*, and promised that no one should control or molest him. Following the *Queen's example*, various *persons of honor* at *Court* frequented his *company* and sent him many *gifts* from time to time. Among others, *Sir Thomas Jones* most nobly offered him his *castle* of *Emlyn* <note>Newcastle Emlyn Castle</note> in *Wales* to live in, free of charge and with all *accommodations*.

His *favor* was strong at *Court*, and the *Queen* herself told him to find some office for her to bestow upon him; yet all the advancement he gained was the <margin>d) 8 Dec. 1594.</margin> (d) *grant* of the *Chancellorship* of *St. Paul's*. On the 27th of *May* 1595, his *patent* <note>A legal document granting a right or title.</note> passed the Great *Seal* for the *Wardenship* of *Manchester*. *He*, his *wife*, *children*, and *family* arrived there on the 14th of *February* 1596, and he was *installed* on the 20th day following. In this *Wardenship*—where he had the unhappiness of being often annoyed by the *turbulent fellows* of that *college*—he died, deserving the *commendations* of all *learned* and *ingenious scholars*, and to be remembered for his remarkable *abilities*.

After *Doctor Dee* came back to *England* (as previously mentioned), *correspondence* was still maintained between him and *Sir Edward Kelley* through letters sent by *Mr. Francis Garland* and others. There was some expectation that *Sir Edward* would come over to England; <margin>e) 23 Dec. 1589.</margin> (e) *Mr. Thomas Kelley* (his *brother*) also gave the *Doctor* hope of it. But at length, *Sir Edward* was locked up as a close *prisoner* by the *Emperor* <note>Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II.</note>. Kelley had managed the *secret* <note>The secret of alchemical transmutation.</note> so unwarily and openly that it had given the *Emperor* cause to keep a strict *eye* over all his *actions*, out of a desire to share in his good fortune. 

Yet it seems the *Emperor* set him at <margin>f) 4 Oct. 1593</margin> (f) *liberty*, and *Doctor Dee* received notice of it the following 5th of *December*. Although he began to grow into the *Emperor's favor* again, hoping to be entertained in his *service* (as he informed *Doctor Dee* by letters in *August* 1595), he was *nevertheless* locked up in *prison* again. Attempting to make his *escape* out of a high *window* by tearing his *sheets* and tying them together to let himself down, he—being a heavy *man*—fell and broke his *leg*, and *died* from the injury. 

According to astrological calculation, the *Ascendant* <note>The sign rising on the eastern horizon at the time of birth or a specific event.</note> was then coming by *Direction* <note>A method in astrology used to predict the timing of events.</note> to the position of the <margin>g) See the chart of his birth.</margin> (g) *Moon* with *Latitude*; she being the *Lady* <note>The planetary ruler.</note> of the 8th house <note>The house associated with death in astrology.</note> in his *birth chart* <note>original: "Radix"</note> and positioned in *Aquarius*. And this is one report of his *death*; there are others, but *Doctor Dee* mentions nothing at all regarding the manner of it.

## Page 365. **A Dialogue between the Father and the Son.**

<margin>
i) Placed on page 338.
</margin>

This dialogue is placed there among the anonymous authors <note>original: "Anonymi"</note> because I did not know the author at the time. However, I later came across the entire work <margin>i) Placed on page 338.</margin> and found it to be George Ripley's <note>George Ripley (c. 1415–1490) was one of England's most famous alchemists, best known for his work *The Compound of Alchemy*.</note>, which is titled the *Mystery of Alchemists*. This fragment was merely drawn from it, only dressed up with a different title; if the reader compares them, they will easily find this to be true.

Regarding the lack of sense in some parts of it, as well as in other older pieces, I hope the dimness of the candle <note>original: "Taper"</note> will be excused where there was no clearer light to be found. For though (like the sun) they may seem to have some spots, yet the honest reader <note>original: "candid Peruser"</note> must admit they are not without their own special glories. The truth is, some passages through them were so obscure and dark, and the paths I followed so rugged and uneven, that I could neither stay in them without clear embarrassment <note>original: "manifest disparagement"</note> nor leave them without some danger. From the discoveries I brought back from there, I am certain I could have satisfied the reader more if I could have satisfied myself better. However, I did not dare to venture to correct <note>original: "Rectifie"</note> what I found wrong. I thought it better to leave it to the judgment of everyone who takes the pains to study them, rather than force my own interpretation <note>original: "sence"</note> upon them, lest what I judge to be an improvement <note>original: "Emendation"</note>, others might criticize as a gross fault. Furthermore, I always remember the strict command <note>original: "Charge"</note> the general body of philosophers have continually given to those who come after them: not to meddle with or alter any of their works. Even in what I fear are obvious imperfections, I dare not do anything but observe their instructions most strictly. Among them all, this credible and trustworthy philosopher is not unworthy of our notice, as he requires the following:

<margin>
k) Hunting of the Green Lion.

This piece is the work of Sir John Gower <note>John Gower (c. 1330–1408) was a famous English poet and contemporary of Geoffrey Chaucer.</note>, and collected out of his book *On the Confession of the Lover* <note>original: "De Confessione Amantis"</note>. He is placed in the register of our Hermetic <note>original: "Hermetique"; relating to the mystical and alchemical tradition of Hermes Trismegistus.</note> philosophers; he is one who initiated our famous English poet, Geoffrey Chaucer, into the inheritance of this mystery. He was an eminent Poet, and has (*m*) written the story of the *Golden Fleece* like an *Hermetic Philosopher* <note>original: "Hermetique Philosopher"; referring to the tradition of alchemy and mystical philosophy attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>: which *Philosophical* vein is to be traced through several other parts of his *Works*. The first acquaintance between *Him* and *Chaucer* began at the *Inner Temple* <note>One of the four Inns of Court in London, where lawyers were trained</note>, where Sir *John Gower* studied the *Laws*, and where *Chaucer* came to follow the same course of studies upon his return from *France*. He was (says *Pits*) a (*n*) noble and learned Man, resembling Geoffrey [Chaucer] almost in every thing, and who surely had the same proposed end for all their studies <note>original: "Galfrido fere per omnia similem, quique eundem prorsus habuit omnium studiorum suorum propositum finem"</note>. They soon perceived the similarity of their manners and quickly joined in *Friendship* and *Labors*; they had daily meetings and familiarity, and all their endeavor was to refine and polish their *Mother Tongue*, so that the clear footprints of *Roman Eloquence* might appear in our *English Speech*.

This appears by *Chaucer's* sending to *Gower* his *Troilus and Criseyde* <note>original: "Troylus and Cressida"</note> after he had finished it, for his review and amendments.

And surely these two added so much splendor and ornament to our *English idiom* <note>original: "Ideome"</note> as no others had before them; for they walked side-by-side <note>original: "set foote to foote"</note> and lovingly competed over who should bring the most honor to his Country. Both endeavored to overcome and to be overcome by each other, being not only the memorialists but *Imitators* of that ideal:

Yet because taste can be disgusting,
Flavor <note>original: "Sapor"</note> is not profitable here.
Yet for certain parts that can be separated,
A taste may well be appropriate <note>original: "convenable"</note>
To make a test <note>original: "assay"</note> before combining elements,
To see whether they are well-made or not.
Nevertheless, a wise man has sufficient help
Using color and smell to achieve his purpose.
For many men can choose good wine
By color and smell when it is high quality;
But for new wine that has not been refined <note>original: "fined"</note>,
The true taste is the most reliable <note>original: "fuertie"</note> test of all.
For smelling has only one organ,
Discerning nothing but gaseous <note>original: "fumous"</note> things alone;
But taste has six organs <note>likely referring to different regions of the tongue or mouth</note> without doubt,
To sense the quality of things both inside and out,
Which Nature ordained against danger and conflict,
For the greater safety of living things.
An ape chooses its food <note>original: "meate"</note> by smelling,
But men and parrots <note>original: "popinjayes"</note> trust in tasting;
For many things have a good smell
Which are found to be very bad to the taste:
For they may be abominably sour,
Over-sharp, too bitter, or truly horrific,
Or venomous, stinking, or over-strong;
Taste is the judge and prevents such harm <note>original: "wronge"</note>.
Ancient authors wrote in olden times
That there are exactly nine flavors <note>original: "Sapors"</note>,
Which you may learn in half an hour:
Such as a sharp taste, oily <note>original: "unctuous"</note>, and sour,
Which three signify subtle matter;
And another three testify to matter of medium <note>original: "meane"</note> quality,
Such as a biting taste, salty, and insipid <note>original: "weerish"</note> also;

The same degrees of the same complexion,

With a medium substance in the second degree,
The taste of it must necessarily be saltish;
When a thing is hot and dry in the third degree,
With a thick substance, there is bitterness;

<meta>This page continues Chapter 5 of Thomas Norton's Ordinal of Alchemy, focusing on the four "testimonies" or essential components of the alchemical work, specifically introducing the fourth: Liquor.</meta>

# Chap. 5.
## Norton's

In your works, take heed of every circumstance,
Wisely considering your four testimonies;
Three have now passed; the fourth is Liquor.

Liquor is the comfort of this work;
Liquor gives evidence to a scholar <note>original: "Clerke"</note>
By which to fasten his elements,
And also to loosen them for certain purposes;
Liquor joins the Male with the Female Wife,
And causes dead things to return to life;
Liquors cleanse with their washing <term>ablution: the act of washing or cleansing, often in a ritual or chemical sense</term>,
Liquors are the chief nutrition for our Stone;
Without liquor, no food <note>original: "Meate"</note> is good;
Liquors convey all nourishment and food
To every part of the human body,
And so they do for us in alchemy.
You must consider the purity
Of all your liquors and their quantity;
And how thick or thin they are,
Otherwise, you shall gain little from them;
But not in the way that physicians mention,
For the Elixir is a thing of a second intention; <note>In scholastic philosophy and alchemy, a "second intention" refers to a more refined, secondary level of operation or conceptualization beyond the initial physical state.</note>
Therefore, you shall find more wondrous natures
In its working than in any other kind;
Physicians say the thicker urine is,
The more it signifies humidity,
Whereas with us, thick liquor has dryness <term>ficcity: dryness</term>,
And subtle <note>original: "futtill"</note> liquor betokens humidity.

Many liquors are required
For the appetite of our Stone.
In the *Book of Turba* <note>original: "Tarba"; referring to the *Turba Philosophorum*, a famous alchemical text</note>, Aristeus stated <note>original: "deposed"</note>
How air was secretly enclosed in water,
Which bore up the earth with its airy might.
->Pythagoras<-

<summary>This page introduces "Liquor" as the fourth essential element in alchemical practice, explaining its role in cleansing, nourishing, and binding elements together. It contrasts alchemical principles with standard medicine, noting that in alchemy, thickness indicates dryness rather than humidity.</summary>
